question_text: Which of the following numerical abnormality is seen in Edward syndrome is?
explanation:
Explanation:

Edward syndrome is a chromosomal disorder caused by the presence of an extra chromosome 18. It is characterized by severe developmental delay, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, congenital heart defects, and growth restriction. Most affected infants have a poor prognosis, with high mortality in the first year of life.

Chromosomal Abnormalities

  • Down's Syndrome (Trisomy 21) (Option B): Three copies of chromosome 21, karyotype 47XY +21.
  • Patau's Syndrome (Trisomy 13) (Option A): Three copies of chromosome 13. Characteristics: Severe intellectual disability, organ defects, early mortality.
  • Edward's Syndrome (Trisomy 18): Three copies of chromosome 18. Characteristics: Growth deficiencies, heart defects, high mortality rate.
  • Klinefelter's Syndrome (XXY): Found only in males; nondisjunction during gametogenesis results in 47 chromosomes. Characteristics: Infertility, gynecomastia, and reduced testosterone levels.
  • Turner's Syndrome (45XO): Found only in females; loss of one X chromosome leads to a karyotype of 45X. Characteristics: Short stature, infertility, and heart defects.
  • Triple X Syndrome (47XXX): Fertilization of an XX oocyte by an X sperm; phenotypically female with two Barr bodies. Characteristics: May have no significant abnormalities, taller than average.

Key takeaways:

Chromosomal abnormalities include Down's (Trisomy 21), Patau's (Trisomy 13), Edward's (Trisomy 18), Klinefelter's (XXY), Turner's (45XO), and Triple X (47XXX) syndromes, each characterized by distinct physical and developmental traits.

question_text: SRY gene is present in
explanation:
• The development of genital system begins during the fourth week of intrauterine life (IUL).
  • The genetic sex (genotype XY or XX) of embryo is established at time of fertilization, but gonads do not acquire male or female morphological characteristics till seventh week of the development.
  • Initially (week 1-6 of development) the gonads are structurally similar and hence this is called indifferent stage of gonad.
  • From seventh week onward, the development proceeds in different directions in males and females, and gonadal sex can then be determined morphologically.
  • By 12th week some male and female characteristics of the external genitalia can also be recognized.
  • By the end of 20th week phenotypical differentiation is complete.
  • This difference of development between male and female is because of chromosomal and hormonal factors.
  • The phenotypical differentiation is determined by SRY gene located on the short arm of Y chromosome (Yp11).
  • The SRY gene encodes for a protein called testis determining factor (TDF). The presence of TDF leads to development of male genital organs. As the indifferent gonad develops into the testis, the Leydig and Sertoli cells differentiate to produce testosterone and Mullerian inhibiting factor (MIF). This results in phenotypically male embryo.
  • In the absence of the TDF, testosterone, and MIF, the indifferent gonads will develop into ovary and embryo will be phenotypically female.

Reference: Textbook Embryology by Vishram Singh, 3rd Edition, Page No - 289

question_text: A 2-day-old male newborn is examined in the nursery. He has characteristic facial features suggestive of a chromosomal disorder. On examination of the hands, a single transverse crease is noted across the palm. Which of the following conditions is most likely associated with this finding?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The presence of a single transverse palmar crease (also called simian crease) is a well-recognised feature in Down syndrome (Trisomy 21).
  • It results from abnormal development of palmar flexion creases during fetal life.
  • While it may occasionally be seen in normal individuals, its presence along with typical dysmorphic features and hypotonia strongly suggests Down syndrome.

Explanation of other options:

Turner syndrome (Option A): Characterised by short stature, webbed neck, shield chest, and streak ovaries, but does not show a single palmar crease.

Klinefelter syndrome (Option B): Features include tall stature, gynecomastia, small testes, and infertility; hand findings are not typical.

Edwards syndrome (Option D): Associated with rocker-bottom feet, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, micrognathia, but not a single palmar crease.

Key Takeaways:

  • Single palmar crease (Simian crease) is strongly associated with Down syndrome, but can also occur in a small percentage of normal individuals.
  • Recognising dysmorphic features in newborns is crucial for early diagnosis of chromosomal disorders.

question_text: Which of the following is not an example of autosomal dominant inheritance?
explanation:
Explanation:

Most inborn errors of metabolism follow an autosomal recessive pattern, as they usually involve loss-of-function mutations in enzyme systems

Autosomal dominant inheritance:

  • Marfan's syndrome
  • Achondroplasia
  • Brachydactyly
  • Neurofibromatosis
  • Huntigton's disease
  • Osteogenesis imperfecta

Autosomal recessive inheritance:

  • Cystic fibrosis
  • Inborn errors of metabolism
  • Hemoglobinopathies, e.g., sickle cell anemia and thalassemia.

X-linked dominant inheritance:

  • Vitamin D resistant rickets
  • Hypophosphatemia
  • Xg blood group

X-linked recessive inheritance:

  • Haemophilia
  • Colour blindness
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Duchenne muscular dystrophy

Y-linked inheritance:

  • Hypertrichosis
  • Webbed toes
  • Porcupine man

Multifactorial inheritance:

  • Cleft lip
  • Cleft palate
  • Club foot
  • Congenital dislocation of hip
  • Congenital heart disease.

Key takeaways:

Inborn errors of metabolism, as they are typically inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. In contrast, examples of autosomal dominant inheritance include Marfan syndrome, neurofibromatosis, and Huntington's disease. Therefore, inborn errors of metabolism are not correct examples of autosomal dominant inheritance.

question_text: What is artherosclerosis?
option_a: Thickening of tunica intima and calcification of tunica media
option_b: Loss of elasticity of tunica media and accumulation of lipid in the myointimal cells
option_c: Thickening of tunica intima and accumulation of lipid in the myointimal cells
option_d: Formation of fibrofatty plaques in tunica intima and calcification of tunica media
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Atherosclerosisis defined as theformation of fibrofatty plaques in the tunica intimaandcalcification of the tunica media.
  • It arises and progresses as an inflammatory response of the vessel wall to chronic multifactorial injury due to hyperlipidaemia, hypertension, smoking or diabetes mellitus.

Characteristics of Atherosclerosis:

  • Thickening of Tunica Intima:
    • Migration and proliferation ofsmooth muscle cellsfrom the tunica media.
    • Accumulation oflipidsinmyointimal cellsand macrophages, leading to plaque formation.
  • Formation of Fibrofatty Plaques:
    • Development ofatheromas(fibrofatty plaques) within the tunica intima that narrow the arterial lumen.
  • Calcification:
    • Occurs in thetunica media, contributing toarteriosclerosis, resulting in loss of elasticity.
  • Age-related Changes:
    • Thickening and lipid accumulation can lead to significant changes in artery structure, impactingblood flowandpressure.
  • Health Implications:
    • Atherosclerosis is a leading cause ofcardiovascular diseases, increasing the risk ofheart attackandstroke.
    • It may lead toaneurysm formationdue to weakened arterial walls, which can be life-threatening if ruptured.

Key Takeaway:

Atherosclerosisinvolves theformation of fibrofatty plaquesandcalcificationwithin the arterial walls, leading tonarrowing of the lumen, which poses significant risks forcardiovascular events.

question_text: All of the following cell containing chromosome 44XY, Except;
explanation:
Explanation:

Spermatid contains a haploid set of chromosomes (22 + X or 22 + Y). It is formed after the second meiotic division of the secondary spermatocyte, resulting in cells with half the chromosomal complement of the parent cell.

Spermatogenesis:

  • Definition: The process of forming spermatozoa from primordial germ cells (PGCs)/spermatogonia in the seminiferous tubules of the testis.
  • Dormancy: PGCs remain dormant in the seminiferous tubules until puberty.
  • Initiation at Puberty: Upon reaching puberty, PGCs undergo a series of divisions to form spermatogonia.
  • Stages of Spermatogenesis:
    • Spermatogonia (Diploid): The initial germ cells that undergo mitosis.
    • Primary Spermatocytes (Diploid): Result from the division of spermatogonia and undergo meiosis I (Option D).
    • Secondary Spermatocytes (Haploid): Formed after meiosis I, these undergo meiosis II.
    • Spermatids (Haploid): Result from meiosis II; they undergo maturation.
    • Spermatozoa (Haploid): Mature sperm cells that are released into the seminiferous tubules.
  • Spermatogonium type A is a diploid cell (44 + XY) that undergoes mitotic divisions to maintain the germ cell line (Option B).
  • Spermatogonium type B is also diploid (44 + XY) and differentiates into the primary spermatocyte (Option C).

Key takeaways:

A spermatid contains 23 chromosomes (22 autosomes + 1 sex chromosome X or Y) after meiosis, while the other cells listed (spermatogonium type A, spermatogonium type B, and primary spermatocyte) contain 44 autosomes and 2 sex chromosomes (44XY).

question_text: All of the following statements regarding Sickle Cell Anemia is true, EXCEPT:
option_b: Patients usually presents before the age of 6 months
option_c: There is a positive correlation between HBS and polymerization of HBS
option_d: Reccurent infections is the most common cause of death
explanation: Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder, caused by an amino acid substitution of valine for glutamine in the sixth position on the beta-globin chain. Onset of the disease starts during the first year of life especially after 6 months of age, when hemoglobin F levels falls, as a signal is sent to switch from production of gamma globin to beta globin. Hemoglobin S is unstable and polymerizes during hypoxemia and acidosis, leading to sickling of red blood cells. Patients develops jaundice, pigmented gallstones, spleenomegaly, and poorly healing ulcers over the lower tibia. Acute painful episodes can occur due to acute vaso-occlusion by clusters of sickled red cells during infection, dehydration, or hypoxia. Common sites of acute painful episodes include the bones and the chest. question_text: What is the type of the X chromosome?
explanation:
Explanation:

The X chromosome is submetacentric, meaning its centromere is placed slightly off-centre, producing one long arm (q-arm) and one shorter arm (p-arm). This asymmetry is a characteristic feature seen on karyotyping

Morphological types of chromosomes:

  • Depending upon the location of centromere, the chromosomes are classified into four types.
  • Metacentric (Option A): Centromere is in the middle.
  • Submetacentric: Centromere is located close to the middle.
  • Acrocentric (Option C): Centromere is located close to the end of chromosome.
  • Telocentric (Option D): Centromere is located at the end of the chromosome.

Key takeaways:

question_text: In case of pregnancy which of the following condition occurs in the uterus?
explanation:
• Atrophy: The muscles which are not used for long times become thin and weak. This is called disuse atrophy. Muscular 'wasting' (reduction in size) is a feature of lower motor neuron paralysis and generalized debility.
  • Hypertrophy: Adequate or excessive use of particular muscles causes their better development, or even hypertrophy
  • Hyperplasia: Increase in number of smooth muscle fibres. Usually occurs in uterus during pregnancy.
  • Hypoplasia: It is the incomplete development or underdevelopment of an organ or tissue. Hence, organs or tissue affected by hypoplasia have a below average number of cells. There are different types of hypoplasia, depending on what tissue is affected.

Key takeaways : Hypertrophy refers to the increase in the size of existing muscle fibers due to use, while hyperplasia refers to the increase in the number of muscle fibers, often occurring in the uterus during pregnancy.

question_text: The emphysema is characterised by:
option_a: Over secretion of mucous in the bronchus
option_c: Enlarged alveoli with destruction of interalveolar septum
option_d: Widen and thickened wall of the bronchi
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Emphysema is a condition of the lung characterized by permanent enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchiole.
  • This enlargement is accompanied by destruction of the alveolar wall.
  • Thus, significant surface area for gas exchange is lost in this disease.
  • It is caused by impairment of synthesis of elastic fibres and other components of septum.
  • Emphysema is often caused by chronic inhalations of foreign particulate material, such as coal dust, textile fibers, and construction dust.
  • The most common cause, however, is cigarette smoking.
  • Over secretion of mucous in the bronchus (Option A): True for chronic bronchitis, not emphysema.
  • Spasmodic narrowing of the bronchi (Option B): Characteristic of bronchial asthma, not emphysema.
  • Widen and thickened wall of the bronchi (Option D): Related to bronchiectasis, not emphysema.

Key Takeaways:

  • Emphysema is characterized by enlarged alveoli and destruction of interalveolar septa due to loss of elastic tissue.
  • Chronic bronchitis involves overproduction of mucus, while bronchial asthma is marked by spasmodic airway narrowing.

question_text: The given finding is associated with?
explanation:
Explanation:

Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) results from the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21. Individuals often present with characteristic facial features, intellectual disability, and various medical complications. One hallmark feature is a single transverse palmar crease (simian crease), observed in about half of those affected, making this the correct association.

Aetiology:

  • Caused by meiotic nondisjunction in maternal or paternal gametes.
  • Occurs in approximately 1 in 800-1000 live births.
  • Overexpression of genes on chromosome 21 leads to the clinical phenotype.

Key Clinical Features:

  • General: Intellectual disability, flat facial profile, upward-slanting eyes with epicanthic folds, small nose with flattened bridge, narrow palate, small teeth, furrowed protruding tongue, hypotonia, small brachycephalic skull, dysplastic ears.
  • Hands and Feet: Short, broad hands, clinodactyly of the fifth finger, simian crease, sandal gap between the first and second toes.

Comorbidities:

  • Heart: 40-60% have congenital heart disease (AVSD, VSD, ASD, PDA, TOF).
  • GI: 12% have atresias (e.g., duodenal), increased risk of annular pancreas, and Hirschsprung disease.
  • Eyes: Risk of cataracts, strabismus, nystagmus, decreased visual acuity.
  • Hearing: 40-60% have conductive hearing loss; routine assessment recommended.
  • Thyroid: Hypothyroidism in 13-54%.
  • Skeletal: Atlanto-occipital instability in 10-30%; monitor with lateral neck X-ray.
  • Growth: Slower linear growth; potential obesity; hypotonia improves with age.
  • Malignancy: Increased risk of leukemia and transient lymphoproliferative syndrome.
  • Neurology: Early-onset Alzheimer's due to APP gene on chromosome 21.

Explanation of other options:

Trisomy 13 (Option A): Trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome, results from an extra chromosome 13, leading to severe developmental issues and congenital abnormalities. While hand anomalies are common, a simian crease isn't typically present.

Klinefelter's syndrome (Option C): Klinefelter's syndrome in males with an extra X chromosome (XXY) leads to male hypogonadism and physical differences, but it's not usually linked to a simian crease.

Trisomy 18 (Option D): Trisomy 18, or Edwards syndrome, stems from an extra chromosome 18, leading to severe developmental delays, intellectual disabilities, and congenital anomalies. While hand abnormalities may occur, a simian crease isn't a defining trait.

question_text: A child came to the orthopaedic department with frontal bossing of skull, brachydactyly, saddle nose and proximal limb shortening. He was diagnosed as the case of achondroplasia. Which of the following is incorrect regarding achondroplasia?
option_c: Short limbs with a normal trunk
explanation:
• Achondroplasia:
    • Key points:
      • Most common form of dwarfism: True, it is indeed the most prevalent type.
      • Short limbs with a normal trunk: Characteristic feature of achondroplasia.
      • FGFR3 gene mutation: It is caused by a mutation in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 gene.

Why Not Others:

  • A (Most common form of dwarfism): Correct, as achondroplasia is indeed the most common form.
  • C (Short limbs with a normal trunk): True; this is a defining feature of the condition.
  • D (FGFR3 gene mutation): Correct, as this mutation is responsible for the disorder.

Key Takeaways:

  • Correct answer: Option B, Autosomal recessive condition.
  • Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant condition, not recessive, characterized by specific skeletal features including short limbs and a normal trunk due to an FGFR3 gene mutation.

question_text: A geneticist is counseling a couple after the diagnosis of Klinefelter syndrome in their son. They ask about the inheritance pattern. Which of the following statements is true regarding Klinefelter syndrome?
option_a: It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern
option_b: It is caused by a non-disjunction event during meiosis
option_c: It can only occur in males with an XXY genotype
option_d: It is always associated with severe intellectual disability
explanation:
• Non-disjunction event during meiosis:
    • Mechanism: Klinefelter syndrome arises from a nondisjunction during meiosis, leading to an extra X chromosome in males (47,XXY).
    • Genetic Basis: This chromosomal anomaly results from the failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate properly during cell division.

Why not the other options?

  • A) Inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern:
    • Explanation: This statement is incorrect as Klinefelter syndrome is not inherited in a classical Mendelian fashion; it results from a random chromosomal error, not a dominant genetic trait.
  • C) Only occurs in males with an XXY genotype:
    • Explanation: While 47,XXY is the most common form, Klinefelter syndrome can also present in variants such as 48,XXXY, which can have similar clinical features.
  • D) Always associated with severe intellectual disability:
  • Explanation: This is misleading; while some cognitive impairment may occur, many individuals with Klinefelter syndrome have normal intelligence, and cognitive effects vary widely among affected individuals.

Key Takeaways:

  • Klinefelter syndrome is primarily caused by a nondisjunction event during meiosis, resulting in an extra X chromosome.
  • The condition does not follow traditional inheritance patterns and can present with various genotypes beyond the classic 47,XXY.

question_text: In a 38-year-old smoker there is enlargement of airspace distal to the terminal bronchioles, barrel shaped chest and flattened diaphragm and no cyanosis. There will be decrease in which following membrane transport?
explanation:
Diagnosis: Emphysema, characterized by destruction of alveolar walls and loss of surface area for gas exchange.

Gases along the respiratory membrane are transported by diffusion.

Option B: Decreased Diffusion of gases due to:

  • Reduced surface area
  • Increased membrane thickness

Diffusion depends on:

  • Area, concentration gradient, lipid solubility (directly proportional)
  • Membrane thickness, particle size (inversely proportional)

Why Not Others:

Option A: Secondary Active Transport:

Not primarily affected in emphysema; this transport mechanism is more related to solute movement rather than gas diffusion.

Option C: Endocytosis:

This process involves the intake of substances into the cell and is not directly related to gas exchange.

Option D: Exocytosis:

This involves the release of substances from the cell and is not impacted by the conditions present in emphysema.

Key takeaways:

Secondary active transport, endocytosis, and exocytosis are not primarily affected in emphysema as they relate to solute transport or cell substance exchange, rather than gas exchange.

question_text: Which of the following statements is NOT true about the ABO blood group system?
option_a: Contain antibodies to A and B
option_c: Antibodies are naturally present since birth
explanation:
Explanation:

The ABO blood group system is based on the presence or absence of A and B antigens (agglutinogens) on the surface of red blood cells and corresponding antibodies (agglutinins) in the plasma.

Therefore:

  • It is false that ABO antibodies are present since birth - they develop postnatally.
  • Newborns lack significant anti-A or anti-B antibodies.

Key Takeaways:

  • ABO antigens: Carbohydrate in nature.
  • ABO antibodies: Naturally acquired postnatally.
  • Predominant class: IgM (pentameric, efficient at agglutination).
  • Newborns lack ABO antibodies.

question_text: A 50yr old man presents with paresthesia, Hb- 6.8 g/dl. Peripheral smear shows macrocytes and neutrophils with hyper segmented nuclei. Endoscopy reveals atrophic gastritis. Which of the deficiency is most likely?
explanation:
Pernicious Anemia a Type 2 Hypersensitivity in which Abs are formed against Intrinsic Factor thus Inhibits the Binding of intrinsic factor+B12

  • Pernicious anemia commonly accompanies gastric atrophy and achlorhydria. Normal gastric secretions contain a glycoprotein called intrinsic factor, secreted by the same parietal cells that secrete hydrochloric acid.
  • Intrinsic factor must be present for adequate absorption of vitamin B 12 from the ileum. That is, intrinsic factor combines with vitamin B12 in the stomach and protects it from being digested and destroyed as it passes into the small intestine.
  • Then, when the intrinsic factor-vitamin B 12 complex reaches the terminal ileum, the intrinsic factor binds with receptors on the ileal epithelial surface, which in turn makes it possible for the vitamin B 12 to be absorbed.
  • In the absence of intrinsic factor, only about 1/50th of the vitamin B 12 is absorbed. In addition, without intrinsic factor, an adequate amount of vitamin B 12 is not made available from the foods to cause young, newly forming red blood cells to mature in the bone marrow. The result is pernicious anemia

question_text: A 62-year-old man was brought to the emergency department with severe, sudden-onset chest pain radiating to the left arm. ECG showed ST segment elevation in precordial leads. He is diagnosed as the case of Myocardial Infarction. Which one of the following is incorrect localization of area of myocardial infarction?
option_a: Anterior wall MI - I, aVL, V1-V4
option_b: Inferior wall MI - II, III, aVF
option_c: Posterior wall MI - I, aVL, V1-V6
option_d: Septal wall MI - I, aVL, V1-V2
explanation:
• Anterior Wall Myocardial Infarction:
    • Identified by ST elevation in leads I, aVL, V1-V4.
    • Involves the left anterior descending artery.
  • Inferior Wall Myocardial Infarction:
    • Associated with ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF.
    • Typically involves the right coronary artery.
  • Posterior Wall Myocardial Infarction:
    • Correct localization should involve reciprocal ST depressions in leads V1 to V3 and not ST elevations in I, aVL, V1-V6.
    • Often presents with dominant R waves in V2 and V3.
  • Septal Wall Myocardial Infarction:
    • Recognized by ST elevation in leads I, aVL, V1-V2.
    • Typically involves the septal branches of the left anterior descending artery.

Why Not Other Options

  • A: Anterior wall MI is accurately localized to leads I, aVL, V1-V4.
  • B: Inferior wall MI is correctly associated with leads II, III, aVF.
  • D: Septal wall MI corresponds to leads I, aVL, V1-V2.

Key Takeaways:

The incorrect localization is for posterior wall MI, which does not show ST elevations in leads I, aVL, V1-V6 but instead exhibits reciprocal ST depressions in leads V1 to V3. Accurate ECG interpretation is crucial for effective diagnosis and treatment of myocardial infarctions.

question_text: Kartagener syndrome is associated with defects in which of the following structures?
explanation:
Explanation:

Kartagener Syndrome, also known as Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD), is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by structural or functional defects in cilia. This leads to ineffective mucociliary clearance and multiple clinical manifestations.


Explanation of other options:

Microvilli (Option A): Microvilli are finger-like extensions of the plasma membrane that increase the absorptive surface area (especially in the small intestine). Defects here lead to malabsorption, not ciliary dysfunction.

Microtubules (Option B): While cilia contain microtubules in their 9+2 arrangement, the syndrome specifically refers to defective cilia function, not generalized microtubule disorders.

Microfilaments (Option D): Microfilaments (actin filaments) are responsible for maintaining cell shape, motility, and intracellular transport, but they are not involved in the mucociliary clearance defects seen in Kartagener syndrome.

Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3519024/

question_text: A 58-year-old factory worker, who has worked in the insulation industry for over 30 years, develops progressive shortness of breath. His wife has tried to get him to go to the doctor, and he finally relents with the appearance of hemoptysis. A chest x-ray is consistent with an alveolitis from asbestos inhalation. Which of the following is the major route for removal of small particles from the alveoli?
explanation:
The lung has a variety of mechanisms to remove particulate matter from the inspired gas. Large particles become deposited in the mucus layer that lies within the bronchi.

The mucus is swept up and out of the bronchioles by the ciliated epithelial cells that line the bronchioles.

Smaller particles remain suspended in the inspired gas and reach the alveoli. Alveolar macrophages remove these particles by phagocytosis.

The macrophages are usually removed from the lung through the lymphatic or blood circulation.

Reference: Ganong, pp 664-665. Kasper et al., pp 1522-1523. Levitzky, pp 216-221. Stead et al., pp 276-277.

question_text: A 25-year-old man returning from a country with endemic malaria was given primaquine for prevention of malaria. Shortly after starting the drug, he presented with dark urine. Which of the following effects did primaquine have on his red blood cells?
option_a: It damaged the cells by acting as a free radical scavenger or antioxidant.
option_b: It exerted more oxidative stress on his red blood cells than the cells could handle.
option_c: It inhibited G6PD and therefore led to an increase in the concentration of oxidized glutathione.
option_d: It irreversibly reduced oxidized glutathione to GSH.
explanation:
G6PD Deficiency: Leads to reduced NADPH production, which is crucial for maintaining reduced glutathione (GSH).

Option B: Oxidative Stress: In individuals with G6PD deficiency, primaquine increases oxidative stress beyond what their red blood cells can manage.

Result: This leads to hemolysis, which explains the presentation of dark urine due to hemoglobinuria.

Why not other options:

Option A: It Damaged the Cells by Acting as a Free Radical Scavenger or Antioxidant: This is incorrect as primaquine does not act as an antioxidant; instead, it increases oxidative stress in G6PD-deficient individuals.

Option C: It Inhibited G6PD and Therefore Led to an Increase in the Concentration of Oxidized Glutathione: Primaquine does not inhibit G6PD; rather, it causes oxidative stress due to the lack of reduced glutathione, resulting from G6PD deficiency.

Option D: It Irreversibly Reduced Oxidized Glutathione to GSH: This is misleading as primaquine does not directly reduce oxidized glutathione to GSH; instead, it exacerbates oxidative stress, leading to hemolysis in G6PD-deficient individuals.

Key takeaways:

After starting primaquine, the 25-year-old man experienced dark urine due to oxidative stress on his red blood cells, which exceeded their capacity to manage it, especially in the context of G6PD deficiency.

question_text: A 78-year-old female complaints of vertigo, intermittent weakness of right lower limb since 2 days, severe headache. On physical examination plethoric face and conjunctive injection, over all dusky cyanotic complexion, pulse 60 BPM, regular, BP 250/110 mm Hg. CBC shows RBC count: 7 to 8 million/mm3, Hematocrit - 60 to 70% and also increase in WBCs and platelets. Which of the following statement is true?
option_a: In this disease the viscosity of blood is drastically decreased
option_b: Given clinical case is of chronic myeloid leukemia
option_c: In this case, there is infective lesion in bone marrow
option_d: Given clinical case is of polycythemia Vera
explanation:
• Polycythemia Vera (PCV) is a myeloproliferative disorder characterized by increased RBCs, WBCs, and platelets. Erythropoietin levels are reduced in PCV. Erythromelalgia is also seen in PCV.
  • Key findings in PCV include:
    • High RBC count and hematocrit (60-70%).
    • Plethoric appearance (red, flushed face) and dusky cyanosis due to increased blood viscosity.
    • BP 250/110 mm Hg and slowed circulation.
  • Increased blood viscosity leads to complications like headaches, vertigo, and thrombotic events.

Why Not Other Options

  • A (Increased blood viscosity, not decreased): Blood viscosity is drastically increased in PCV, causing circulatory issues, not decreased.
  • B (Chronic myeloid leukemia): CML primarily affects WBCs and presents with different clinical features, lacking the characteristic high RBCs and hematocrit seen in PCV.
  • C (Infective lesion in bone marrow): PCV is not caused by infection but by a genetic mutation (JAK2 mutation) in hematopoietic stem cells.

Key Takeaways:

  • Correct Diagnosis: Polycythemia Vera (PCV).
  • Main Issue: Increased RBC production, elevated blood viscosity, and associated symptoms like plethoric face and hypertension.
  • Other myeloproliferative disorders: Essential thrombocytosis, CML, Myelofibrosis.

question_text: Which immunoglobulin is present in serum/plasma at the highest concentration?
explanation:
Explanation:

IgG

  • Main serum immunoglobulin (≈80% of total antibodies).
  • Found both intravascularly & extravascularly.
  • Only antibody crossing the placenta → provides passive immunity to the newborn.
  • Functions: complement activation, opsonization, neutralisation of toxins/viruses, role in chronic inflammation.
  • Clinical application: Anti-Rh(D) IgG given to Rh-negative mothers prevents isoimmunisation.

Explanation of other options:

IgM (Option C):

  • Largest antibody ("millionaire molecule"), pentameric with J chain, valency = 10.
  • Mostly intravascular (≈80%).
  • It is the first antibody produced by the fetus (≈20 weeks).
  • Short-lived; very potent in complement activation & opsonization (500-1000× IgG).

IgA (Option B):

  • Found in secretions (colostrum, saliva, tears).
  • Exists as monomer (serum) & dimer (secretory IgA with J chain & secretory piece).
  • Provides mucosal immunity; resistant to proteases; activates the alternative complement pathway.

IgE (Option D):

  • Present in very low serum concentration.
  • Heat-labile; binds strongly to mast cells & basophils.
  • Mediates Type I hypersensitivity (allergies, asthma, hay fever).
  • Defense against parasites via mast cell degranulation

question_text: A 10-month-old boy presents with recurrent oral lesions and respiratory infections. Laboratory investigations reveal reduced B cell, T cell, and NK cell counts along with reduced adenosine deaminase levels. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis based on the history of recurrent oral lesions and respiratory infections in an infant, along with reduced B cell, T cell, and NK cell counts and adenosine deaminase levels, is suggestive of severe combined immunodeficiency.

Severe combined immunodeficiency is a group of genetically diverse disorders with defects in both humoral and cell-mediated immunity.

Explanation of other options:

Agammaglobulinemia (Option A): Agammaglobulinemia is an X-linked recessive disorder and arises from mutations in the Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) gene, which disrupts signalling from the pre-B cell receptor, leading to failure of B-cell precursors to mature into functional B cells and causing markedly reduced immunoglobulin levels. Clinically, the disorder manifests after about six months of age with recurrent bacterial respiratory infections, susceptibility to certain viral and protozoal infections, absence of plasma cells, underdeveloped lymphoid tissues, and normal T-cell function.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (Option B): Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by misfolded α1-antitrypsin protein, most often the PiZ variant, which accumulates in hepatocytes, leading to endoplasmic reticulum stress and impaired inhibition of neutrophil elastase, resulting in lung and liver damage. Clinically, it may manifest in infancy with severe liver disease progressing to cirrhosis, while pulmonary emphysema develops due to unchecked neutrophil elastase activity.

DiGeorge syndrome (Option C): DiGeorge syndrome arises from developmental failure of the thymus due to defects in the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, most commonly linked to a 22q11 deletion involving the TBX1 gene. This results in deficient T-cell-mediated immunity, hypocalcemic tetany from absent parathyroids, and congenital malformations of the heart and great vessels, often accompanied by abnormal facial features. Clinically, patients show low T-cell counts, reduced resistance to fungal and viral infections, and depletion of T-cell zones in lymphoid organs, while immunoglobulin levels may be normal or reduced depending on the degree of T-cell deficiency.

question_text: What is the enzyme defect if a child with anemia, thrombocytopenia, bony pain, and hepatosplenomegaly shows a "crumpled tissue paper" appearance on light microscopy of bone marrow aspirate?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical features point to Gaucher disease, a lysosomal storage disorder inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

  • The underlying defect is in the enzyme beta-glucosidase (also called glucocerebrosidase).
  • This defect causes the accumulation of glucosylceramide (glucocerebroside) within macrophages.
  • These engorged macrophages are termed Gaucher cells, which display the classic "crumpled tissue paper" appearance on bone marrow aspirate due to fibrillary inclusions in the cytoplasm.
  • The infiltration of Gaucher cells in bone marrow, liver, and spleen explains the clinical findings of anemia, thrombocytopenia, bony pain, and hepatosplenomegaly.

Explanation of incorrect options:

Sphingomyelinase (Option B):

  • Deficiency of this enzyme leads to Niemann-Pick disease.
  • In this condition, bone marrow aspirates reveal foamy histiocytes packed with lipid-filled cytoplasm, not the crumpled tissue paper appearance.

Hexosaminidase (Option C):

  • Defective in Tay-Sachs disease.
  • It does not typically cause anemia, thrombocytopenia, or bony pain.
  • Histopathology may demonstrate an "onion-skin" appearance of lysosomes, which is distinct from Gaucher disease.

Glucose-6-phosphatase (Option D):

  • Deficiency results in Von Gierke disease (Glycogen storage disease type I).
  • Patients present with hepatosplenomegaly and sometimes bone pain, but anemia and thrombocytopenia are not characteristic.
  • The hallmark is hypoglycemia with glycogen accumulation, not Gaucher cells.

question_text: An elderly patient presents with signs of atherosclerosis. His diet is high in saturated fats, and lab tests show elevated LDL levels. Which type of fatty acid is primarily associated with increased cardiovascular risk?
explanation:
• Saturated fatty acids:
    • Saturated fatty acids, found in animal products (like red meat, butter, and cheese) and tropical oils (such as coconut and palm oil), are primarily associated with increased cardiovascular risk.
    • They raise LDL (bad) cholesterol levels, which contribute to atherosclerosis (plaque buildup in the arteries), increasing the risk of heart disease.
  • Monounsaturated fatty acids:
    • Monounsaturated fatty acids, found in foods like olive oil, avocados, and nuts, are heart-healthy.
    • They can lower LDL cholesterol and reduce cardiovascular risk when replacing saturated fats in the diet.
  • Polyunsaturated fatty acids:
    • Polyunsaturated fatty acids, found in foods like fish, flaxseeds, and walnuts, are also heart-protective.
    • Certain types, like omega-3 fatty acids, have anti-inflammatory effects and lower the risk of cardiovascular disease.
  • All of the above:
    • While saturated fats are linked to increased cardiovascular risk, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats are generally heart-healthy.
    • This makes all of the above incorrect in the context of increased cardiovascular risk.

Why Not Others:

  • Option A: Monounsaturated fatty acids
    • Monounsaturated fats are heart-healthy and can lower LDL cholesterol, which reduces cardiovascular risk, not increases it.
  • Option B: Polyunsaturated fatty acids
    • Polyunsaturated fats have protective effects, such as reducing inflammation and triglycerides, thereby reducing cardiovascular risk.
  • Option D: All of the above
    • While saturated fats increase cardiovascular risk, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats are beneficial and do not contribute to atherosclerosis or increased LDL levels.

Key Takeaways:

  • Saturated fats are linked to increased cardiovascular risk due to their role in raising LDL cholesterol.
  • Monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats have heart-protective effects, reducing LDL cholesterol and inflammation.
  • Trans fatty acids (found in processed foods) should be avoided as they raise LDL cholesterol and lower HDL cholesterol, increasing cardiovascular risk.

  • Topic: Fatty acid in cardiovascular disease
  • PYQ: Good to know

question_text: An 8-year-old boy presents to the OPD for evaluation of a subcutaneous xanthoma on his right elbow. Which of the following types of Familial hyperlipoproteinemias is the most likely underlying condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely underlying familial hypercholesterolemia in a patient with subcutaneous xanthoma, elevated cholesterol and LDL, with normal triglycerides and a positive family history of cardiovascular events is familial hyperlipoproteinemia type IIa.

The various hyperlipoproteinemias are summarised in the table given below.

Explanations of other options:

Type I (Option A): Familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency (Type I), a form of hyperlipoproteinemia, is characterised by markedly elevated triglyceride levels due to absent or defective lipoprotein lipase (LPL) activity or a deficiency of apo C-II, which inactivates LPL. Patients typically show reduced levels of both low-density lipoproteins (LDL) and high-density lipoproteins (HDL), yet despite the lipid abnormalities, there is no associated increase in the risk of coronary artery disease.

Type IIb (Option C): Type IIb hyperlipoproteinemia is a multifactorial and more common form of hypercholesterolemia compared to type IIa, characterised by elevation of both LDL and VLDL. This pattern significantly increases the risk of atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease.

Type III (Option D): Familial type III hyperlipoproteinemia, also called Familial type III hyperlipoproteinemia, also called remnant removal disease or dysbetalipoproteinemia, occurs due to defective clearance of lipoprotein remnants by the liver, caused by an apo E abnormality. This results in accumulation of chylomicron and VLDL remnants (β-VLDL), leading to hypercholesterolemia, xanthomas, and atherosclerosis.

question_text: A male patient reports imbalance, numbness in the feet, and muscle weakness. On further history, he mentions taking high doses of multivitamin supplements regularly for the past year. What is the most likely underlying cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • While multivitamins supply essential nutrients, an overdose can result in toxicity with noticeable symptoms.
  • The patient's reported symptoms, including numbness, muscle weakness, and difficulty walking, are characteristic of nerve damage that can arise from high doses of Vitamin B6 supplements.
  • This occurs because vitamin B6 can build up in the system and become toxic, with a particular impact on the peripheral nerves.

Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine) Toxicity:

Vitamin B6 is vital for many bodily functions, like amino acid metabolism, neurotransmitter production, and the creation of red blood cells, but excessive levels can cause harm.

  • Causes of Vitamin B6 Toxicity:
    • Excessive Supplementation: The most frequent cause is the long-term use of high-dose vitamin B6 supplements (over 100 mg daily).
    • Self-medication: Individuals might unknowingly consume unsafe amounts when using B6 supplements for conditions like premenstrual syndrome (PMS), depression, or carpal tunnel syndrome.
  • Symptoms of Vitamin B6 Toxicity:
    • Neurological Symptoms:
      • Peripheral neuropathy
      • Sensory ataxia
      • Muscle weakness
      • Cognitive disturbances
    • Other Symptoms:
      • Skin lesions: Can include painful and irritated skin that often looks like a rash.
      • Gastrointestinal discomfort: High doses may lead to nausea or heartburn.
  • Toxic Dose and Safety:
    • The established tolerable upper intake level (UL) for vitamin B6 is 100 mg per day for adults. Regularly surpassing this limit can cause toxicity.
    • Toxicity usually happens with doses significantly higher than the UL, particularly when taken for a prolonged period (months or years).
  • Treatment:
    • Stopping the excess intake allows most symptoms of vitamin B6 toxicity, especially peripheral neuropathy, to reverse or improve. However, the recovery of nerve damage can be slow, and in severe situations, it may be permanent.
  • Prevention:
    • Limit Supplementation: One should not consume vitamin B6 supplements in amounts greater than the recommended daily allowance (RDA) without guidance from a healthcare professional.
    • Dietary Intake: Achieving toxic levels through food alone is unlikely because the body effectively manages absorption from dietary sources.

Explanation of other options:

Vitamin D toxicity (Option A): Symptoms associated with Vitamin D toxicity can include elevated blood calcium levels, weakness, nausea, vomiting, intense thirst, polyuria (frequent urination), weight loss, and difficulty speaking.

Vitamin C toxicity (Option C): Vitamin C is crucial for skin health and immune function, but consuming too much can lead to gastrointestinal issues, including diarrhea and nausea.

Vitamin A toxicity (Option D): Toxicity from Vitamin A can manifest as dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and blurred vision. In cases of extremely high intake, it can also cause liver damage and result in birth defects in pregnant women.

question_text: A patient presents with ataxia, anaemia, and sensory neuropathy. Laboratory tests show elevated total homocysteine and methylmalonic acid levels. Production of which of the following amino acids could be affected?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario of ataxia, anaemia, and sensory neuropathy, along with elevated total homocysteine and methylmalonic acid levels, suggests vitamin B12 deficiency, which affects the production of methionine.

  • The term vitamin B12 is used as a generic descriptor for the cobalamins and for practical purposes, is available only from foods of animal origin, with no plant sources.
  • As a result, strict vegetarians (vegans) are at high risk of deficiency. Though trace amounts may be produced by bacteria on fruit surfaces, nutritional needs are generally met either through animal foods or preparations derived from bacterial fermentation.
  • Absorption of vitamin B12 requires binding to intrinsic factor, a glycoprotein secreted by the stomach's parietal cells.
  • Dietary vitamin B12 is first freed from food proteins by gastric acid and pepsin, then binds to cobalophilin from saliva.
  • In the duodenum, pancreatic enzymes degrade cobalophilin, releasing vitamin B12 so it can bind to intrinsic factor. Pancreatic insufficiency can therefore lead to deficiency due to impaired release of vitamin B12 from cobalophilin.
  • Absorption occurs in the distal ileum via receptors that recognise only the intrinsic factor-vitamin B12 complex, not free vitamin.
  • The vitamin also undergoes enterohepatic circulation, being excreted in bile and reabsorbed in the ileum.
  • Two enzymes require vitamin B12: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase.
  • The first catalyses the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA, derived from amino acids and odd-chain fatty acids, into succinyl-CoA.
  • Deficiency impairs this process, causing methylmalonyl-CoA buildup and urinary methylmalonic acid excretion, which can be used as a marker of deficiency.
  • Methionine synthase uses vitamin B12 to convert homocysteine into methionine, and production of methionine is impaired in vitamin B12 deficiency.
  • Deficiency of vitamin B12 also causes functional folate deficiency, known as the "folate trap."
  • This occurs because methionine synthase, a B12-dependent enzyme, is required to convert methyltetrahydrofolate into tetrahydrofolate, the active form needed for DNA synthesis.
  • Without vitamin B12, methyltetrahydrofolate accumulates and cannot be used, producing secondary folate deficiency despite adequate folate levels.
  • The deficiency disrupts folic acid metabolism, leading to impaired DNA synthesis and megaloblastic anaemia.
  • Neurological damage also occurs, with irreversible spinal cord degeneration due to impaired methylation of myelin proteins, specifically linked to methionine deficiency in the nervous system.

Explanation of other options:

Tyrosine (Option A): Phenylalanine hydroxylase converts phenylalanine into tyrosine with tetrahydrobiopterin as a cofactor. When the diet supplies enough of the essential amino acid phenylalanine, tyrosine does not need to be obtained from food and is considered nutritionally nonessential.

Glutamine (Option B): The enzyme glutamine synthetase carries out amidation of glutamate to glutamine and requires ATP and a divalent metal cation such as Mg2+.

Cysteine (Option C): Cysteine is not an essential dietary amino acid because it can be synthesised from methionine, which is essential. Methionine is first converted to homocysteine, which then combines with serine to form cystathionine. The breakdown of cystathionine yields cysteine and homoserine. In vitamin B12 deficiency, since homocysteine production is not impaired, synthesis of cysteine remains unaffected.

question_text: A 40-year-old woman who underwent ileal resection presents with features of anaemia despite a balanced diet. Her RBC count is 2.8 million/mm<sup>3</sup>, and serum iron is 164 mcg/dL. Which of the following is most likely to be found in her?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical scenario of anaemia with reduced RBC count and normal serum iron in a patient after ileal resection is suggestive of megaloblastic anaemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency.

  • Megaloblastic anaemia arises due to defective DNA synthesis, which results in ineffective blood cell production and distinct morphological abnormalities, notably the presence of unusually large erythroid precursors and red cells.
  • The main subtypes include pernicious anaemia, caused by vitamin B12 deficiency, and folate deficiency anaemia.
  • Both vitamin B12 and folic acid act as coenzymes in the synthesis of thymidine, a DNA base, and their deficiency disrupts DNA synthesis, leading to defective nuclear maturation and delayed or blocked cell division.
  • Other causes of megaloblastic anaemia are summarised in the table below.
  • Peripheral blood typically shows macrocytic and oval-shaped red cells (macro-ovalocytes), which are larger than normal and may appear hyperchromic but lack central pallor.
  • Neutrophils are often larger and display nuclear hypersegmentation with five or more lobes instead of the usual three to four, as shown below.
  • The marrow is usually hypercellular due to an increase in hematopoietic precursors, with megaloblastic changes evident at all stages of erythroid development.
  • Despite delayed nuclear maturation, cytoplasmic growth and haemoglobin synthesis proceed normally, producing nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony.
  • Vitamin B12 obtained from the diet is initially released from food proteins through the action of gastric acid and pepsin, after which it attaches to salivary cobalophilin.
  • In the duodenum, pancreatic enzymes break down cobalophilin, liberating vitamin B12 so it can then bind to intrinsic factor. If pancreatic function is impaired, this release step is defective, resulting in vitamin B12 deficiency. Absorption finally takes place in the terminal ileum, where receptors specifically recognise the intrinsic factor-vitamin B12 complex, but not the free vitamin itself. Hence, ileal resection leads to vitamin B12 deficiency and, in turn, megaloblastic anaemia.

Explanation of other options:

Iron deficiency anaemia (Option A): Causes of iron deficiency include inadequate dietary intake, defective absorption, heightened physiological demand, or persistent blood loss. Absorption of iron predominantly takes place in the duodenum.

Aplastic anaemia (Option C): The causes of aplastic anaemia often involve exposure to chemicals and drugs, such as chemotherapy agents and benzene, which suppress marrow in a dose-related and reversible manner. It can also be due to idiopathic causes or acquired stem cell defects.

Hemolytic anaemia (Option D): Hemolytic anaemias are characterised by a reduced lifespan of red blood cells, which leads to elevated erythropoietin levels and compensatory erythropoiesis. Clinically, they present with anaemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly due to increased red cell destruction, while intravascular hemolysis additionally produces hemoglobinemia, hemoglobinuria, and hemosiderinuria. Excess bilirubin from ongoing hemolysis contributes to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and persistent cases may result in gallstone formation from heme pigment deposits.

question_text: An Indian female on a strict vegetarian diet, consuming high fibre, presents to OPD with features of anemia. Her peripheral blood smear is given below. Which of the following deficiency is characteristic to the finding?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's history is highly suggestive of Vitamin B12 deficiency. Clinical features and history include:

  • Strict vegetarian diet: Vitamin B12 is naturally found almost exclusively in animal products (meat, eggs, dairy). Strict vegetarians (vegans) are at high risk for deficiency.
  • Anemia: The peripheral blood smear show macrocytic ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils, which are characteristic hallmarks of megaloblastic anemia caused by either Vitamin B12 or Folate deficiency.
  • In an Indian context, where vegetarianism is common, B12 deficiency is far more prevalent than folate deficiency as a cause of megaloblastic anemia, as folate is present in many plant foods (green leafy vegetables, legumes). B12 is the characteristic deficiency in this demographic.

Explanation of other options:

Vitamin B9 (Folate) (Option A): Folate deficiency also causes megaloblastic anemia, it is less likely in this scenario. A high-fibre, vegetarian diet is typically rich in folate from vegetables and legumes. B12 deficiency is the more probable cause given the dietary restrictions.

Iron (Option C): Iron deficiency causes microcytic hypochromic anemia, characterized by small, pale red blood cells (RBCs), which is the opposite of the macrocytic RBCs seen in B12/folate deficiency.

Copper (Option D): Copper deficiency can cause a anemia that may be microcytic or sideroblastic, but it is rare and not specifically linked to a vegetarian diet. It is not the characteristic finding here.

Key Takeaways:

  • Vitamin B12 deficiency is a common cause of megaloblastic anemia in strict vegetarians.
  • The peripheral blood smear in megaloblastic anemia shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils (≥5 lobes).

question_text: All of the following are key properties of cancer cells, except:
explanation:
Option A & Option B: Cancer cells are self-sufficient in growth signals and are insensitive to antigrowth signals.

Option C: Cancer cells are resistant to apoptosis.

Option D: They have Limitless replicative growth potentials

Cancer cells are characterized by certain key properties. They

  1. Proliferate rapidly;
  2. Display diminished growth control;
  3. Display increased genomic mutations at the level of the nucleotide, small and large insertions and deletions (indels), and gross chromosomal rearrangements, duplications and loss;
  4. Display loss of contact inhibition in culture in vitro;
  5. Invade local tissues and spread, or metastasize, to other parts of the body;
  6. They are self-sufficient in growth signals and are insensitive to antigrowth signals;
  7. Stimulate local angiogenesis; and
  8. are often able to evade apoptosis.
    • These properties are characteristic of cells of malignant tumours. It is metastasis that is generally responsible for the deaths of patients who have cancer.
    • By contrast, cells of benign tumours also show diminished control of growth, but do not invade local tissue or spread to other parts of the body.

Six major biologic features of cancer cells

question_text: A patient presents with multiple colonic polyps and was diagnosed with colorectal cancer. He has a strong family history of HNPCC. Which of the following DNA repair mechanism defects is responsible for her condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The DNA repair mechanism defective in HNPCC is mismatch repair.

  • DNA repair is vital for preserving genomic stability and preventing the spread of mutations, whether within somatic or germ cells.
  • Since DNA is constantly exposed to chemical, physical, and biological insults, cells require efficient systems for detecting and correcting DNA lesions.
  • Eukaryotic cells possess five principal repair pathways:
  • Nucleotide excision repair (NER)
  • Mismatch repair (MMR)
  • Base excision repair (BER)
  • Homologous recombination (HR)
  • Nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ).
  • These pathways involve numerous proteins, many of which have counterparts in prokaryotes.
  • Mutations in DNA repair genes often result in human diseases, as summarised in the table below.

Explanation of other options:

Base excision repair (Option A): Base excision repair is associated with MUTYH-associated polyposis.

Nucleotide excision repair (Option B): Nucleotide excision repair can result in xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome, and trichothiodystrophy.

Double-strand break repair (Option D): There are two pathways by which double-strand break repair occurs - Nonhomologous end joining and homologous repair. Some disorders associated with this include SCID, ATLD, and Bloom syndrome.

question_text: A patient who is diagnosed with HNPCC, which of the following is the most common repair associated with it?
explanation:
Option A: A defect in mismatch repair can lead to Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer(HNPCC).

Option B: A defect in Base excision repair can lead to MUTYH-associated polyposis(MAP).

Option C: A defect in Nucleotide excision repair can lead to Xeroderma pigmentosum(XP), Cockayne syndrome(CS) & Trichothiodystrophy(TTD).

Option D: A defect in Homologous recombination repair can leads to Ataxia Telangiectasia(AT) -like disorder, Nijmegen breakage syndrome(NBS), Bloom syndrome(BS), Werner syndrome(WS), Rothmund-Thomson syndrome(RTS) and Breast cancer susceptibility 1 and 2(BRCA1, BRCA2).

Repair of damaged DNA is critical for maintaining genomic integrity and thereby preventing the propagation of mutations, either horizontally(somatic cells) or vertically(germ cells). DNA is subjected to a huge array of chemical, physical and biologic assaults on a daily basis, hence efficient recognition and repair of DNA lesions is essential. Consequently, eukaryotic cells contain five major DNA repair pathways. The mechanisms of DNA repair include nucleotide excision repair(NER); mismatch repair(MMR); base excision repair(BER); homologous recombination(HR); and nonhomologous end-joining(NHEJ) repair pathways

question_text: You see a child in clinic who is well below average height. You note that the child has short limbs, normal trunk size, macrocephaly, and a variety of other skeletal abnormalities. Yoususpect that the child has achondroplasia. Select from the following list the test that would best confirm your diagnosis:
option_b: Assays for enzymes involved in the metabolism of GAGs
option_d: Gene tests for abnormalities of the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3)
explanation:
• Achondroplasia is caused by mutations in the FGFR3 gene.
    • The best known of the chondrodysplasias is achondroplasia, the most common cause of short-limbed dwarfism.
    • Affected individuals have short limbs, normal trunk size, macrocephaly, and a variety of other skeletal abnormalities.
    • The condition is often inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, but many cases are due to new mutations.
    • Achondroplasia is not a collagen disorder but is due to mutations in the gene encoding fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3).
    • Fibroblast growth factors are a family of more than 20 proteins that affect the growth and differentiation of cells of mesenchymal and neuroectodermal origin. Their receptors are transmembrane proteins and form a subgroup of four in the family of receptor tyrosine kinases. FGFR3 is one member of this subgroup and mediates the actions of FGF3 on cartilage. In almost all cases of achondroplasia that have been investigated, the mutations were found to involve nucleotide 1138 and resulted in substitution of arginine for glycine (residue number 380) in the transmembrane domain of the protein, rendering it inactive. No such mutation was found in unaffected individuals.

Reference: Harper 32nd edition, Page no. 643, 645

question_text: A patient presented with severe generalized pain and has had multiple similar episodes in the past, especially after strenuous exercise. Blood examination revealed anemia with elongated (sickle-shaped) red blood cells instead of normal biconcave cells. A diagnosis of sickle cell anemia was made. Which amino acid substitution is responsible for this condition?
option_a: Substitution of valine by glutamic acid at the 6th position
option_b: Substitution of glutamic acid by valine at the 6th position
option_c: Substitution of valine by glutamic acid at the 5th position
option_d: Substitution of glutamic acid by valine at the 5th position
explanation:
Explanation:

Sickle cell anemia results from a single-point mutation in the β-globin gene, where glutamic acid is replaced by valine at the 6th position of the β-globin chain. This creates an abnormal hemoglobin known as HbS.

Pathophysiology:

  • HbS Polymerization: After deoxygenation, HbS molecules aggregate to form rigid polymers, distorting RBCs into a sickle shape. This promotes hemolysis and vascular occlusion.
  • Vaso-occlusion: Sickled cells obstruct capillaries, leading to ischemia, pain crises, and organ damage.
  • Endothelial Dysfunction: Free hemoglobin released during hemolysis consumes nitric oxide (NO), generating oxidative stress and worsening vascular injury.
  • Sterile Inflammation: Cell-free heme and ischemia-reperfusion injury trigger ROS formation, TLR4 activation, neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) release, and inflammasome activation, fueling further inflammation and vaso-occlusion.
  • Thus, the key molecular defect is the E6V mutation (Glu → Val at position 6), which alters hemoglobin solubility and underlies the disease pathology.

question_text:
Septic shock is a serious medical condition.
Because
Septic shock causes multiple organ injury leading to low blood pressure and abnormalities in cellular metabolism.
option_a: If both statements are true and causally related
option_b: If both statements are true but not causally related
option_c: If the first statement is true and second is false
option_d: If the first statement is false and second is true
explanation:
Septic shock is caused by the host response to bacterial or fungal infections; it is characterized by endothelial cell activation, vasodilation, edema, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and metabolic derangements. In septic shock, the skin may be warm and flushed owing to peripheral vasodilation. The primary threat to life is the underlying initiating event (e.g., myocardial infarction, severe hemorrhage, bacterial infection). However, the cardiac, cerebral, and pulmonary changes rapidly aggravate the situation. If patients survive the initial period, worsening renal function can provoke a phase dominated by progressive oliguria, acidosis, and electrolyte imbalances.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg-116-118

explanation:
The consequences of traumatic brain injury may be internal and subtle. The parasagittal cortex is anchored to arachnoid villi, whereas the lateral aspects of the cerebrum move more freely. question_text: A 40-year-old woman on screening found to have abnormal findings in Pap smear. On pathologist advice cervical biopsy was performed which reveals atypical squamous cells throughout the entire thickness of the epithelium, with no evidence of epithelial maturation (shown in the image). The basal membrane appears intact. What is the appropriate diagnosis?
explanation:
The normal process by which the cervical squamous epithelium matures is disturbed in CIN, as evidenced morphologically by changes in cellularity, differentiation, polarity, nuclear features, and mitotic activity. In CIN-1 (mild dysplasia), the most pronounced changes are seen in the basal third of the epithelium. However, in this case, abnormal cells are present throughout the entire thickness of the epithelium. In CIN-2 (moderate dysplasia, choice c), most of the cellular abnormalities are in the lower and middle thirds of the epithelium. CIN-3 is synonymous with severe dysplasia and carcinoma in situ and shows abnormal cells occupying the full thickness of the epithelium, with no evidence of epithelial maturation. Invasive carcinoma (choice b) features extension of neoplastic cells through the basal membrane. Dysplasia is not synonymous with squamous metaplasia (choice e).

question_text: A 54-year-old female presented with 3 month history of intermittent vaginal bleeding. Pelvic examination reveals a left adnexal mass. A uterine curettage shows complex endometrial hyperplasia without atypia. A CT scan of the abdomen reveals a 5 cm mass replacing the left ovary. The patient undergoes hysterectomy and bilateral salpingooophorectomy. Histologic examination of the ovarian mass is shown in the image. Which of the following is the appropriate pathologic diagnosis?
explanation:
(a) The lesion is composed of sheets of uniform cells divided into poorly demarcated lobules by delicate fibrous septa containing a lymphocytic infiltrate.

(b) Granulosa cell tumor is the prototypical functional neoplasm of the ovary associated with estrogen secretion. The tumor is derived from sex cord stromal cells. Most granulosa cell tumors occur after the menopause. Microscopically, granulosa cell tumors display haphazard orientation of the nuclei about a central degenerative space (Call-Exner bodies), which results in a characteristic follicular histologic pattern. Three fourths of granulosa cell tumors secrete estrogens. Consequently, endometrial hyperplasia is a common presenting sign.

(c) Cystadenocarcinoma are common ovarian tumors that are often bilateral. The serous type is typically unilocular. As the name indicates, they are cystic in appearance. They may be benign, borderline, or malignant. Benign tumors have a smooth cyst wall with small or absent papillary projections. Borderline tumors have increasing amounts of papillary projections.

question_text:
In which of the following condition the cell can recover to its original state when the stress is eliminated?
i.Hypertrophy
ii.Hyperplasia
iii.Atrophy
iv.Metaplasia
option_a: Only i, ii and iii are correct
option_b: Only i and iii are correct
option_c: Only ii and iv are correct
explanation:
• Adaptation are reversible changes in the size, number, phenotype, metabolic activity, or functions of cells in response to changes in their environment.

CELLULAR ADAPTATIONS TO STRESS:

  • Hypertrophy: Increased cell and organ size, often in response to increased workload; induced by growth factors produced in response to mechanical stress or other stimuli; occurs in tissues incapable of cell division
  • Hyperplasia: Increased cell numbers in response to hormones and other growth factors; occurs in tissues whose cells are able to divide or contain abundant tissue stem cells.
  • Atrophy: Decreased cell and organ size, as a result of decreased nutrient supply or disuse, associated with decreased synthesis of cellular building blocks and increased breakdown of cellular organelles and autophagy.
  • Metaplasia: Change in phenotype of differentiated cells, often in response to chronic irritation, that makes cells better able to withstand the stress, usually induced by altered differentiation pathway of tissue stem cells. This may result in reduced functions or increased propensity for malignant transformation

Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10th ed Pg:54

question_text: Pap smear with hyperchromatic nuclei pleomorphism with low maturation index involving almost all thickness. What is this called?
explanation:
The described Pap smear findings of hyperchromatic nuclei, pleomorphism, and low maturation index involving almost all thickness, are indicative of (Choice B) Dysplasia.

Here's a more detailed explanation:

  • Dysplasia: Refers to disordered growth of cells, which can be a precursor to cancer, it does not always progress to cancer.
  • Hyperchromatic nuclei: Nuclei that appear darker than normal due to increased DNA content.
  • Pleomorphism: Variation in the size, shape, and staining of cells, which is a sign of abnormal cell growth.
  • Low maturation index: A low proportion of mature cells compared to immature cells, indicating a disruption in the normal cell development process.
  • Involving almost all thickness: This suggests that the abnormal changes are widespread within the cervical tissue.

Incorrect choices explanation:

  • (Choice A): Metaplasia: A change in cell type, (replacement of one type of cell with another type) not necessarily indicative of dysplasia or cancer.
  • (Choice C): Hyperplasia: An increase in the number of cells but size remains the same. Not necessarily indicative of dysplasia or cancer.
  • (Choice D): Carcinoma: Cancer, a more advanced stage of abnormal cell growth.

Key takeaway: Hyperplasia Examples: Physiological - Pregnant uterus. Pathological - Endometrial hyperplasia. Metaplasia Examples: Physiological: In cervix during menstruation - squamous metaplasia; Pathological - Barrett's esophagus.

question_text: A 35-year-old chronic smoker presents with an oral lesion, as shown in the image below. Which is the stain used to identify this pathology?
explanation:
Explanation:

Toluidine blue is the most appropriate supravital stain for identifying oral or vocal cord lesions in smokers.

  • It is particularly useful in detecting early changes or abnormalities in cells before they undergo irreversible damage or cell death.
  • It is a valuable tool for identifying dysplasia, precancerous lesions, and early-stage cancer.

Explanation for other options:

Congo Red (Option B) is primarily used to identify amyloid deposits under polarised light. It is not useful for detecting dysplasia or squamous cell carcinoma in oral lesions or vocal cords.

Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) (Option C) are commonly used for routine histopathology to examine tissue structure. H&E is used to assess the overall architecture of tissue, such as looking for signs of malignancy or dysplasia.

Oil Red O (Option D) is used to stain lipids in tissues and is commonly used to identify cell fat content, such as in lipid-rich lesions or tissue samples.

Reference:

Histological Stains: A Literature Review and Case Study - PMC

question_text: A 45-year-old male patient presented with a history of productive cough since 4 months, and he had such symptoms every year since 3 years. He gave a history of excessive smoking from long duration due to stress. What will be the histopathological findings in such disease in airway if biopsy is taken, image of which is shown below. What is the correct answer?
option_a: Thickening of the bronchiolar wall due to smooth muscle hypertrophy
option_b: Enlargement of mucus-secreting glands of trachea and bronchi
option_c: Chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate (lymphocytes and macrophages)
explanation:
The characteristic microscopic features of chronic bronchitis are chronic inflammation of the airways (predominantly lymphocytes and macrophages); thickening of the bronchiolar wall due to smooth muscle hypertrophy, deposition of extracellular matrix in the muscle layer, and peribronchial fibrosis; goblet cell hyperplasia; and enlargement of the mucus-secreting glands of the trachea and bronchi. Of these, the most striking change is an increase in the size of the mucous glands. This increase can be assessed by the ratio of the thickness of the mucous gland layer to the thickness of the wall between the epithelium and the cartilage (Reid index).

Reference: Robbins 10th Ed, pg 681

question_text:
Assertion: In the habitual cigarette smoker, ciliated columnar epithelial cells of trachea and bronchi are often replaced by stratified squamous epithelial cells.
Reason: In the habitual cigarette smoker, the stratified squamous epithelial cells are better to withstand chronic irritation by smoke.
option_a: If both statements are true and causally related
option_b: If both statements are true but not causally related
option_c: If the first statement is true and second is false
option_d: If the first statement is false and second is true
explanation:
In brief, metaplasia is a reversible cellular change seen in habitual smokers, where ciliated columnar epithelial cells are replaced by stratified squamous epithelial cells due to chronic irritation. This change, while more robust, reduces protective functions and can, if persistent, initiate malignancy.

  • Metaplasia Definition: Metaplasia is a reversible cellular change where one cell type replaces another, often due to environmental stress.
  • Example in Smokers: In habitual smokers, ciliated columnar epithelial cells in the respiratory tract are often replaced by stratified squamous epithelial cells in response to chronic irritation.
  • Effects: This change makes the epithelium more durable but compromises protective mechanisms like mucus and ciliary action. In most cases, metaplasia is undesirable as it reduces the organ's functionality.
  • Malignant Transformation Risk: Persistent factors causing metaplasia can potentially lead to malignancy in metaplastic tissue.

Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 9th ed Pg:37

question_text: Which of the following is the mediator of bronchial asthma?
explanation:
• The asthmatic airway is marked by accumulation of mucus in the bronchial lumen secondary to an increase in the number of mucus-secreting goblet cells in the mucosa and hypertrophy of sub mucosal glands; intense chronic inflammation due to recruitment of eosinophils, macrophages, and other inflammatory cells; thickened basement membrane; and hypertrophy and hyperplasia of smooth muscle cells.
  • Inhaled allergens (antigen) elicit aTH2-dominated response favouring IgE production and eosinophil recruitment. On reexposure to antigen (Ag), the immediate reaction is triggered by Ag-induced cross-linking of IgE bound to Fc receptors on mast cells.
  • These cells release preformed mediators that directly and via neuronal reflexes induce bronchospasm, increased vascular permeability, mucus production, and recruitment of leukocytes.
  • Leukocytes recruited to the site of reaction (neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils; lymphocytes and monocytes) release additional mediators that initiate the late phase of asthma.
  • Several factors released from eosinophils (e.g., major basic protein, eosinophil cationic protein) also cause damage to the epithelium.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg-504

question_text: Identify the marked structure on the given biopsy of prostate tisuue.
explanation:
Explanation:

The structure shown in the prostate biopsy image above is corpora amylacea, which is commonly seen in Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) (also referred to as nodular hyperplasia)

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)

  • The most common benign prostate condition in men over 50 years of age.
  • Affects both glandular epithelium and connective tissue stroma to variable degrees.
  • Most common site of origin: Submucosal glands of the periurethral transitional zone.
  • Role of hormones in BPH:
    • DHT (Dihydrotestosterone)
      • DHT, derived from testosterone via 5-alpha reductase, binds to androgen receptors in the prostate, promoting cellular proliferation and contributing to prostatic enlargement.
    • Estrogen
      • Estrogen levels increase relative to testosterone in ageing men, influencing prostate growth through the activation of estrogen receptors, particularly ER-α, in the prostatic tissue.
  • Secondary changes in the bladder (due to increased force of contraction of detrusor muscles):
    • Collagen deposition
    • Detrusor muscle hyperplasia
    • Detrusor muscle hypertrophy.
  • Clinical features
  • Complications:
    • Retention
    • Haematuria
    • Urinary infection
    • Stone formation

Microscopy

  • Hyperplasia (increase in the number of cells) of both stromal and epithelial components of the prostate gland.
    • The stromal cells include fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells, while the epithelial cells line the glandular structures of the prostate.
  • Unlike prostate cancer, BPH is characterised by the absence of atypical cells with high mitotic activity or dysplastic changes in the glandular architecture.
  • The cells in BPH retain their normal morphology but increase in number, leading to glandular enlargement.
  • Corpora amylacea are round, basophilic structures commonly seen in the histopathology of BPH.
    • They are composed of proteinaceous material often found in the prostatic acini and ducts.
  • BPH is not associated with significant infiltration of inflammatory cells such as lymphocytes or plasma cells.

Explanation of other options:

Corpora arenecea (Option A): These are calcified structures found in the pineal gland and other areas of the brain, such as the choroid plexus. They comprise calcium phosphate, calcium carbonate, magnesium phosphate, and ammonium phosphate.

Psammoma bodies (Option B): Small, calcified, round structures found in various tissues, often linked to certain tumours. They are composed of calcium and can appear in the brain, thyroid, ovaries, and other organs. They are commonly seen in meningiomas, papillary thyroid carcinoma, ovarian serous cystadenocarcinoma, endometrial carcinoma, and choroid plexus tumours.

Amyloid deposits (Option D): Amyloid deposits are abnormal buildups of misfolded proteins that form insoluble fibrils, impairing normal tissue function in amyloidosis. They can be detected using Congo red staining, which produces an apple-green colour under polarized light.A

question_text: Which of the following can be aptly considered as the definition of a hamartoma?
option_a: Proliferation of native cells in tissue
option_b: Proliferation of cells in a foreign site
explanation:
• Hamartoma is a mass of disorganized tissue resembling the involved site, such as the lung or the liver. 
  • Although historically thought of as developmental malformations, hamartomas have clonal chromosomal aberrations that are acquired through somatic mutations and are best considered unusual benign neoplasms.

Explanation of Other Options:

Option B) Proliferation of cells in a foreign site: Describes a choristoma, not a hamartoma. A choristoma is normal tissue located in an abnormal (ectopic) location.

Option C) Malignant proliferation of native tissue: This defines a carcinoma or sarcoma, depending on the cell origin. Hamartomas are benign, not malignant.

Option D) Acquired dysplasia: Dysplasia refers to abnormal cellular growth and maturation, often a precursor to malignancy, but it does not describe a hamartoma.

Reference:

Robbins and Kumar, Basic Pathology, 11th Edition, Page 188

question_text: Following statements are true for defining Dysplasia EXCEPT:
option_a: Pleomorphism and nucleomegaly with high N: C ratio
option_d: Increased mitosis, frequent at abnormal locations(other than basal)
explanation:
• Dysplastic epithelium is recognized by a loss in the uniformity of individual cells and in their architectural orientation.
  • Dysplastic cells exhibit considerable pleomorphism and often possess abnormally large, hyperchromatic nuclei.
  • Mitotic figures are more abundant than usual and frequently appear in abnormal locations within the epithelium.
  • In dysplastic stratified squamous epithelium, mitoses are not confined to the basal layers, where they normally occur, but may be seen throughout the epithelium.
  • In addition, there is considerable architectural anarchy.
  • For example, the usual progressive maturation of tall cells in the basal layer to flattened squames on the surface may be lost and replaced by a disordered hodgepodge of dark basal-appearing cells.
  • When dysplastic changes are severe and involve the entire thickness of the epithelium, the lesion is referred to as carcinoma in situ, a preinvasive stage of cancer.

Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10th ed, Pg: 194.
