question_text: A 54-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis complaints of weakness and fatigue. She states that her stools have recently become black after taking a new nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). Gastroscopy shows numerous superficial, bleeding mucosal defects. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
(a) Acute hemorrhagic gastritis is characterized by necrosis of the mucosa and is commonly associated with the intake of aspirin, other NSAIDs, alcohol, or ischemic injury. The factor common to all forms of acute hemorrhagic gastritis is thought to be the breakdown of the mucosal barrier, which permits acid induced injury. Mucosal injury causes bleeding from superficial erosions. Defects in the mucosa may extend into the deeper tissues to form an ulcer. The necrosis is accompanied by an acute inflammatory response and hemorrhage, which may be severe enough to result in exsanguination and hypovolemic shock.

question_text: Following figure demonstrates A Masson trichrome preparation showing complete replacement of virtually all glomeruli by blue-staining collagen. What can be the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• It is a case of chronic glomerulonephritis. Classically, the kidneys are symmetrically contracted, and their surfaces are red-brown and diffusely granular when the underlying disorder affects blood vessels or glomeruli.
  • Kidneys damaged by chronic pyelonephritis are typically unevenly involved and have deep scars. Microscopically, the feature common to all cases is advanced scarring of the glomeruli, sometimes to the point of complete sclerosis.This obliteration of the glomeruli is the end point of many diseases, and it is impossible to ascertain from such kidneys the nature of the initial lesion. There also is marked interstitial fibrosis, associated with atrophy and dropout of many of the tubules in the cortex, and diminution and loss of portions of the peritubular capillary network.
  • The small- and medium-sized arteries frequently are thick-walled, with narrowed lumina, secondary to hypertension. Lymphocytic (and, rarely, plasma cell) infiltrates are present in the fibrotic interstitial tissue.
  • As damage to all structures progresses, it may become difficult to ascertain whether the primary lesion was glomerular, vascular, tubular, or interstitial. Such markedly damaged kidneys have been designated end-stage kidneys.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th edition, Page- 573

question_text: Which of the following glomerular lesion is seen in reflux nephropathy?
explanation:
• Chronic Reflux-Associated Pyelonephritis (Reflux Nephropathy):Chronic reflux-associated pyelonephritis is the most common cause of chronic pyelonephritis. It results from superimposition of a UTI on congenital vesicoureteral reflux and intrarenal reflux. Both the reflux and the attendant renal damage may be unilateral or bilateral, the latter potentially leading to chronic renal insufficiency.
  • One or both kidneys may be involved, either diffusely or in patches. Even when involvement is bilateral, the kidneys are not equally damaged and therefore are not equally contracted. This uneven scarring is useful in differentiating chronic pyelonephritis from the more symmetrically contracted kidneys associated with vascular sclerosis (often referred to as benign nephrosclerosis) and chronic GN.
  • The hallmark of chronic pyelonephritis is scarring involving the pelvis or calyces, or both, leading to papillary blunting and marked calyceal deformities.

Focal segmental glomerular sclerosis (fsgs) is a frequently encountered cause of nephrotic syndrome, accounting for 40% of cases in adults and 20% in children. [1] in fsgs, some (not all) glomeruli are sclerosed (focal), and each involved glomerulus is only partially affected (segmental).

Fsgs occurs in following settings:

  • As a primary disease( idiopathic fsgs)
  • In association with other known conditions, such as hiv infection, heroin addiction, sickle cell disease,and morbid obesity
  • As secondary event,reflecting scarring of previously active necrotizing lesions,in cases of focal glomerulonephritis( ig a nephropathy)
  • As a component of adaptive response to loss of renal tissue ( renal ablation),whether from congenital anomalies(unilateral agensis or renal dyspalsia) or aquired causes (reflux nephropathy) , or advancing stages of other renal disorders ,such as hypertensive nephropathy.
  • In uncommon inherited forms of nephrotic syndrome where the disease may be caused by mutations in genes that encodes protiens localized to the slit diaphragm ,e.g; podocin , α actinin 4, and trpc6.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th edition, Page- 566

question_text: A 24-year-old man presented with a 4-month history of progressive swelling in his ankles and abdomen. Urinalysis shows heavy proteinuria (>4 g per 24 hours) but no evidence of inflammatory cells or RBCs. Laboratory studies reveal hyperlipidemia and hypoalbuminemia. Serum creatinine level is normal. The patient responds well to treatment with corticosteroids, but edema and proteinuria recur the following year. The steroid treatment is repeated with the same results. Upon the third recurrence of edema and proteinuria, the patient becomes steroid resistant. A renal biopsy is shown in the image. All of following statements are true regarding the diagnosis; except:
option_a: Light microscopy shows focal and segmental sclerosis of the glomeruli
option_b: Sclerotic region shows increase matrix and collapse of capillary
option_c: Immunofluorescence study shows deposition of IgG, IgA and C3 in sclerotic area and/or in mesangium
option_d: Electron microscopy shows diffuse effacement of foot process in sclerotic and nonsclerotic area
explanation:
• By light microscopy, the focal and segmental lesions may involve only a minority of the glomeruli and may be missed, if the biopsy specimen contains an insufficient number of glomeruli.
  • In the sclerotic segments, there is collapse of capillary loops, increase in matrix, and segmental deposition of plasma proteins along the capillary wall (hyalinosis), which may become so pronounced as to occlude capillary lumens.
  • By immunofluorescence microscopy, IgM and C3 may be present in the sclerotic areas and/or in the mesangium.
  • On electron microscopy, both sclerotic and nonsclerotic areas show diffuse effacement of foot processes, and there may also be focal detachment of the epithelial cells and denudation of the underlying GBM.

question_text: A 55-year-old man with a poorly controlled chronic medical condition suddenly loses consciousness. He is found to be deeply comatose, and a CT scan reveals a large intracerebral bleed. The gross appearance of the brain at autopsy is shown in the image below. What is the most common underlying cause for such a lesion?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The image shows a large, destructive, intraparenchymal hemorrhage located deep within the cerebral hemisphere, in the region of the basal ganglia. This type of spontaneous deep intracerebral bleed is known as a hypertensive hemorrhage.
  • Chronic systemic hypertension is the single most common cause. It leads to a condition called hyaline arteriolosclerosis, which weakens the walls of the small, penetrating arteries that supply the basal ganglia, thalamus, and pons (e.g., the lenticulostriate arteries).
  • These weakened vessels are prone to rupture, leading to a sudden and catastrophic hemorrhage directly into the brain parenchyma.

Explanation of Other Options:

Chronic alcoholism (Option A): Chronic alcoholism is more commonly associated with an increased risk of traumatic hemorrhages (e.g., subdural hematomas from falls) or hemorrhage related to coagulopathy from liver disease, not spontaneous deep parenchymal bleeds of this type.

Metastatic carcinoma (Option B): While some metastases are prone to hemorrhage (e.g., melanoma, RCC, choriocarcinoma), they are typically multiple and located at the gray-white junction, not as a single massive bleed in the basal ganglia.

Multiple sclerosis (Option C): Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune demyelinating disease. Its characteristic lesions are white matter plaques, which do not bleed.

Key Takeaways:

The location of a spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage is a strong clue to its underlying etiology:

  • Deep Gray Matter (Basal Ganglia, Thalamus), Pons, Cerebellum: Most common cause is Hypertension.
  • Lobar (Superficial, at Gray-White Junction): Most common cause in the elderly is Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy. Can also be from AVMs or hemorrhagic metastases.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Chapter 28, Page 1257.

question_text: Ground glass appearance is associated with which of the following hepatitis viruses?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ground glass appearance is associated with chronic hepatitis B virus.

The general morphologic features of viral hepatitis are described below.

Acute viral hepatitis:

  • The liver can appear normal, enlarged (due to inflammation), or shrunken in cases of acute liver failure with massive necros
  • Microscopically, there is a portal and lobular inflammatory infiltrate, mainly lymphocytes, with plasma cells and eosinophils.
  • Hepatocyte damage occurs via necrosis or apoptosis, often with pigmented macrophages cleaning up debris.
  • Severe cases may show confluent necrosis progressing to panlobular or bridging necrosis, sometimes leading to liver failure.

Chronic viral hepatitis:

  • Over time, fibrosis increases, progressing from portal and periportal fibrosis to bridging fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis.
  • The key microscopic feature is portal lymphocytic or lymphoplasmacytic inflammation with fibrosis. Inflammatory cells may cross the limiting plate, causing interface activitywith hepatocyte injury.
  • Distinctive features in specific types:
    • Hepatitis B: Hepatocytes may show a 'ground-glass' appearance due to swollen endoplasmic reticulum filled with HBsAg as shown below
    • Hepatitis C: Shows lymphoid aggregatesor follicles in portal tracts, often with steatosis (especially with genotype 3).
    • Bile duct injury: Can occur in hepatitis C, mimicking biliary disease, but usually focal.
  • Liver biopsy:
    Commonly used to confirm chronic hepatitis, assess inflammatory grade, and stage fibrosis. Staging helps guide therapy.

question_text: A 45-year-old man with a long-standing history of chronic inflammation presents with fatigue, pallor, and weakness. Laboratory studies show microcytic hypochromic anaemia. Further workup indicates impaired iron metabolism due to cytokine-mediated inhibition of ferroportin. Which cytokine is most likely responsible for this effect?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • This patient's features are consistent with anaemia of chronic disease (ACD), characterised by microcytic hypochromic anaemia due to disrupted iron metabolism.
  • The key cytokine involved is Interleukin-6 (IL-6), which plays a central role in the pathogenesis of ACD. I
  • n chronic inflammation, IL-6 stimulates the liver to produce hepcidin(HEPatic bacterioCIDal proteIN), a peptide that regulates iron balance.
  • Hepcidin binds to ferroportin, the iron exporter on enterocytes and macrophages, leading to:
  • Reduced iron absorption from the gut.
  • Decreased serum iron and transferrin saturation.
  • Inhibition of iron release from ferritin stores → increased ferritin levels.
  • Decreased total iron-binding capacity (TIBC).

Explanation of other options:

IL-1 (Option A): Important in systemic inflammation, but does not directly regulate hepcidin or ferroportin.

IFN-γ (Option C): Produced by Th1 cells; causes immune-mediated stem cell damage, leading to aplastic anaemia.

TNF-α (Option D): A strong pro-inflammatory cytokine, but it does not directly control ferroportin activity like IL-6 does.

question_text: Macrophages play an important role in phagocytosis and chronic inflammation. Which of the following cells perform the same function in the liver?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Kupffer cells are specialised macrophages located within the liver sinusoids.
  • They perform phagocytosis, removing pathogens, damaged cells, and cellular debris from the bloodstream.
  • Kupffer cells regulate immune responses and contribute to chronic inflammation when needed.
  • Functionally, they are the liver equivalent of macrophages, performing innate immune surveillance and debris clearance.

Explanation of Other Options:

Hepatocytes (Option A) are the main functional cells of the liver responsible for various metabolic functions, such as detoxification, synthesis of proteins, and storage of nutrients. While hepatocytes are involved in many liver functions, they do not primarily perform phagocytosis and chronic inflammation.

Merkel cells (Option B) are specialised cells found in the skin and are involved in the sensation of touch and tactile discrimination. They are not present in the liver or involved in phagocytosis or chronic inflammation.

Sinusoidal cells (Option C) refer to the cells lining the sinusoids in the liver, which are specialised blood vessels.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: What is the TYPE OF STONE IN Chronic cholecystitis?
explanation:
Bile is comprised of bile salts, acids and cholesterol. The bile salts and acids are usually enough to break down the cholesterol; however, in those with gallbladder disease this is not the case.

In these people, the cholesterol is left to sit in the gallbladder and solidify because the bile itself does not contain enough bile salts to break it down.

LOOK AT OTHER STONES ALSO

Pigmented stones

Pigment stones are made from a combination of calcium salts and bilirubin. Bilirubin is the end result of the liver breaking down hemoglobin (red blood cells). These stones are typically seen in developing countries and can be the result of several different risk factors including:

  • Hemolytic anemias (like sickle-cell disease or hereditary spherocytosis)
  • Biliary tract infections
  • Prolonged use of proton-pump inhibitors
  • Erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP)

Mixed Stones

  • This type of stone is typically made up of anywhere from 20 to 80 percent cholesterol and bile pigments such as calcium carbonate, palmitate phosphate and bilirubin. Because mixed stones contain a fair amount of calcium, they can easily be seen on x-rays.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th edition, Page-674

question_text: Which of the following interventions is linked to a longer lifespan?
option_d: Pharmacological intervention with proton pump inhibitors
explanation:
Explanation:

Of the options provided, caloric restriction is the best-documented intervention linked to extending lifespan.

Explanations of other options:

Regular moderate exercise for 30 min (Option A): It offers several health benefits, including enhanced cardiovascular function, improved metabolism, and a lower risk of chronic illnesses. However, unlike caloric restriction, its impact on directly extending lifespan is less well established, though it does support a longer health span.

Decrease stress (Option B): Chronic stress leads to multiple harmful health outcomes that can shorten lifespan. While stress management strategies may enhance overall health and potentially extend longevity, the connection is more indirect and inconsistent.

Pharmacological intervention with proton pump inhibitors (Option D): Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) lower stomach acid and are used in managing GERD and peptic ulcers. Although effective for symptom control, they do not contribute to increased lifespan

question_text: A 35-year-old female on OCPs presented with intermittent abdominal pain and intermittent diarrhea. Appearance of intestine is an image given below. Endoscopy showed ileum involvement with rectal sparing. Which of the following feature is specific to given disease?
explanation:
Why (Choice A) Transmural Involvement is the Best Answer:

  • It is the defining histological feature of Crohn's disease.
  • It explains key complications of Crohn's, such as fistulas, strictures, and abscess formation, which occur due to full-thickness inflammation.
  • Involvement of the ileum with rectal sparing is another classical feature of Crohn's, making transmural involvement the best choice.

Why the Other Options Are Incorrect:

  • (Choice B) Presence of Polyps
    • While inflammatory polyps (pseudopolyps) can be seen in both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, they are not a distinguishing feature.
    • Pseudopolyps result from regenerating mucosa in areas of chronic inflammation but are more commonly associated with ulcerative colitis.
  • (Choice C) Mucosal Edema
    • Mucosal edema occurs in many inflammatory conditions of the gut, including both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.
    • Since it is not exclusive to Crohn's, it cannot be used as a diagnostic hallmark.
  • (Choice D) Lymphocyte Infiltrate
    • Lymphocytic infiltration is a general histopathological feature of inflammation, seen in both Crohn's and ulcerative colitis.
    • Crohn's disease typically shows granulomatous inflammation, which is more specific, while ulcerative colitis shows crypt abscesses.

Key takeaway:

Transmural inflammation is the defining characteristic of Crohn's disease.

The ileum involvement with rectal sparing also points strongly towards Crohn's disease.

Based on the above histopathological findings, what is your probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Microscopic polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis that generally affects capillaries as well as small arterioles and venules. Unlike PAN, all lesions of microscopic polyangiitis tend to be of the same age in any given patient, suggesting a single episode of antibody or immune complex deposition. It is also called hypersensitivity vasculitis or leukocytoclastic vasculitis. The skin, mucous membranes, lungs, brain, heart, gastrointestinal tract, kidneys, and muscle all can be involved. Most cases are associated with MPO-ANCA positivity. Microscopic polyangiitis is characterized by segmental fibrinoid necrosis of the media with focal transmural necrotizing lesions; granulomatous inflammation is absent.

question_text: A patient presents with a 1 month history of cough, chest pain, and dyspnea. Imaging reveals bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Biopsy of a mediastinal lymph node shows non caseating granulomas containing stellate inclusions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis based on the given clinical features of cough, dyspnea, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy along with biopsy revealing stellate inclusion bodies and non-caseating granulomas is sarcoidosis.

  • Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disorder that can affect multiple organs, most frequently the lungs, eyes, and skin, with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy or parenchymal lung disease present in 90% of cases.
  • It often occurs in adults under 40, with higher prevalence in women, and is characterised pathologically by well-formed non-necrotising granulomas composed of epithelioid macrophages and giant cells.
  • These sometimes contain stellate inclusions known as asteroid bodies, as shown below. Another finding commonly seen is laminated concretions composed of calcium and proteins called Schaumann bodies.
  • Immunologic abnormalities include a predominance of CD4+ T cells with elevated Th1 cytokines, increased local cytokine production, and impaired dendritic cell function, leading to granuloma formation.
  • The lungs are a frequent site of involvement, often showing granulomas along lymphatics near bronchi and blood vessels, with possible coalescence into small palpable nodules in advanced disease. Varying stages of fibrosis and hyalinization may be present.
  • Lymph node involvement is seen in almost all cases, especially in the hilar and mediastinal regions, with nodes appearing enlarged and discrete, sometimes calcified.
  • Skin lesions appear in a quarter of patients, ranging from discrete nodules to erythematous plaques or erythema nodosum.
  • Ocular involvement includes iritis or iridocyclitis, which may lead to glaucoma or vision loss, and is often associated with lacrimal gland inflammation and sicca syndrome.
  • Bilateral salivary gland involvement produces Mikulicz syndrome.

Explanation of other options:

Tuberculosis (Option A): Histologically, tuberculosis is characterised by granulomatous inflammation forming predominantly caseating tubercles. These granulomas are composed of a fibroblastic rim with lymphocytes and often contain multinucleated giant cells. Progressive primary tuberculosis frequently mimics acute bacterial pneumonia, presenting with lobar consolidation, enlargement of hilar lymph nodes, and accumulation of pleural fluid.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Option C): Morphologically, granulomatosis with polyangiitis shows upper respiratory tract lesions ranging from sinusitis with mucosal granulomas to ulcerative lesions, often featuring geographic necrosis with vasculitis, necrotising granulomas in the lungs, and renal involvement from focal segmental necrotising glomerulonephritis to crescentic glomerulonephritis. Clinically, it often affects middle-aged men and presents with bilateral pneumonitis, chronic sinusitis, mucosal ulcerations, and renal disease, alongside systemic symptoms such as rash, myalgia, and fever.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (Option D): In hypersensitivity pneumonitis, histological features vary with disease stage. Acute lesions show alveolar damage shortly after antigen exposure, while subacute lesions are bronchiolocentric with interstitial pneumonitis composed of lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages, and non-necrotising granulomas.  Chronic cases reveal interstitial fibrosis, fibroblastic foci, honeycombing, and obliterative bronchiolitis. Clinically, acute episodes present with fever, dyspnea, cough, and leukocytosis within hours of exposure, recurring with re-exposure, whereas prolonged antigen contact can lead to chronic progressive fibrosis, dyspnea, and cyanosis, resembling other chronic interstitial lung diseases.

question_text: A 45-year-old female complains of chronic constipation and anovulatory cycles for the last 6 months. Her vital signs are normal. Physical examination reveals peripheral edema. USG neck examination shows diffusely enlarged thyroid gland. Laboratory investigations shows abnormally low serum levels of T3 and T4. Patient underwent thyroidectomy excised histopathological image of the specimen is shown below. Based on the above findings, what is the appropriate diagnosis?
explanation:
(a) This will show variable sized and dilated colloid filled spaces.

(b) There will be presence of granuloma.

(c) There is extensive infiltration of the parenchyma by a mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate containing small lymphocytes, plasma cells, and well-developed germinal centers. The thyroid follicles are atrophic and are lined in many areas by epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm, termed Hürthle cells, which represent a metaplastic response of the normally low cuboidal follicular epithelium to chronic injury. All of these features are suggestive of autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis.

(d) There should be monotonous uniform infiltration by atypical lymphocytes.

Reference: Robbins 10th Ed pg 1080

question_text: A 49 year old male, chronic smoker and alcoholic came with complaints over epigastric region radiating to back associated with pale-colored stools. Pain usually increases or aggravated by eating or alcohol consumption. CT abdomen done as shown below. Most common cause of the condition discussed above is
explanation:
The patient's symptoms, including epigastric pain radiating to the back, pale-colored stools (steatorrhea), and worsening with food or alcohol consumption, along with the CT findings, strongly suggest chronic pancreatitis.

Most Common Cause: Alcohol (Choice A)

  • Chronic alcohol consumption is the leading cause of chronic pancreatitis (70-80% of cases).
  • Alcohol induces repeated pancreatic injury, leading to progressive inflammation, fibrosis, and loss of exocrine function.
  • Calcifications in the pancreas, seen on CT imaging, are characteristic of chronic alcoholic pancreatitis.

Incorrect choices explanation :

  • (Choice B) Gallstones:
    • Gallstone disease is a major cause of acute pancreatitis, not chronic pancreatitis.
    • Chronic pancreatitis due to gallstones is less common and usually occurs in patients with recurrent acute pancreatitis episodes.
  • (Choice C) Trauma:
    • Trauma can cause acute pancreatitis, but chronic pancreatitis from trauma is rare and usually seen in severe pancreatic injuries.
  • (Choice D) Smoking:
    • Smoking is a risk factor but is not the most common cause.
    • It accelerates the progression of chronic pancreatitis in alcoholics but is not an independent leading cause.

Key takeaway:

  • Chronic, progressive epigastric pain that worsens with meals and alcohol.
  • Malabsorption (steatorrhea, weight loss) due to pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.
  • Diabetes mellitus (late-stage complication due to endocrine dysfunction).
  • Pancreatic calcifications on CT scan or X-ray (a hallmark of chronic disease).

question_text: Which of the following is involved in the development of rheumatoid arthritis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks healthy joint tissues.
  • In genetically susceptible individuals, exposure to specific antigens activates CD4+ T-cells.
  • These T-cells release inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, and interferon-γ, which in turn activate endothelial cells, B-cells, and macrophages.
  • This immune cascade leads to persistent inflammation, joint damage, and the characteristic deformities of RA.

Explanation of other options:

IgE-mediated (Option A): Primarily seen in allergic reactions, not in RA.

Defective cellular and humoral immunity (Option B): RA involves targeted autoimmunity rather than a general immune defect.

Chronic microbial infections (Option D): May trigger or worsen autoimmune responses but are not the primary cause of RA.

question_text: A patient presents with neck swelling. The excision biopsy finding is given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The histopathological image shows signs of chronic granulomatous inflammation, with caseous necrosis (pink areas) and Langerhans giant cells, all suggesting Tuberculosis (TB), a bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Tuberculosis

It can be classified into the following types: Primary and secondary.

Primary tuberculosis

  • It develops in a previously unexposed and, therefore, unsensitised person.
  • The primary organ involved is mostly the lungs.
  • Location:
    • Sub-pleural region.
    • Lower part of the upper lobe & upper part of the lower lobe.
  • Ghon's focus: Grey-white area of inflammation with consolidation.
  • Ghon's complex: Ghon's focus + inflamed regional lymph nodes.
  • Histology: Granulomatous inflammatory reaction with both caseating and non-caseating tubercles.
  • Simon's focus: Occult hematogenous dissemination to the apex of the lung.
  • Fate:
    • 95% of the cases are controlled by immunity, calcified, healed lesions and hilar lymph nodes (Ranke complex).
    • 5% of the cases are progressive (Progressive primary TB).
      • Resembles acute bacterial pneumonia.
      • Lymphohematogenous dissemination may cause tuberculous meningitis and/or miliary TB.

Secondary tuberculosis

  • It arises in a previously sensitised host.
  • It may follow shortly after primary tuberculosis, but more commonly, it appears months to years after the initial infection, usually when the host resistance is weakened.
  • The apical and posterior lobe segments are involved due to high O2 concentration (Puhl's focus).
  • The infraclavicular lesion is called Assman's focus.
  • Regional lymph node involvement is late.
  • Cavitation occurs readily with the erosion of the cavities into an airway.
  • Histology: Active lesions show coalescent tubercles with central caseation (Caseous necrosis).

Disseminated TB: Spread to other organs.

The images below show the aseous necrosis seen in TB.


Explanation of other options:

Sarcoidosis (Option A): An inflammatory condition marked by the development of granulomas. While the exact cause remains unknown, it is thought to result from an abnormal immune response, potentially triggered by genetic and environmental factors. Histologically, it presents with non-caseating granuloma or naked granuloma (lymphocytic collar absent).

Histoplasmosis (Option C): Histoplasmosis is a fungal infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum. Its pathogenesis is unclear but clinically resembles tuberculosis with primary pulmonary involvement, chronic lung disease, extrapulmonary spread, and widespread infection in immunocompromised individuals. Histologically, granulomas may necrose, consolidate, and later calcify with a tree-bark appearance.

Brucellosis (Option D): A bacterial infection caused by Brucella, which is transmitted from animals to humans. Symptoms include fever, fatigue, joint pain, and abdominal pain. It can lead to complications like osteoarticular infections. Treatment involves antibiotics, typically doxycycline and rifampin. It does not show caseous necrosis and Langerhans giant cells.

question_text:
True about Dentigerous cyst:
A. Arises in relation to unerupted teeth
B. It most commonly encroaches maxillary antrum
C. Mandibular third molar is common site

explanation:
• Dentigerous cyst is defined as a cyst that originates around the crown of an unerupted tooth and is thought to be the result of fluid accumulation between the developing tooth and the dental follicle.
  • Radiographically, these are unilocular lesions most of them associated with impacted third molar (wisdom) teeth. Histologically, they are lined by a thin layer of stratified squamous epithelium. Often, there is a dense chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate in the connective tissue stroma.

question_text: All of the following are true about TGF-beta except?
option_a: Involved in the development of fibrosis in lung, liver and kidneys that follows chronic inflammation
option_b: Stimulates fibroblast migration and proliferation, increased synthesis of collagen and fibronectin
option_c: Increased degradation of ECM due to inhibition of metalloproteinases
option_d: Anti-inflammatory cytokine, limits and terminates inflammatory responses
explanation:
• TGF- beta causes decreased degradation of ECM due to inhibition of metalloproteinases.
  • Transforming growth factor(TGF) is the most important cytokine for the synthesis and deposition of connective tissue proteins.
  • Produced by most of the cells in granulation tissue, including alternatively activated
  • Stimulates fibroblast migration and proliferation, increased synthesis of collagen and fibronectin and decreased degradation of ECM due to inhibition of metalloproteinases.
  • TGF is involved in the development of fibrosis in lung, liver and kidneys that follow chronic inflammation - liver cirrhosis, systemic sclerosis(scleroderma), fibrosing diseases of the lung(idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, pneumoconioses and drug radiation-induced pulmonary fibrosis), end-stage kidney disease and constrictive pericarditis.
  • TGF is also an anti-inflammatory cytokine that serves to limit and terminate inflammatory responses by inhibiting lymphocyte proliferation and the activity of other leukocytes.

question_text: Which substance acts as a key mediator in chronic inflammation?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • TGF-β (Transforming Growth Factor-beta)is a central mediator in chronic inflammation.
  • While IL-1and TNF-α are important in initiating and sustaining acute inflammation, TGF-β is more involved in the chronic phase, where it promotes tissue repair, fibrosis, and immune regulation.
  • It drives fibrosisby stimulating extracellular matrix deposition.
  • It modulates immune responses, helping control excessive inflammation.
  • It contributes to tissue regenerationand maintenance of immune homeostasis.

Explanation of other options:

IL-1 (Option A): Primarily involved in the acute inflammatory response and fever induction.

TNF-α (Option B): Key cytokine in acute and subacute inflammation, promoting leukocyte recruitment and systemic effects, but not the dominant mediator in chronic fibrosis.

None (Option D): Incorrect, since TGF-β clearly plays a role.

question_text: Multiple sinuses from infection of great toe is mainly caused by: September 2007
explanation: Ans. B: Actinomycetes Mycetoma is a chronic localized granulomatous inflammatory lesion common in the tropics and sub-tropics. Multiple siAuses, soft tissue swelling and discharge of coloured granules characterize a mycetoma foot. Chronic sinuses discharging granules are caused by (1) Eumycetes (true fungi), (2) Schizomycetes, which includes Actinomycosis (aerobic higher filamentous bacteria) and Botryomycosis (bacterial infection). - Actinomycosis is often caused by Actinomadura or Nocardia species wherein it gains entry after penetrating trauma (splinter, gravel or thorn prick). Young males are commonly affected and 75% of the lesions occur in the lower limbs. The disease slowly progresses from a nodule to multiple sinuses discharging coloured granules. Involvement of bone is late following dermal and soft tissue spread. - Botryomycosis (a misnomer), a chronic suppurative infection is caused by bacteria involving skin or viscera . This rare condition mimics a deep mycotic infection and is often caused by mimics a deep mycotic infection and is often caused by Staphylococcus or Pseudomonas species of bacteria. The feet and hands are commonly affected and penetrating trauma may be a predisposing factor. It usually presents as a nodule, sinus or ulcer, which is initially localized. The diagnosis of actinomycosis is based on clinical findings, demonstration of characteristic granules and culture of the organism from a deep tissue biopsy. Immunological studies (counter immuno electrophoresis and ELISA) are also used. Botryomycosis is diagnosed based on a positive gram's stain and culture; negative fungal cultures and demonstration of the characteristic botryomycotic granules at histopathology from a deep biopsy. In endemic areas, subcutaneous swelling with sinuses should be considered as mycetoma unless proved otherwise. The differential diagnosis includes chronic osteomyelitis, tuberculosis and chronic abscesses.

question_text: A 48-year-old male patient presented with symptoms of sinusitis, nasopharyngeal ulcer and chronic cough. Laboratory findings revealed deranged kidney function test and PR3-ANCA positivity. Urine analysis shows presence of proteinuria and RBCs. Chest X-ray shows bilateral nodular lesions in lung. A transbronchial lung biopsy specimen shows a necrotizing inflammatory process involving the small peripheral pulmonary arteries and arterioles. Based on the above findings, what is your probable diagnosis?
explanation:
(a) Polyarteritis nodosa most often involves small muscular arteries, and sometimes veins. It causes necrosis and microaneurysm formation, followed by scarring and vascular occlusion, mainly in the kidney, gastrointestinal tract, and skin of young to middle aged adults.

(b) Antineutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibody (ANCA) associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis) is a form of hypersensitivity reaction to an unknown antigen characterized by necrotizing granulomatous inflammation that typically involves small to medium- sized vessels, although many organ sites may be affected. Pulmonary and renal involvement can be life-threatening. C-ANCAs (antibodies mainly directed against neutrophil proteinase 3) are found in more than 90% of cases.

(c) Kaposi sarcoma can produce plaque like to nodular masses that are composed of irregular vascular spaces lined by atypical-appearing endothelial cells; skin involvement is most common, but visceral organ involvement can occur.

(d) Granuloma pyogenicum is an inflammatory response that can produce a nodular mass, often on the gingiva or the skin.

Reference: Robbins 10th Ed pg 514

question_text: A 34-year-old woman presented with fever, migratory arthritis of lower large joints, tachycardia. Murmur is pansystolic. On echo mitral regurgitation is present. The biopsy shows the following, identify:
explanation:
During acute RF, focal inflammatory lesions are found in various tissues. Distinctive lesions in the heart-called Aschoff bodies-are composed of foci of T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells, and plump activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells.

These macrophages have abundant cytoplasm and central round to ovoid nuclei (occasionally binucleate) in which the chromatin condenses into a central, slender, wavy ribbon (hence the designation "caterpillar cells").

Reference: Robin's basic pathology 10th edition, pg 561

question_text: 34-year-old male presents weak pulses in upper limbs, BP 90/60 mm Hg, retinal hemorrhages present, On biopsy, Granulomatous inflammation, replete with giant cells and patchy medial necrosis, is seen. Diagnosis
explanation:
Takayasu arteritis classically involves the aortic arch. In a third of patients, it also affects the remainder of the aorta and its branches, with pulmonary artery involvement in half of cases; coronary and renal arteries may be similarly affected. There is irregular thickening of the vessel wall with intimal hyperplasia; when the aortic arch is involved, the great vessel lumens can be markedly narrowed or even obliterated

Such narrowing explains the weakness of the peripheral pulses. Histologically the changes range from adventitial mononuclear infiltrates with perivascular cuffing of the vasa vasorum to intense mononuclear inflammation in the media. Granulomatous inflammation, replete with giant cells and patchy medial necrosis, is also seen. The histology is essentially indistinguishable from giant cell (temporal) arteritis. As the disease progresses, collagenous scarring, with admixed chronic inflammatory infiltrates, occurs in all three layers of the vessel wall. Occasionally, aortic root involvement causes dilation and aortic valve insufficiency.

Reference: Robin's basic pathology 10th edition, pg 512

question_text: Granulomatous condition causing hypercalcemia include all of the following, except:

Sarcoidosis, Tuberculosis (TB) and Berylliosis are typical Granulomatous disorders causing hypercalcemia. Granulomatous causes of Hypercalcemia Infective Causes Tuberculosis Berylliosis Histoplasmosis Coccidoimycosis Pneumocystis Granulomatous Leprosy Cat-Scratch Disease  Non-Infective Cause Sarcoidosis (Most common) Wegner's Granulomatosis Inflammatory Bowel Disease Histiocytosis-X Foreign body Granulomas Almost every single disease associated with Granuloma formation has been reported to cause Hypercalcemia

question_text: A 59-year-old male patient presented with persistent and sever cough with foul smelling expectorant since 3 weeks, sometime associated with hemoptysis, dyspnea along with orthopnea. Chest X-ray was done which shows opacities in bilateral lower lobe and also prominent vascular marking. Which one of the following statements is true regarding the disease?
option_a: Grossly there is airway dilation sometimes up to 4 times
option_b: There is ulceration, squamous metaplasia with acute and chronic inflammatory infiltrate
option_c: Long-standing may form peribronchial fibrosis and bronchial wall leading to obstruction
explanation:
Classical history of bronchiectasis

(a) Bronchiectasis usually affects the lower lobes bilaterally, particularly air passages that are vertical, and is most severe in the more distal bronchi and bronchioles. The airways are dilated, sometimes up to four times normal size.

(b) The histologic findings vary with the activity and chronicity of the disease. In the full-blown, active case there is an intense acute and chronic inflammatory exudation within the walls of the bronchi and bronchioles, associated with desquamation of the lining epithelium and extensive ulceration.

(c) Fibrosis of the bronchial and bronchiolar walls and peribronchiolar fibrosis develop in more chronic cases, leading to varying degrees of subtotal or total obliteration of bronchiolar lumens

Reference: Robbins 10th Ed, pg 687

question_text: A 57-year-old man with a history of recurrent chest infections presents with a chronic, productive cough yielding foul-smelling sputum. The gross pathology of his lung at autopsy is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• The hallmark clinical symptom of bronchiectasis is a chronic, productive cough with a large volume of purulent and often foul-smelling sputum. Hemoptysis is also a common feature.
  • The image displays the characteristic gross findings of severe bronchiectasis. The cut surface of the lung shows markedly and permanently dilated bronchi and bronchioles, which can be followed all the way to the pleural surface. These dilated airways are typically filled with mucopurulent secretions and appear as cystic spaces.
  • Bronchiectasis is a condition of permanent, abnormal dilation of the airways due to the destruction of the muscular and elastic components of their walls, most commonly resulting from chronic necrotizing infections.

Explanation of Other Options:

Asthma (Option A): In fatal asthma, the lungs are overinflated, and the bronchi are occluded by thick mucus plugs, but there is no permanent, destructive dilation of the airway walls.

Emphysema (Option B): Emphysema involves the destructive enlargement of the airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles (the alveoli), not the bronchi themselves. Grossly, it appears as large, empty air sacs or bullae.

Small cell carcinoma (Option D): Small cell carcinoma is a central lung tumor that typically arises from the main bronchi and forms a perihilar mass. It would not cause the widespread, cystic dilation of the distal airways seen in the image.

Key Takeaways:

  • Bronchiectasis is a condition of permanent, irreversible dilation of the bronchi and bronchioles.
  • The key clinical symptom is a chronic cough with copious, foul-smelling, purulent sputum.
  • Grossly, the dilated airways can be seen extending to the pleural surface of the lung.

Reference:

Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page Number: 687.

question_text: A 56-year-old male with a 65-pack-per-year smoking history presents to his family physician for a check-up. He has not seen a doctor in 15 years. question_text: Laminated concretions of calcium and proteins seen in sarcoidosis. What are they known as?

question_text: A 21-year-old previously healthy man who owns a pet shop presents with a 14-day history of asymptomatic left submental swelling. The swelling was approximately 1 x 2 cm, non-tender, rubbery, and non fluctuant with limited mobility. The patient was prescribed 250 mg of amoxicillin 3 times a day for 7 days without appreciable effect. Upon histopathological examination, the given finding is seen. Identify the diagnosis?
explanation:
The patient's submental lymphadenopathy, history of pet shop ownership (likely exposure to cats), and lack of response to amoxicillin suggest Cat Scratch Disease (CSD), caused by Bartonella henselae, a gram-negative bacillus.

Incorrect Choices explanation :

  • (Choice A) Crohn's Disease
    • Crohn's primarily affects the gastrointestinal tract, not isolated lymph nodes.
    • Non-caseating granulomas are present in Crohn’s, but there is no necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with stellate abscesses, which are characteristic of CSD.
  • (Choice B) Berylliosis
    • Occurs in industrial workers exposed to beryllium (e.g., aerospace, nuclear, electronics industries).
    • Non-caseating granulomas in the lungs, mimicking sarcoidosis.
    • No history of beryllium exposure in this patient.
  • (Choice D) Syphilis
    • Treponema pallidum infection, presenting with painless genital ulcers (primary syphilis) or generalized lymphadenopathy (secondary syphilis).
    • Histology shows plasma cell infiltrates, not necrotizing granulomas.
    • No sexual history or other syphilitic symptoms in this case.

Key takeaway:

  • Caused by Bartonella henselae, transmitted via scratches, bites, or flea exposure from cats.
  • Chronic lymphadenopathy (submandibular, axillary, cervical, or inguinal nodes) lasting weeks to months.
  • Lymph nodes are non-tender, rubbery, and firm, with possible necrosis and granuloma formation.
  • Histopathology shows necrotizing granulomas with stellate microabscesses (a hallmark feature).
  • Serology (IgG/IgM for Bartonella) or PCR confirms the diagnosis.

Ulcerative colitis (Option D) is a chronic inflammatory condition limited to the colon and rectum. It presents with bloody diarrhoea, tenesmus, and abdominal pain. No itchy skin lesions are associated with ulcerative colitis.

question_text: What is the tumour marker for a carcinoid tumour?
explanation:
Explanation:

The key tumour marker for carcinoid tumours is 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid), the main breakdown product of serotonin found in urine.

  • Origin: Carcinoid tumours arise from neuroendocrine (argentaffin) cells that produce serotonin and other vasoactive mediators such as bradykinin, histamine, prostaglandins, and kallikrein.
  • Typical sites: Most often the mid-gut (small intestine) with liver metastases, but they can also occur in the bronchi or ovaries.
  • Clinical manifestations:
    • Recurrent flushing and skin pruritus due to histamine release
    • Diarrhoea and abdominal cramps from excess serotonin
    • Wheezing or dyspnoea caused by bronchospasm
    • Pellagra-like symptoms (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia) due to niacin deficiency
    • Carcinoid heart disease, most commonly right-sided valvular lesions such as tricuspid regurgitation
  • Diagnostic tests:
    • 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA measurement is the primary investigation.
    • Serum serotonin and chromogranin A levels are often elevated.
    • Imaging with an octreoscan helps locate the primary tumour or metastases.

question_text: A 34-year-old woman presented with fever migratory arthritis of lower large joints, tachycardia, murmur is pansystolic. On echo mitral regurgitation is present. The biopsy shows the following?
explanation:
The histopathological image shows a collection of fibrinoid necrosis with surrounding inflammatory cells, including activated macrophages (Anitschkow cells) and multinucleated giant cells. This is characteristic of an Aschoff body, which is pathognomonic for rheumatic heart disease.

The clinical presentation of a 34-year-old woman with fever, migratory arthritis, tachycardia, pansystolic murmur, and mitral regurgitation is highly suggestive of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) leading to rheumatic heart disease (RHD).

  • (Choice A) Aschoff body (Correct Answer)
    • Found in rheumatic heart disease, particularly in myocarditis.
    • Composed of central fibrinoid necrosis, surrounding inflammatory cells, and characteristic Anitschkow cells (caterpillar cells).
    • Associated with rheumatic fever, which follows Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A strep) infection.

Incorrect choices explanation:

  • (Choice B) Granuloma annulare
    • A benign skin condition presenting as dermal palisading granulomas.
    • No association with cardiac pathology or rheumatic fever.
  • (Choice C) Granulomatous vasculitis
    • Seen in conditions like Giant cell arteritis or Wegener's granulomatosis (GPA).
    • Typically affects vessels, not myocardium.
  • (Choice D) Epithelioid granuloma
    • Seen in tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, and fungal infections.
    • Composed of epithelioid histiocytes and Langhans giant cells, which are absent in the given histology.

Key takeaway:

  • The histology, clinical features, and echocardiographic finding of mitral regurgitation strongly support acute rheumatic fever (ARF) with myocarditis, confirming the presence of an Aschoff body.
  • Correct answer: (Choice A) Aschoff body.

question_text: A 45-year-old patient with a history of chronic liver disease presents with nausea, vomiting, oedema, and ascites. On examination, liver function tests are markedly deranged, and evaluation confirms a diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma. The pathogenesis of this malignancy is most likely linked to:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in this patient with chronic liver disease is most strongly associated with aflatoxin exposure.
  • Aflatoxins are toxic metabolites produced by Aspergillus flavusand related fungi, which commonly contaminate improperly stored grains and nuts.
  • Aflatoxin B1is the most potent type and induces a characteristic mutation in the p53 tumour suppressor gene (codon 249, G→T transversion), promoting malignant transformation.

HCC typically arises in the background of cirrhosis, which can be due to:

  • Chronic alcohol intake
  • Chronic hepatitis B or C infection
  • Metabolic liver disorders
  • Non-alcoholic steatohepatitisAflatoxin exposure

Explanation of other options:

Benzol (Option A): Used in the petrochemical, rubber, paint, and printing industries, benzene exposure is linked to bone marrow suppression and haematological malignancies (e.g., AML) rather than hepatocellular carcinoma.

Arsenic (Option B): Chronic arsenic exposure, often from contaminated water, is associated with skin, lung, and bladder cancers. While it may cause liver injury, it is not a leading cause of HCC compared to aflatoxin.

Vinyl chloride (Option D): This compound is primarily linked to angiosarcoma of the liver, a rare vascular malignancy, rather than HCC.

question_text: A 12-year-old child presents with a persistent cough for 15 days. On examination, cervical lymphadenopathy is found. Biopsy of the lymph node is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical history (chronic cough, cervical lymphadenopathy) combined with the biopsy showing caseating granulomas (central necrosis surrounded by epithelioid macrophages and lymphocytes) strongly supports the diagnosis of Tuberculosis.

Types of granulomas and examples

Causes of granuloma formation

  • Infectious causes: TB, leprosy, syphilis, malaria (Durck's granuloma), cat scratch disease, lymphogranuloma venereum, Q fever.
  • Non-infectious causes: Sarcoidosis, Crohn's disease, giant cell arteritis, Churg-Strauss syndrome, berylliosis, foreign body reactions.

Explanation of other options:

Leprosy (Option B): May form granulomas, but not typically caseating; classically non-caseating.

Sarcoidosis (Option C): Produces non-caseating "naked" granulomas, not caseating ones.

Syphilis (Option D): Can cause granulomas, but tuberculosis is the prototype of caseating granulomas.

Key Takeaways:

  • Caseating granuloma = hallmark of tuberculosis.
  • Granulomas may be infectious or non-infectious.
  • Histology remains a gold standard clue in TB diagnosis.

question_text: Which of the following cells plays a key role in phagocytosis and chronic inflammation in the liver?
explanation:
Explanation for answer:

Kupffer cells: Specialised macrophages located in the liver sinusoids, essential for phagocytosisand managing chronic inflammation. They clear pathogens, cellular debris, and aged red blood cells as blood passes through the liver.

Explanation of other options:

Hepatocytes (Option A): Main functional cells of the liver responsible for metabolic activities, but they do not perform phagocytosis.

Ito cells (Option B) / Hepatic stellate cells: Found in the space of Disse between hepatocytes and sinusoidal endothelial cells. They store vitamin A and regulate sinusoidal blood flow. When the liver is injured, it transforms into myofibroblast-like cells, secretes TGF-β, and contributes to fibrosis by producing excess collagen.

Sinusoidal endothelial cells (Option C): Line the liver sinusoids and allow exchange of materials between blood and liver cells. Their fenestrated structure helps filter blood and regulate molecular movement, but they are not primary phagocytes.

question_text: Which of the following disorders presents with repeated catalase-positive infections?
explanation:
Explanation:

Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD) is characterised by increased susceptibility to recurrent infections caused by catalase-positive organisms.

  • Cause: Defect in NADPH oxidase, an enzyme complex in phagocytes.
  • Mechanism: Defect in NADPH oxidase leads to the inability to produce the reactive oxygen species (ROS) required to kill certain bacteria and fungi.
  • Clinical Presentation: Recurrent infections, particularly with catalase-positive organisms like Staphylococcus aureus, Aspergillus), granuloma formation.

Explanation of other options:

X-linked hypogammaglobinemia (Option A): Also known as X-linked Agammaglobulinemia (XLA) or Bruton's agammaglobulinemia, is a genetic disorder caused by mutations in the BTK gene on the X chromosome, leading to low immunoglobulin levels and impaired B cell development. It results in recurrent bacterial infections, but not specifically catalase-positive organisms.

SCID (Option B): Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is a genetic disorder that impacts both humoral and cell-mediated immunity, occurring in two forms: X-linked and autosomal recessive. Infants typically present with thrush, diaper rash, and failure to thrive, and some may develop Graft-Versus-Host Disease (GVHD) due to maternal T cells. Treatment includes hematopoietic stem cell transplantation or gene therapy.

Chediak Higashi Syndrome (Option D): An autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the LYST gene that leads to defective phagosome-lysosome fusion, neutropenia, and delayed microbial killing. Giant granules appear in leukocytes, and there are abnormalities in melanocytes (albinism), nerve cells (defects), and platelets (bleeding disorders).

question_text: A sandblasting worker develops cough and hemoptysis. Chest X-ray is suggestive of tuberculosis. Which occupational lung disease is strongly associated with this?
explanation:
Explanation:

Silicosis is the most common occupational lung disease, caused by inhalation of crystalline silica. It predisposes to tuberculosis due to impaired macrophage function.

Silicosis:

  • Cause:Inhaled crystalline silica (quartz, cristobalite, tridymite).
  • Pathogenesis:Silica → macrophage phagocytosis → inflammasome activation (IL-1, IL-18) → fibrosis.
  • Occupations at risk:Sandblasting, stone cutting, mining, foundry work.
  • Forms:
    • Acute:Heavy exposure, rapid onset, silico-tuberculosis, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis.
    • Chronic (simple/complicated):Decades of exposure, progressive fibrosis, dyspnea.
  • Morphology:Nodules in hilar nodes, upper lobes; hard collagenous scars; pleural thickening; eggshell calcification of lymph nodes.
  • Complications:Pulmonary TB, progressive massive fibrosis, lung cancer (↑ 2x).

Explanation of other options:

Asbestosis (Option A): This condition results from the inhalation of asbestos fibers. It primarily causes pulmonary fibrosis and is associated with an elevated risk of both lung carcinoma and mesothelioma. However, it does not have a direct correlation with tuberculosis.

Anthracosis (Option C): Also known as 'coal miner's lung,' this develops from the inhalation of coal dust. It may lead to chronic bronchitis or emphysema, but it is not directly associated with tuberculosis.

Siderosis (Option D): Caused by inhalation of iron oxide dust, commonly affecting workers such as welders. It can produce pulmonary fibrosis, but it does not substantially increase the likelihood of tuberculosis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Silicosis = commonest pneumoconiosis.
  • Silicosis strongly predisposes to TB.
  • Classic finding: eggshell calcification.

question_text: A 35-year-old woman with a long history of dyspnea, chronic cough, sputum production, and wheezing dies of respiratory failure following a bout of pneumonia. question_text: A chronic smoker with a 20-year history of working in a cement factory is diagnosed with mesothelioma. What is the most likely causative agent for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

Mesothelioma is primarily caused by exposure to asbestos fibres, which is a known risk factor for this type of cancer.

  • Long-term exposure to asbestos, especially in industries such as cement factories, is the most common occupational cause of mesothelioma.
  • Asbestos exposure is a well-established risk factor for developing laryngeal, ovarian, colon, lung, and pleural cancers.
  • Lung mesothelioma is a more specific tumour associated with asbestos exposure. It is common, but it is less prevalent than Adenocarcinoma.

Explanation for other options:

Silicosis (Option A) is caused by the inhalation of silica dust, commonly seen in industries such as mining and construction. While silica exposure can lead to lung fibrosis, it is not a direct cause of mesothelioma.

Coal worker pneumoconiosis (Option C), also known as black lung disease, results from the inhalation of coal dust. This condition affects the lungs but is not linked to mesothelioma.

Bagassosis (Option D) is caused by the inhalation of mouldy sugarcane dust and can lead to lung disease, but it is not associated with mesothelioma.

Key Takeaways:

  • Adenocarcinoma of the lung is the most common malignancy associated with asbestos exposure.
  • Mesothelioma is the most specific malignancy due to asbestos exposure.

question_text: Which of the following is not true about the given condition?
option_a: It is associated with elevated levels of growth factors
option_b: It has greater amount of collagen and vascularity
option_c: It does not spread beyond wound site
option_d: Wide excision may be done as a treatment
explanation:
The image clearly shows keloids, which are raised, firm, and rubbery or shiny scars that extend beyond the original wound site. This is a key characteristic that distinguishes keloids from hypertrophic scars, which remain confined to the boundaries of the initial injury.

(Choice C) it does not spread beyond wound site: This is FALSE. This is the defining characteristic of keloids. They DO spread beyond the original wound site.

Incorrect choices explanation :

(Choice A) it is associated with elevated levels of growth factors: This is TRUE. Keloids are associated with an overproduction of collagen, driven by elevated levels of growth factors like TGF-beta.

(Choice B) it has a greater amount of collagen and vascularity: This is TRUE. Keloids contain an excessive amount of collagen, leading to their raised and firm appearance. They also tend to have increased vascularity compared to normal scars.

(Choice D) wide excision may be done as a treatment: This is TRUE, but with caveats. Wide excision is a treatment option, but it's important to note that it often leads to recurrence, and additional treatments like radiation or corticosteroids are often used in conjunction with excision.

Why (Choice C) is the Correct Answer

The statement that keloids do not spread beyond the wound site is incorrect. This is the fundamental difference between keloids and hypertrophic scars.

Key takeaway:

Keloid:

Predisposition: Certain individuals are more prone to developing keloids, including people of African descent.

Location: Keloids are more common in certain areas of the body, such as the chest, shoulders, and earlobes.

question_text: p53 induced cell cycle arrest occurs in:
explanation:
p53-mediated cell cycle arrest may be considered the primordial response to DNA damage. It occurs late in the G1 phase and is caused mainly by p53-dependent transcription of the CDKI gene CDKN1A(p21). The p21 protein inhibits cyclin–CDK complexes and prevents phosphorylation of RB, thereby arresting cells in the G1 phase. Such a pause in cell cycling is welcome, because it gives the cells "breathing time" to repair DNA damage. The p53 protein also induces expression of DNA damage repair genes. If DNA damage is repaired successfully, p53 upregulates transcription of MDM2, leading to its own destruction and relief of the cell cycle block. If the damage cannot be repaired, the cell may enter p53- induced senescence or undergo p53-directed apoptosis.

The figure describes The role of p53 in maintaining the integrity of the genome. Activation of normal p53 by DNA-damaging agents or by hypoxia leads to cell cycle arrest in G1 and induction of DNA repair, by transcriptional upregulation of the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor CDKN1A(p21) and the GADD45 genes. Successful repair of DNA allows cells to proceed with the cell cycle; if DNA repair fails, p53 triggers either apoptosis or senescence. In cells with loss or mutations of TP53, DNA damage does not induce cell cycle arrest or DNA repair and genetically damaged cells proliferate, giving rise eventually to malignant neoplasms.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg: 211.

question_text: Which of the following best describes the lesions seen in Kaposi sarcoma?
explanation:
Explanation:
Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumour caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8). It is most commonly seen in association with AIDS and serves as an AIDS-defining condition, though it can also occur in other contexts.

Types

  1. Classic KS- Affects older men of Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, or Eastern European descent. Presents as persistent red-purple plaques or nodules, often on the lower extremities. Usually localized and indolent.
  2. Endemic African KS- Seen in HIV-negative individuals, usually under 40. It may involve lymph nodes and has a variable course from slow-growing to aggressive.
  3. Transplant-associated KS-Develops in immunosuppressed transplant recipients, particularly those on T-cell-suppressive drugs. Often aggressive and may regress if immunosuppression is reduced.
  4. AIDS-associated (epidemic) KS- The most common HIV-related malignancy. Involves skin, lymph nodes, and viscera, often with widespread dissemination.

Pathogenesis
HHV8 infection is central, with viral proteins promoting angiogenesis and cell survival. KS development is aided by impaired immune surveillance, particularly diminished T-cell immunity. Mutations in host cells may also contribute to tumor progression.

Morphology
Lesions evolve in stages:

  • Patch stage- Red-purple macules with irregular vascular channels and inflammatory cells.
  • Plaque stage- Raised, violaceous lesions with jagged vascular spaces, hemosiderin, and inflammatory infiltrates.
  • Nodular stage- Solid masses of spindle cells with small vessels, red cell extravasation, and frequent mitoses.
  • Clinical Features
  • The course varies widely. Classic KS tends to remain localised to the skin, while AIDS-related KS is often aggressive and systemic.
  • Prognosis depends on the form and extent of disease. Treatments include surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, antiretroviral therapy for HIV-related KS, and, in transplant patients, reducing immunosuppression.
  • Newer strategies target angiogenesis and VEGF-related pathways.

question_text: A patient had lipoma excision surgery 5 weeks ago and now presents with a scar confined to the original incision site. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • It results from excessive collagen deposition, rapid tissue proliferation, and activity of myofibroblasts.
  • Hypertrophic scars usually improve over time and have a lower tendency to recur compared to keloids.

Explanation of other options:

Keloid (Option A): A keloid is a type of scar that extends beyond the original wound boundaries and does not regress over time. It is more commonly seen in African American individuals and typically develops following deep dermal injuries.

Exuberant Granulation (Option B & D): Excessive granulation tissue occurs when tissue grows above the level of the surrounding skin, a condition often referred to as 'proud flesh.' This overgrowth interferes with reepithelialization, thereby delaying proper wound healing. Management typically involves cauterization or surgical excision to remove the excess tissue and promote normal healing.

question_text: Familial HNPCC has a defect in?
explanation:
Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC), also known as Lynch Syndrome, is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes. These mutations lead to microsatellite instability (MSI), a hallmark of HNPCC-related cancers.

Key Genetic Defect:

  • The DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes involved in HNPCC include:
    • MLH1
    • MSH2
    • MSH6
    • PMS2
    • EPCAM (indirectly affects MSH2 expression)
  • Function of MMR Genes:
    • These genes help in detecting and correcting base mismatches during DNA replication.
    • When defective, they cause accumulation of errors in microsatellites, leading to microsatellite instability (MSI-H) and an increased risk of colorectal, endometrial, gastric, and other cancers.

Incorrect choices explanation:

  • (Choice A) Nucleotide excision repair (NER)
    • This pathway repairs bulky DNA adducts (e.g., UV-induced pyrimidine dimers).
    • Defective in Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP), not HNPCC.
  • (Choice B) Base excision repair (BER)
    • Repairs small, non-bulky base lesions (e.g., deaminated bases, alkylated bases).
    • Defective in MUTYH-associated polyposis (MAP), not HNPCC.
  • (Choice C) Point mutations
    • Point mutations occur in many genetic disorders but are not the primary defect in HNPCC.
    • HNPCC is specifically associated with MMR gene mutations and microsatellite instability, not just simple point mutations.

Key takeaway:

HNPCC (Lynch Syndrome) is caused by defects in the mismatch repair (MMR) genesr.

question_text: In healing by first intention, macrophages appear on day?
explanation:
• In healing by first intention, macrophages appear on day 3.
  • When the injury involves only the epithelial layer, the principal mechanism of repair is epithelial regeneration, also called primary union or healing by the first intention.
  • Within 24 to 48 hours, epithelial cells from both edges have begun to migrate and proliferate along the dermis, depositing basement membrane components as they progress. The cells meet in the midline beneath the surface scab, yielding a thin but continuous epithelial layer that closes the wound.
  • Within 24 hours, neutrophils are seen at the incision margin, migrating toward the fibrin clot. They release proteolytic enzymes that begin to clear the debris. Basal cells at the cut edge of the epidermis begin to show increased mitotic activity.
  • By day 3, neutrophils have been largely replaced by macrophages and granulation tissue progressively invades the incision space. Collagen fibers are now evident at the incision margins. Epithelial cell proliferation continues, forming a covering approaching the normal thickness of the epidermis.
  • By day 5, neovascularization reaches its peak as granulation tissue fills the incisional space. These new vessels are leaky, allowing the passage of plasma proteins and fluid into the extravascular space. Thus, new granulation tissue is often edematous.
  • During the second week, there is continued collagen accumulation and fibroblast proliferation.
  • By the end of the first month, the scar comprises a cellular connective tissue largely devoid of inflammatory cells and covered by an essentially normal epidermis.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition, chapter 3, pg 104

question_text: During the process of wound healing, which cells are the first to arrive at the site of the wound due to chemotaxis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Neutrophils are the initial cells to migrate to the site of tissue injury in response to chemotactic signals. They play a vital role in the early wound healing stages by eliminating pathogens, dead tissue, and debris.

Events in wound healing:

  • Day 0:Platelets and fibrin form a blood clot.
  • Day 1:Blood clot persists, recruitment of neutrophils (acute inflammation).
  • Day 2:Continued clot presence with neutrophil accumulation; thin epithelial covering forms.
  • Day 3:Macrophages replace neutrophils; chronic inflammation begins; granulation tissue (angiogenesis) starts.
  • Day 5:Peak granulation tissue formation and maximum neovascularisation; collagen bridging begins.
  • Day 21 (3rd week):Maximum collagen deposition (Type I collagen).

Healing by primary vs. secondary intention:

  • Primary intention:Rapid closure of a clean, surgically incised wound with minimal tissue loss, forming a small scar (e.g., surgical scar).
  • Secondary intention:Wound left open to granulate and epithelialise, healing with contraction, producing larger scars (e.g., road traffic accident).

Explanation of other options:

Monocytes (Option B): Arrive later, transform into macrophages.

Macrophages (Option C): Replace neutrophils by day 3, promoting granulation tissue and collagen deposition.

Lymphocytes (Option D): Participate in chronic inflammatory responses, not the earliest phase of wound healing.

Key Takeaways:

  • Neutrophils → first responders.
  • Macrophages → essential for later tissue repair and angiogenesis.
  • Collagen type I → predominant by 3rd week.

question_text: A 47-year-old woman has had increasing pain and deformities in her hands and feet for the past 10 years. On physical examination, joint shows swelling, erythema, and tenderness. RA typically affects small joints of the hands and feet. The synovium becomes grossly edematous, thickened, and hyperplastic, transforming its smooth contour to one covered by delicate and bulbous villi. The characteristic histologic features include

question_text: Stunning of myocardium without any acute coronary syndrome is:
explanation:
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (also called stress-induced cardiomyopathy or "broken heart syndrome") is a condition characterized by transient left ventricular systolic dysfunction in the absence of acute coronary syndrome (no coronary artery occlusion).

Why is Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy the Correct Answer?

  • Stunning of the myocardium occurs due to acute catecholamine surge in response to emotional or physical stress.
  • Reversible dysfunction of the left ventricular apex ("apical ballooning") is seen on echocardiography.
  • No evidence of significant coronary artery disease (CAD) on angiography.
  • Typically affects postmenopausal women after extreme emotional distress.

Incorrect Choices explanation :

  • (Choice A) Subendocardial Infarction
    • Occurs due to partial ischemia of the myocardium caused by acute coronary syndrome (ACS).
    • Shows ST-segment depression on ECG and troponin elevation.
    • Not a stress-induced phenomenon without ACS.
  • (Choice B) Restrictive Cardiomyopathy
    • Characterized by diastolic dysfunction and stiff ventricular walls due to fibrosis or infiltration (e.g., amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis).
    • Not associated with myocardial stunning or catecholamine stress.
  • (Choice D) Transmural Infarction
    • Involves full-thickness myocardial necrosis due to complete coronary artery occlusion.
    • Associated with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).
    • Permanent myocardial damage, unlike Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, which is reversible.

Key takeaway :  Takotsubo cardiomyopathy leads to myocardial stunning without acute coronary syndrome (ACS).

question_text: All are hereditary causes of thrombosis except:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is a rare acquired condition marked by clonal expansion of hematopoietic stem cells lacking GPI anchor proteins and is not a hereditary cause of thrombosis.
  • PNH blood cells are deficient in three GPI-linked proteins that regulate complement activity:
    • CD55 (decay-accelerating factor)
    • CD59 (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis)
    • C8-binding protein.
  • Pathogenesis:
    • It results from acquired mutations in the phosphatidylinositol glycan complementation group A gene (PIGA), an enzyme that is essential for the synthesis of certain membrane-associated complement regulatory proteins.
  • Clinical features:
    • It causes intravascular haemolysis and anaemia
    • Haemoglobinuria (red-brown colour) (most noticeable in early morning urine)
    • Hypoplastic bone marrow failure, aplastic anaemia and myelodysplastic syndrome
  • Management
    • Transfusion
    • Folate supplements
    • Prophylaxis or treatment of thrombosis
    • Anti-complement C5 monoclonal antibody.

Explanation of other options:

Protein S deficiency (Option B): A genetic disorder that predisposes to abnormal blood clot formation (thrombosis). Protein C and its cofactor Protein S are vitamin K-dependent natural anticoagulants that inactivate factors Va and VIIIa, thereby regulating thrombin generation. Deficiency of either protein increases the risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), and other thrombotic complications.

Antithrombin deficiency (Option C): An autosomal dominant inherited disorder that increases the risk of abnormal blood clotting (thrombosis). Antithrombin (AT) is a serine protease inhibitor (SERPIN) that inactivates coagulation factors IIa, IXa, Xa, and XIa. Deficiency leads to a higher risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), and other thrombotic events. Heparin and fondaparinux act by enhancing AT activity, forming the basis of their anticoagulant effect.

Homocystinuria (Option D): An autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CBS gene, resulting in cystathionine β-synthase deficiency. This leads to accumulation of homocysteine and methionine in the blood. Clinical features include ectopia lentis (lens dislocation), intellectual disability, seizures, Marfan-like skeletal abnormalities, osteoporosis, thrombosis, and hyperpigmentation.

• An embolus is a detached intravascular solid, liquid, or gaseous mass that is carried by the blood from its point of origin to a distant site, where it often causes tissue dysfunction or infarction.
  • Pulmonary emboli originate from deep venous thromboses and are responsible for the most common form of thromboembolic disease.
  • Deep vein thrombosis (dvt) occurs when a blood clot (thrombus) forms in one or more of the deep veins in the body, usually in the legs. Deep vein thrombosis can cause leg pain or swelling. Sometimes there are no noticeable symptoms. You can get dvt if you have certain medical conditions that affect how the blood clots.

Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10ᵗʰ ed Pg:112

question_text: Which of the following is not a part of the criteria for diagnosis of Kawasaki disease?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The diagnostic criteria for Kawasaki Disease include non-purulent conjunctivitis rather than purulent conjunctivitis.

Kawasaki Disease

  • An acute febrile illness primarily affecting children under 4 years old, characterised by large- to medium-sized vessel arteritis, particularly involving the coronary arteries.
  • Infectious agents (mostly viruses) trigger the disease in genetically predisposed individuals.
  • It may result from a delayed-type hypersensitivity response directed against cross-reactive or newly uncovered vascular antigens.
  • Cytokine production and polyclonal B-cell activation result in autoantibodies to ECs and SMCs that precipitate the vasculitis.

Clinical Features (Mnemonic: CREAM-F).

  • Conjunctivitis: Non-exudative & non-purulent
  • Rash: Polymorphous, non-vesicular (Option B ruled out)
  • Oedema or erythema of hands & feet).
  • Lymphadenopathy
    • Cervical, often unilateral and non-suppurative. (Option D ruled out)
  • Mucosal involvement
    • Erythema or fissures or crusting at times, referred to as strawberry tongue. (Option A ruled out)

    • Fever: Most important constitutional symptom
  • It can lead to severe cardiovascular complications, including coronary artery aneurysms and myocardial infarction.

question_text: Which is the commonest site of thrombosis?
explanation:
• Venous thrombi (phlebothrombosis) are almost invariably occlusive; they frequently propagate some distance toward the heart, forming a long cast within the vessel lumen that is prone to give rise to emboli.
  • Because these thrombi form in the sluggish venous circulation, they tend to contain more enmeshed red cells, leading to stasis or thrombi.
  • The veins of the lower extremities are most commonly affected (90% of venous thromboses); however, venous thrombi also can occur in the upper extremities, periprostatic plexus, or ovarian and periuterine veins, and under special circumstances they may be found in the dural sinuses, portal vein, or hepatic vein.

Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10ᵗʰ ed Pg:110

question_text:
Infarcts due to venous thrombosis are seen in
i. Testis
ii. Brain
iii. Ovary
iv. Kidney
option_a: Only i, ii and iii are correct
option_b: Only i and iii are correct
option_c: Only ii and iv are correct
explanation:
An infarct is an area of ischemic necrosis caused by occlusion of the vascular supply to the affected tissue. Infarction primarily affecting the heart and the brain is a common and extremely important cause of clinical illness. Roughly 40% of all deaths in the United States are a consequence of cardiovascular disease, with most of these deaths stemming from myocardial or cerebral infarction. Pulmonary infarction is a common clinical complication, bowel infarction often is fatal, and ischemic necrosis of distal extremities (gangrene) causes substantial morbidity in the diabetic population. Arterial thrombosis or arterial embolism underlies the vast majority of infarctions. Less common causes of arterial obstruction include vasospasm, expansion of an atheroma secondary to intraplaque hemorrhage, and extrinsic compression of a vessel, such as by tumor, a dissecting aortic aneurysm, or edema within a confined space (e.g., in anterior tibial compartment syndrome). Other uncommon causes of tissue infarction include vessel twisting (e.g., in testicular torsion or bowel volvulus), traumatic vascular rupture, and entrapment in a hernia sac. Although venous thrombosis can cause infarction, the more common outcome is simply congestion; typically, bypass channels rapidly open to provide sufficient outflow to restore the arterial inflow. Infarcts caused by venous thrombosis thus usually occur only in organs with a single efferent vein (e.g., testis or ovary).

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10ᵗʰ ed,Pg-114
