question_text: Which of the following is the first sign in any vascular injury?
explanation:
Normal hemostasis.

  • (A) After vascular injury, local neurohumoral factors induce a transient vasoconstriction.
  • (B) Platelets bind via glycoprotein Ib (GpIb) receptors to von Willebrand factor (VWF) on exposed ECM and are activated, undergoing a shape change and granule release.
  • Released ADP and thromboxane A2 (TXA2) induce additional platelet aggregation through platelet GpIIb-IIIa receptor binding to fibrinogen, and form the primary hemostatic plug.
  • (C) Local activation of the coagulation cascade (involving tissue factor and platelet phospholipids) results in fibrin polymerization, 'cementing' the platelets into a definitive secondary hemostatic plug.
  • (D) Counterregulatory mechanisms, mediated by tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA, a fibrinolytic product) and thrombomodulin, confine the hemostatic process to the site of injury.

Reference :Robbins, 10th edition, page number - 102

question_text: Which of the following is not a component of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura?
explanation:
Explanation:

Thrombosis is not a component of Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP).

Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)

  • It is an acute autoimmune disorder mediated by antibodies against ADAMTS-13 (a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with a thrombospondin type 1 motif).
  • It is characterised by a pentad of findings:
    • MAHA (microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia) (Option D ruled out)
    • Thrombocytopenia (Option B ruled out)
    • Renal failure (Option C ruled out)
    • Neurologic findings
    • Fever
  • Pathogenesis:
    • It is caused by a deficiency in a plasma enzyme called ADAMTS13 (vWF metalloprotease).
    • ADAMTS13 degrades very high-molecular-weight multimers of vWF. In its absence, large multimers accumulate in plasma and tend to promote spontaneous platelet activation and aggregation.
    • Superimposition of endothelial cell injury (caused by some other condition) may further promote the formation of platelet aggregates, thus exacerbating TTP.
    • It leads to microvascular occlusion by platelet thrombi, which affects key organs, principally the brain and kidneys.
  • Treatment:
    • Emergency plasma exchange.
    • Glucocorticoids, aspirin and rituximab also have a role in management.

question_text: How does Total Plasma Exchange (TPE) help in managing Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)?
option_c: TPE removes anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies and thereby restores ADAMTS13 protease activity
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Total Plasma Exchange (TPE) is the cornerstone of therapy for TTP.
  • It acts by removing circulating autoantibodies against ADAMTS13, thereby allowing the enzyme to regain its normal function.
  • ADAMTS13 is a metalloprotease that cleaves ultra-large von Willebrand factor (vWF) multimers. Without this cleavage, large vWF multimers persist, causing platelet aggregation and widespread microvascular thrombosis.
  • By restoring ADAMTS13 activity, TPE reduces thrombotic burden and prevents organ damage.

Explanation of other options:

TPE removes von Willebrand factor (Option A): TPE does not directly remove vWF; instead, it targets anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies, which are the underlying problem.

TPE removes antiplatelet antibodies(Option B): It is not antiplatelet antibodies that are removed in TTP.

TPE replenishes coagulation factors(Option D): Unlike in coagulation factor deficiencies, TTP pathology is due to defective vWF processing, not missing clotting factors. Hence, replenishment of coagulation factors is not the mechanism of benefit.

Key takeaway:

Treatment of TTP

  • Plasma Exchange (PEX) + Corticosteroids
    • PEX removes both ADAMTS13 autoantibodies and ultra-large vWF multimers.
    • Corticosteroids suppress the reticuloendothelial system and reduce autoantibody formation.
    • Typical regimen: exchange of one plasma volume (~40 mL/kg) per session.
    • Prednisolone: 1 mg/kg/day.
  • Rituximab
    • Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody.
    • Targets B-cells, effective in refractory or relapsed TTP.
  • Caplacizumab
    • Humanized monoclonal antibody fragment that binds the A1 domain of vWF, blocking platelet adhesion.
    • Shows strong potential for use in acute TTP.
  • Other therapies (in resistant cases):
    • Splenectomy
    • Vincristine
    • Cyclosporine
    • Cyclophosphamide

Reference:

NIH Guidelines

question_text: A 24-year-old female with malar rash, oral ulcers, joint pains, thrombocytopenia, and positive anti-Smith antibody. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), an autoimmune disease that typically affects young women. It presents with the following features:

  • Malar rash (a butterfly-shaped rash across the cheeks and nasal bridge),
  • Recurrent oral ulcers,
  • Joint pain (classically non-erosive arthritis),
  • Thrombocytopenia,
  • Positive anti-Smith (anti-Sm) antibodies, which are highly specific for SLE.

Although conditions such as scleroderma, Sjögren syndrome, and rheumatoid arthritis may have overlapping clinical manifestations, the presence of anti-Sm antibodies is most specific to SLE, confirming the diagnosis.

SLE is a chronic autoimmune disorder characterised by the production of multiple autoantibodies including antinuclear antibodies (ANA), anti-double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), and anti-Sm. These antibodies form immune complexes that deposit in tissues, leading to inflammation and organ damage. The condition is significantly more common in women.

Clinical manifestations of SLE:

  • Skin:Malar rash, photosensitivity, discoid lesions, and mucosal ulcers.
  • Joints:Non-erosive arthritis, most frequently affecting the hands, wrists, and knees.
  • Renal:Lupus nephritis, ranging from asymptomatic proteinuria to severe renal failure. This is a major contributor to morbidity and mortality in SLE.
  • Cardiovascular:Pericarditis, myocarditis, increased risk of atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease.
  • Pulmonary:Pleuritis, pleural effusion, pulmonary hypertension, and interstitial lung disease.
  • Neurologic:Neuropsychiatric symptoms, which may include headaches, cognitive dysfunction, seizures, and psychosis.
  • Hematologic:Anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and an increased risk of thrombotic complications.

Explanation of other options:

Scleroderma (Option A): Characterized by skin thickening and tightening; may present as CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia).

Sjögren Syndrome(Option B): Autoimmune disorder causing dry eyes and dry mouth (sicca symptoms); commonly associated with anti-SSA (Ro) and anti-SSB (La) antibodies.

Rheumatoid Arthritis (Option D): Chronic inflammatory arthritis with erosive joint changes, often involving small joints; associated with anti-CCP antibodies and rheumatoid factor.

Key Takeaways:

  • SLE = autoimmune, systemic, women of reproductive age.
  • Anti-Sm = specific marker.

question_text: A young patient presents with a significant retroperitoneal haemorrhage and reports episodes of knee joint swelling following strenuous physical activity. There is no history of mucosal bleeding. Which coagulation factor deficiency is most likely responsible for this presentation?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's symptoms (large retroperitoneal haemorrhage and knee swelling) suggest haemophilia, which is typically caused by deficiencies in Factor VIII (Haemophilia A) or Factor IX (Haemophilia B).

  • This condition is characterised by spontaneous or trauma-induced joint and muscle bleeds but not mucosal bleeding, which is distinct from von Willebrand disease or platelet dysfunction.
  • Haemophilia C is due to factor 11 deficiency, an autosomal recessive condition. Bleeding episodes are generally milder than in Haemophilia A and B.

Explanation for other options:

GP1b/IX (Option B): This is associated with Bernard-Soulier syndrome, a platelet disorder characterised by defective platelet adhesion. It leads to mucosal bleeding, which is absent in this case.

Von Willebrand factor (Option C) deficiency causes von Willebrand disease, which primarily results in mucosal bleeding (e.g., nosebleeds, gum bleeding) and not typically large retroperitoneal haemorrhages or joint bleeds.

Lupus anticoagulant (Option D): This is associated with antiphospholipid syndrome, leading to an increased risk of thrombosis (clots), not bleeding. It does not explain the bleeding symptoms described in this patient.

Key Takeaways:

question_text: A 14-year-old boy presents with acute onset of right flank pain, which developed after he helped his father paint the ceiling of his bedroom. Physical examination demonstrates an area of ecchymosis in the right flank that is tender to palpation. The patient has a lifelong history of easy bruising. His brother shows the same tendency. The serum level of clotting factor VIII is less than 2% of normal. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism for bleeding tendency in this patient?
option_a: Circulating antibodies directed against factor VIII
option_b: Decreased hepatic synthesis of multiple coagulation factors
option_d: Genetic defect involving the factor VIII gene
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely underlying mechanism is a genetic defect involving the factor VIII gene, resulting in Hemophilia A.

Diagnosis Breakdown:

The clinical presentation is classic for a hereditary coagulation disorder:

  • Demographics: Young male patient.
  • Family History: History of easy bruising and a brother with similar symptoms, suggesting an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern.
  • Trigger: Bleeding (flank ecchymosis/hematoma) occurred after physical exertion (painting the ceiling). Deep tissue bleeding is characteristic of coagulation factor deficiencies rather than platelet disorders.
  • Lab Findings: Factor VIII level <2% confirms severe deficiency.
  • Pathophysiology of Hemophilia A: Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in the F8 gene, which encodes coagulation factor VIII. It affects approximately 1 in 5,000 to 10,000 males. The deficiency prevents the formation of the intrinsic tenase complex, leading to impaired thrombin generation and bleeding diathesis (hemarthroses, deep muscle hematomas, and post-traumatic bleeding).

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Circulating antibodies directed against factor VIII (Option A): This describes Acquired Hemophilia A, an autoimmune condition where autoantibodies inhibit Factor VIII. It typically presents in older adults or postpartum women and lacks a lifelong or familial history of bleeding.
  • Decreased hepatic synthesis of multiple coagulation factors (Option B): Severe liver disease causes a deficiency in most clotting factors. However, Factor VIII is often normal or elevated in liver disease because it is also synthesized by endothelial cells, not just hepatocytes. Furthermore, liver disease would not present with an isolated Factor VIII deficiency in a young boy with a specific family history.
  • Deficiency of vitamin K (Option C): Vitamin K deficiency impairs the synthesis of factors II, VII, IX, and X (and proteins C and S). It does not affect Factor VIII levels.

Key Takeaway:

Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a genetic defect in the Factor VIII gene. It is characterized by deep tissue bleeding (muscles, joints), a prolonged aPTT, and low Factor VIII levels.

question_text: A young boy presents with joint swelling after a fall. Lab investigations show normal PT and raised aPTT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis based on the clinical features of joint swelling after a fall, along with normal PT and raised aPTT, is haemophilia.

  • Bleeding disorderscan result from either inherited or acquired deficiencies in clotting factors.
  • Such deficiencies typically cause symptoms likelarge bruises, hematomas, or prolonged bleeding after injuries or surgeries.
  • Unlike platelet-related bleeding, which often causes small pinpoint haemorrhages, clotting factor deficiencies usually lead to bleeding in deeper tissues, such as the gastrointestinal tract, urinary tract, and joints (hemarthrosis). (Option D ruled out)
  • Common examples include persistent bleeding after minor procedures like tooth extraction or recurrent joint bleedsafter slight stress.
  • Hereditary deficiencies generally involve a single clotting factor.
  • The most important include factor VIII deficiency (haemophilia A) and factor IX deficiency (haemophilia B).
  • In clinical testing, the coagulation cascade is evaluated by separating it into extrinsic and intrinsic pathways

Haemophilia A:

Haemophilia B (Christmas Disease, Factor IX Deficiency)

  • Haemophilia B results from factor IX deficiencyand is clinically indistinguishable from haemophilia A.
  • It is inherited as an X-linked recessive disorderand shows variable severity depending on the mutation.
  • Like haemophilia A, patients present with prolonged PTT and normal PT, and the diagnosis is confirmed by factor IX assays.
  • The condition is treated with infusions of recombinant factor IX.

Explanation of other options:

Von-Willebrand disease (Option A): Von Willebrand disease is an autosomal dominant disorder that usually presents with mild bleeding, often unnoticed until triggered by surgery or dental procedures, with common symptoms including spontaneous bleeding from mucous membranes, wounds, or menorrhagia. Laboratory findings show reduced plasma levels of active vWF, decreased ristocetin cofactor activity, and, in type 1 and type 3 disease, a prolonged PTT due to reduced stability of factor VIII, despite normal platelet counts.

Iron deficiency anemia (Option C): The clinical features of anaemia arise from reduced hemoglobin and oxygen delivery to tissues. Patients typically appear pale and experience weakness, malaise, easy fatigue, and breathlessness on mild exertion.

question_text: Which of the following is not true regarding Von Willebrand disease?
option_b: Quantitative defects are seen in subtypes 1 and 3 one willebrand disease
explanation:
Why is Choice (C) Incorrect?

  • Hemarthrosis (bleeding into joints) is NOT a usual presentation of VWD.
  • Hemarthrosis is more characteristic of Hemophilia A or B (Factor VIII or IX deficiency), which affects the coagulation cascade more severely.
  • VWD usually presents with mucocutaneous bleeding such as epistaxis, menorrhagia, easy bruising, and prolonged bleeding from minor cuts.

Why Are the Other Choices Correct?

  1. (Choice A) Normal platelet count → True
    • In VWD, platelet count is normal because it is a platelet function disorder, not a platelet production disorder.
    • However, platelet function is defective due to reduced vWF.
  2. (Choice B) Quantitative defects in subtypes 1 and 3 → True
    • Type 1 VWD: Mild-moderate quantitative deficiency of vWF (most common type, ~70-80%).
    • Type 3 VWD: Severe deficiency/complete absence of vWF (rare but severe).
    • Type 2 VWD: Qualitative defect (dysfunctional vWF rather than decreased quantity).
  3. (Choice D) Produced by endothelial cells → True
    • vWF is primarily synthesized and stored in endothelial cells (Weibel-Palade bodies) and megakaryocytes.
    • It plays a key role in platelet adhesion to damaged blood vessels.

Key takeaway:

Von Willebrand Disease (VWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, caused by deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand Factor (vWF). vWF is a glycoprotein produced by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes, essential for platelet adhesion and stabilization of Factor VIII in coagulation.

question_text: Rapid assessment of entire coagulation pathway in emergency?
explanation:
Unlike traditional tests like prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), TEG is viscoelastic test and assesses platelet function, clot strength, and fibrinolysis

Measurement Parameters:

  • TEG evaluates several key parameters related to clot formation:
    • Reaction Time (R value): Represents the time until the first evidence of a clot is detected.
    • K value: Measures the time from the end of R until the clot reaches 20 mm, indicating the speed of clot formation.
    • Angle: Derived from the tangent of the curve as K is reached, offering similar information to K.
    • Maximum Amplitude (MA): Reflects clot strength.
    • Coagulation Index (CI): An overall assessment that combines the contributions of R, K, angle, and MA.
    • G-value: A log-derivation of MA, representing clot strength in dynes/sec units.
    • Clot Lysis: TEG also measures clot lysis, reported as estimated percent lysis (EPL) and the percentage of clot lysed after 30 minutes (LY30,%).

Reference: Hoffman hematology, 2234

question_text: Defective intrinsic pathway causes:
explanation:
• Based on assays performed in clinical laboratories, the coagulation cascade has traditionally been divided into the extrinsic and intrinsic pathways.
  • The prothrombin time (PT) assay assesses the function of the proteins in the extrinsic pathway (factors VII, X, V, II (prothrombin), and fibrinogen). In brief, tissue factor, phospholipids, and calcium are added to plasma and the time for a fibrin clot to form is recorded.
  • The partial thromboplastin time (PTT) assay screens the function of the proteins in the intrinsic pathway (factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, and fibrinogen). In this assay, clotting of plasma is initiated by the addition of negative charged particles (e.g., ground glass) that activate factor XII (Hageman factor) together with phospholipids and calcium, and the time to fibrin clot formation is recorded.

explanation:
• Hemophilia A is the most common hereditary cause of serious bleeding. It is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by reduced factor VIII activity. It primarily affects males.
  • In symptomatic cases there is a tendency toward easy bruising and massive hemorrhage after trauma or operative procedures. In addition, 'spontaneous' hemorrhages frequently are encountered in tissues that normally are subject to mechanical stress, particularly the joints, where recurrent bleeds (hemarthroses) lead to progressive deformities that can be crippling.
  • Petechiae are characteristically absent. Specific assays for factor VIII are used to confirm the diagnosis of hemophilia A. Typically, patients with hemophilia A have a prolonged PTT that is corrected by mixing the patient's plasma with normal plasma. Specific factor assays are then used to confirm the deficiency of factor VIII.

question_text: Which of the following is the correct statement regarding Hemophilia A?

option_c: Affects mainly males and heterozygous females
explanation:
• Hemophilia A is the most common hereditary cause of serious bleeding. It is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by reduced factor VIII activity. It primarily affects males. Much less commonly, excessive bleeding occurs in heterozygous females, presumably due to preferential inactivation of the X chromosome carrying the normal factor VIII gene (unfavourable lyonization).
  • Approximately 30% of cases are caused by new mutations; in the remainder, there is a positive family history. Severe hemophilia A is observed in people with marked deficiencies of factor VIII (activity levels < 1% of normal). Milder deficiencies may only become apparent in the face of trauma or other hemostatic stresses. The varying degrees of factor VIII deficiency are explained by the existence of many different causative mutations, including deletions, inversions, and splice junction mutations.
  • In symptomatic cases there is a tendency toward easy bruising and massive hemorrhage after trauma or operative procedures. In addition, 'spontaneous' hemorrhages frequently are encountered in tissues that normally are subject to mechanical stress, particularly the joints, where recurrent bleeds (hemarthroses) lead to progressive deformities that can be crippling.
  • Petechiae are characteristically absent. Specific assays for factor VIII are used to confirm the diagnosis of hemophilia A. Typically, patients with hemophilia A have a prolonged PTT that is corrected by mixing the patient's plasma with normal plasma. Specific factor assays are then used to confirm the deficiency of factor VIII.
  • In approximately 15% of those with severe hemophilia A, replacement therapy is complicated by the development of neutralizing antibodies against factor VIII, probably because factor VIII is seen by the immune system as a 'foreign' antigen. In these persons, the PTT fails to correct in mixing studies.

Reference: Robbins, 10th edition, page number - 490

question_text: Which of the following is the most common hereditary bleeding disorder?
explanation:
VON WILLEBRAND DISEASE

  • Von Willebrand disease is caused by the deficiency of Von Willebrand factor. Von Willebrand factor helps blood platelets clump together and stick to the vessel wall, which is necessary for normal blood clotting.
  • Von Willebrand disease is transmitted as an autosomal dominant disorder. It usually presents as spontaneous bleeding from mucous membranes, excessive bleeding from wounds, and menorrhagia.
  • It is underrecognized, as the diagnosis requires sophisticated tests and the clinical manifestations often are quite mild. Actually, this disease is surprisingly prevalent, particularly in persons of European descent.
  • It is estimated that approximately 1% of people in the United States have von Willebrand disease, making it the most common inherited bleeding disorder. People with von Willebrand disease have compound defects in platelet function and coagulation, but in most cases only the platelet defect produces clinical findings.
  • The exceptions are rare in patients with homozygous Von Willebrand disease, in whom there is a concomitant deficiency of factor VIII severe enough to produce features resembling those of haemophilia.

Reference :Robbins, 10th edition. page number - 490

Astrocytes proliferate in reaction to brain injury in the process called gliosis. Endothelial cells are most likely to proliferate in neoplasms. Microglia respond to brain injury with a macrophage-like function. Oligodendroglial cells provide myelination for brain neuronal axons.

question_text: A 60-year-old male patient presents with increasing blood in sputum and weight loss over the past 3 months. An HRCT scan reveals a mass circumscribing the right main bronchus protruding into its lumen. Endobronchial lung biopsy was taken, the histopathological image of which is shown below. Based on the above findings, what is your probable diagnosis?
explanation:
(a) Histologically, squamous cell carcinoma is characterized by the presence of keratinization and/or intercellular bridges. Keratinization may take the form of squamous pearls or individual cells with markedly eosinophilic cytoplasm.

(b) Adenocarcinoma is an invasive malignant epithelial tumor with glandular differentiation or mucin production by the tumor cells. Adenocarcinomas grow in various patterns, including acinar, lepidic, papillary, micropapillary, and solid.

(c) Small cell carcinoma is comprised of relatively small cells with scant cytoplasm, ill-defined cell borders, finely granular nuclear chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli.

(d) Carcinoid tumors occur most often in the wall of the major bronchus and may protrude into its lumen. Histologically, the tumor is composed of organoid, trabecular, palisading, ribbon, or rosettelike arrangements of cells separated by a delicate fibrovascular stroma. Tumor cells are quite regular and have uniform round nuclei with salt and pepper. Chromatin and a moderate amount of eosinophilic cytoplasm.

question_text: A 31-year-old woman had increasingly severe diarrhea 1 week after returning from a trip to Central America. Gross examination of the stools showed mucus and streaks of blood. Diarrhea with mucus and blood in the stools may be caused by several enteroinvasive microorganisms, including Shigella dysenteriae and Entamoeba histolytica. Amebiasis affects the cecum and ascending colon most often, but sigmoid colon, rectum, and appendix can also be involved. Dysentery develops when the amebae attach to the colonic epithelium, induce apoptosis, invade crypts, and burrow laterally into the lamina propria. This recruits neutrophils, causes tissue damage, and creates a flask shaped ulcer with a narrow neck and broad base. Histologic diagnosis can be difficult, since amebae can be similar to macrophages in size and appearance. Clostridium difficile causes pseudomembranous colitis after antibiotic therapy. Dissemination of Cryptosporidium and Strongyloides organisms may occur in immunocompromised patients. Giardia produces a self-limited, watery diarrhea.

question_text: Which amino acid is necessary for the production of nitric oxide in blood vessels?
explanation:
Explanation:

Nitric oxide (NO) is a vital signaling molecule involved in vasodilation and various other physiological processes. Nitric oxide synthesis in blood vessels requires the amino acid arginine, which serves as its precursor.

Steps in Nitric Oxide Synthesis:

  1. Enzyme Involved:
    • Nitric oxide synthase (NOS) converts L-arginine to nitric oxide (NO) and L-citrulline in the presence of oxygen and cofactors like NADPH and tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4).
  2. Physiological Role of NO:
    • NO is a potent vasodilator that relaxes vascular smooth muscle cells, thus regulating blood pressure and improving blood flow.
    • It also has roles in neurotransmission and immune response.

question_text: Which of the following instruments is not used in the colorimetric method for the estimation of hemoglobin?

Explanation:

The instrument shown in the figure in option C is the RBC pipette; it is not used in the colorimetric method for the estimation of haemoglobin (Sahli's method).

Sahli's Method (Acid Hematin Method)

  • A visual comparator technique for estimating hemoglobin.
  • When blood is added to dilute hydrochloric acid (HCl), hemoglobin is converted into brown-colored acid hematin.
  • The solution is diluted until its color matches a permanent brown glass standard by direct visual comparison.

Sahli's Hemoglobinometer Components:

  • Comparator
    • A rectangular plastic box with a slot for the hemoglobin tube. Brown standard glasses on either side allow color matching, and a white opaque back provides uniform illumination. (Option A ruled out)
  • Hemoglobin Tube (Sahli-Adams Tube)
    • Graduated on one side in g% (2-24) and on the other in % (20-140) for hemoglobin estimation. (Optional B ruled out)
  • Hemoglobin Pipette (Sahli's Pipette)
    • Single-marked at 20 μL (0.02 mL); lacks a bulb unlike WBC/RBC diluting pipettes.
  • Stirrer
    • Thin glass rod used to mix the blood-HCl solution in the hemoglobin tube. (Optional D ruled out)

Reference:

Sahli's Method For The Estimation Of Hemoglobin

  • A Coombs test, also known as an antiglobulin test, is of two blood tests used in immunohematology. They are the direct and indirect Coombs tests. The direct Coombs test detects antibodies that are stuck to the surface of the red blood cells.

question_text: Bombay blood group contains?
option_b: Anti A, Anti B, Anti H
explanation:
The Bombay blood group, also known as the hh blood group, is a rare blood type

  1. Antigen Absence: Individuals with the Bombay phenotype do not express the H antigen(also called substance H), which is typically present in blood group O. As a result, they cannot produce the A antigen (substance A) or the B antigen (substance B) on their red blood cells, regardless of their ABO blood group gene alleles. This absence of A and B antigens makes them universal red blood cell donors within the ABO blood group system.
  2. Anti-H Antibodies: The serum of individuals with the Bombay phenotype contains antibodies that react against all red blood cells of normal ABO phenotypes. These antibodies attack not only A and B antigens but also the H antigen, which is unique to the Bombay group. Consequently, people with this rare blood type can donate blood to any member of the ABO system, but they can only receive blood from other individuals with the Bombay phenotype.

  • In addition to ABO blood groups, there's the Rh factor (Rh-positive or Rh-negative). Rh-negative blood can be given to Rh negative patients, and Rh-positive or Rh-negative blood may be given to Rh positive patients.
  • The rules for plasma compatibility are the reverse of red cell compatibility:
    • The universal red cell donor has Type O negative blood.
    • The universal plasma donor has Type AB blood.

question_text: Blood transfusion reactions are mediated by which type of hypersensitivity reaction?
explanation:
Explanation:

Blood transfusion reactions are mediated by type 2 hypersensitivity reactions.

Type II (Antibody-Mediated) Hypersensitivity

  • Definition: In this reaction, antibodiestarget antigens on cell surfaces or within extracellular matrices, leading to cell damage, inflammation, or functional disturbance.
  • Mechanisms:
    • Opsonization and Phagocytosis- Antibody-coated cells are recognized by phagocytes via Fc receptors or complement fragments (C3b, C4b), leading to phagocytosis and destruction. Complement activation may also form membrane attack complexes, causing cell lysis.
    • Antibody-Dependent Cellular Cytotoxicity (ADCC)- Cells coated with IgG are killed by NK cells or macrophages without phagocytosis.
    • Inflammation- Antibodies deposited in tissues activate complement, releasing C3a and C5a, which recruit neutrophils and monocytes. Activated leukocytes release enzymes and reactive oxygen species, damaging tissue.
    • Cellular Dysfunction - Antibodies bind to receptors, either blocking their function (e.g., myasthenia gravis) or stimulating them (e.g., Graves' disease), without necessarily causing inflammation.
  • Clinical Examples:
    • Destruction of cells: Hemolytic transfusion reactions, erythroblastosis fetalis, autoimmune hemolytic anaemia, agranulocytosis, drug-induced cytotoxicity.
    • Tissue injury: Glomerulonephritis, vascular rejection of grafts.
    • Functional disorders: Myasthenia gravis, Graves' disease.

question_text: A 28-year-old woman with beta-thalassemia develops anxiety, hypotension, and fever during a blood transfusion. What is the next appropriate step in management?
option_a: Stop the blood transfusion and restart after stabilisation
option_b: Continue the blood transfusion and perform an ECG
option_c: Investigate for clerical errors in the blood transfusion process
option_d: Administer corticosteroids and monitor vital sign
explanation:
Explanation:

In a patient experiencing hypotension, fever, and anxiety during a transfusion, the immediate priority is to stop the transfusion and stabilise the patient. Prompt cessation prevents worsening of the reaction and allows appropriate evaluation and supportive care.

  • Transfusion Reactions:
    • Adverse responses to blood components can be:
    • Immunologically mediated (via WBCs or antigen-antibody reactions)
  • Infection-related
    • They can be immediate (within hours) or delayed (days to weeks).
  • Management Steps:
    • Stop the transfusion immediately.
    • Provide supportive care (monitor vitals, manage hypotension or respiratory distress).
    • Collect three samples:
      • Blood for blood grouping and cross-match (EDTA vial)
      • Blood for biochemical tests of hemolysis (plain red vial)
      • Urine for hemoglobinuria

Explanation for Other Options:

Continue the blood transfusion and perform an ECG (Option B): Continuing the transfusion may worsen the reaction. The priority is to stop the transfusion before any further monitoring or diagnostics.

Investigate for clerical errors in the blood transfusion process (Option C): Although checking for errors like blood group mismatch is important, the patient must first be stabilised. Investigation is secondary.

Administer corticosteroids and monitor vital signs (Option D): Corticosteroids are sometimes used in allergic transfusion reactions, but they are not first-line for acute reactions like hypotension and fever. Immediate stopping of the transfusion and supportive care are required first.

    • CMV IgM

  • PCR: Detects CMV DNA; quantitative nucleic acid testing (QNAT) via PCR is the most sensitive and specific
  • Treatment:
    • Ganciclovir: Drug of choice
    • Foscarnet: Used in ganciclovir-resistant cases
    • CMV immunoglobulins combined with ganciclovir are used in bone marrow transplant patients

Explanation of other options:

Human papillomavirus (HPV, Option A): A sexually transmitted virus. Low-risk types (6 & 11) cause benign genital warts, while high-risk types (16 & 18) are linked to cervical cancer, vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN), and vulvar carcinoma. Histologically, it shows koilocytes-cells with enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei and perinuclear halos in the superficial epithelium.

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV, Option C): Mainly associated with infectious mononucleosis and some lymphoproliferative disorders. Peripheral blood may show Downey cells-atypical large lymphocytes with vacuolated cytoplasm and a 'ballerina skirt' appearance.

Herpes simplex virus (HSV, Option D):Causes vesicular lesions. Infected cells show intranuclear inclusions, multinucleated giant cells with faceted nuclei, and ground-glass chromatin(Tzanck cells). May also form Lipschutz bodies (Cowdry type A inclusions).

question_text: Which of the following is not routinely screened before performing a blood transfusion?
explanation:
Explanation:

Hepatitis A is not routinely tested before blood transfusion because its primary mode of transmission is fecal-oral rather than through blood. It usually presents as an acute, self-limiting infection without progression to chronic disease; hence the risk of transfusion-related spread is minimal.

  • Screening before transfusion ensures patient safety by minimizing the risk of transmitting infectious diseases.
  • In addition to Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV, screening for syphilis and malaria is also mandatory in many settings.
  • The selection of safe donors, proper testing, and storage are critical steps in transfusion medicine.

Explanation of other options:

Hepatitis B (Option B): Mandatory screening, as it is a blood-borne infection with potential chronicity and serious complications.

Hepatitis C (Option C): Mandatory screening due to its efficient transmission via blood and high risk of chronic liver disease.

HIV 1 / HIV 2 (Option D): Essential screening to prevent transfusion-related transmission of HIV infection.

Key Takeaways:

  • Hepatitis A is not screened as it is not transmitted through blood transfusion.
  • Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV are routinely screened due to their blood-borne transmission risks.
  • Blood safety protocols also include screening for syphilis and malaria.

question_text: A patient received four units of blood transfusion two hours ago and now reports chest discomfort. A chest X-ray reveals bilateral fissure thickening. What is the most likely cause of this presentation?
explanation:
Explanation:

Fluid overload is the most likely cause in this scenario. Transfusion of multiple units of blood, especially in a short period, can result in transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO), leading to symptoms like chest discomfort, shortness of breath, and bilateral fissure thickening on chest X-ray (indicative of pulmonary oedema).

Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload (TACO) is a common but often underrecognised complication of blood transfusions. It has become the leading cause of death related to transfusions since the risk of Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury (TRALI) has decreased.

  • Risk factors:
    • Advanced age
    • Renal failure
    • Pre-existing fluid overload
    • Cardiac dysfunction
    • Administration of large blood volumes
    • Rapid transfusion rates relative to the patient's hemodynamic tolerance
  • Clinical presentation:
    • Dyspnea and hypoxia
    • Bilateral, predominantly alveolar infiltrates seen on chest X-ray
    • Frequent systolic hypertension
    • Elevated brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) levels
    • Fever (in some cases)
  • Prevention:
    • Identifying high-risk patients
    • Close monitoring during transfusion
    • Slowing the transfusion rate (e.g., administering 1 unit of red blood cells over 3-4 hours)
    • Using diuretics in hemodynamically stable patients with a history of TACO
  • Treatment:
    • Stopping the transfusion immediately
    • Administering oxygen
    • Administering diuretics to alleviate symptoms and prevent further complications.

Explanation for other options:

ABO incompatibility reaction (Option A) is a severe reaction that occurs immediately after transfusion and presents with hemolysis, fever, chills, and dark urine rather than chest discomfort or pulmonary findings like bilateral fissure thickening.

Hypocalcemia (Option C) can occur after rapid blood transfusions due to the citrate in blood products, which binds calcium. However, hypocalcemia typically presents with symptoms like tetany, paresthesias, or cardiac arrhythmias rather than chest discomfort and lung findings on X-ray.

Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) (Option D) is a rare but serious complication of blood transfusions, primarily in immunocompromised patients. It presents with skin rash, liver dysfunction, and gastrointestinal symptoms rather than chest discomfort or pulmonary oedema on X-ray.

question_text: Which of the following can be transmitted by most of the blood components?
explanation:
Explanation:

Malaria can be transmitted by most of the blood components.

  • Plasma processing methods have been shown to inactivate most recognized infectious organisms, except for non-lipid-enveloped viruses and prions.
  • All clinically relevant blood components transmit prion disease following a single blood transfusion.
  • Malaria can be transmitted by most blood components (red cells, platelets, white-cell concentrates, cryoprecipitates, and frozen red cells after thawing and washing).
    • Transmission from single-donor FFP has not been reported.
  • In India, the following five diseases are screened:
    • HBV
    • HCV
    • HIV
    • Malaria
    • Syphilis
  • Screening for the diseases mentioned above is mandatory, and transfusing unscreened blood is a medical offence.

Explanation of other options:

Syphilis (Option A): Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum, an organism that does not survive well in stored blood. Thus, transmission of syphilis through blood is extremely rare.

Toxoplasmosis (Option B): Toxoplasmosis is caused by Toxoplasma gondii, which is primarily transmitted through contaminated food, soil, or cat feces. It is not spread via all blood components.

Filarial infection (Option D): Filarial diseases are caused by parasites like Wuchereria bancrofti, which is transmitted by mosquito bites, not through blood transfusions, and does not involve all blood components

question_text: A 65-year-old female presents complaining of severe fatigue, which began 4 months ago and has gradually worsened. On examination she has moderate hepatosplenomegaly with normal examination of the heart, lungs, and skin. A complete blood count shows a leukocyte count of 150 × 10^9 cells/L, hemoglobin level of 9.8 g/dL, and platelet count of 424 ×  10^9 cells/L. A peripheral blood smear shows immature leukocyte forms as well as teardrop-shaped erythrocytes and nucleated red cells. Cytogenetic testing is negative for the BCR-ABL1 translocation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Here's the reasoning:

  • Clinical Presentation:
    • Severe fatigue.
    • Hepatosplenomegaly (enlargement of the liver and spleen).
    • Abnormal complete blood count (CBC).
  • CBC Findings:
    • Leukocyte count of 150 × 10^9 cells/L (elevated white blood cells).
    • Hemoglobin level of 9.8 g/dL (low hemoglobin).
    • Platelet count of 424 × 10^9 cells/L (elevated platelets).
  • Peripheral Blood Smear:
    • Immature leukocyte forms.
    • Teardrop-shaped erythrocytes (dacrocytes).
    • Nucleated red cells.
  • Cytogenetic Testing:
    • Negative for the BCR-ABL1 translocation, which is characteristic of chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML).

Myelofibrosis is a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by the proliferation of abnormal bone marrow cells, which leads to fibrosis (scarring) of the bone marrow. This condition can result in anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, and a characteristic blood picture with teardrop-shaped red blood cells (dacrocytes) and nucleated red cells. It often presents with fatigue and discomfort due to the enlarged spleen and liver.

The absence of the BCR-ABL1 translocation rules out CML. While acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) can also present with anemia and leukocytosis, the chronicity of the symptoms and presence of fibrosis make myelofibrosis a more likely diagnosis in this case. β-thalassemia major typically presents earlier in life with severe anemia and would not explain the leukocytosis and hepatosplenomegaly.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th edition, page number -483

question_text: A 35-year-old patient presents with colicky abdominal pain, joint pain, and palpable purpura. Urinalysis reveals the presence of red blood cells only, with no significant proteinuria.Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The constellation of palpable purpura, abdominal pain, arthralgia, and isolated hematuria (without heavy proteinuria) is classic for IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura, HSP).

Pathophysiology: Immune complex (IgA) deposition in capillaries, venules, and arterioles leads to leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

  • Epidemiology: More common in children but can affect adults.
  • Urinalysis:Typically shows RBCs ± RBC casts with minimal proteinuria.

Explanation for Other Options:

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Option B): A necrotising small-medium vessel vasculitis with granuloma formation. Classically causes upper & lower respiratory tract symptoms (chronic sinusitis, nasal ulcers, hemoptysis) and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Palpable purpura and abdominal colic without involvement of the lungs or ENT are atypical.

Microscopic polyangiitis (Option C): ANCA-associated small vessel vasculitis presenting with pulmonary capillaritis (hemoptysis) and rapidly progressive GN. It lacks the IgA-mediated skin/GI features and typically causes more severe renal proteinuria than seen here.

Behçet's disease (Option D): Characterised by recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis, and variable-vessel vasculitis. Palpable purpura with isolated hematuria and abdominal colic is not typical.

question_text: What should be the sequence of events during collection of blood sample?
option_a: Ask the patient his name → ®Verify from file → Label the sample at bedside → Collect blood
option_b: Look at the file → Collect sample → Label the sample at bedside
option_c: Prelabel the sample vials → Check the file for patient details → Collect sample
option_d: Collect sample → Confirm name from file → Label the sample vial
explanation:
WHO guidelines on drawing blood: best practices in phlebotomy

The following is the recommended sequence of events during collection of blood sample:

  1. Select the site: Blood is usually collected from veins, capillaries, and arteries. Venous blood is collected from the anticubital vein most commonly. Blood is also collected from the vein of arms, dorsum of hands. Long cephalic vein is also used where non-availability of the former veins. Infant's femoral vein is used for collection of blood.
  2. Prepare the patient: Explain the procedure to the patient and obtain consent. Position the patient comfortably and ensure that the patient is relaxed.
  3. Prepare the equipment: Ensure that all the equipment is ready and within reach. The equipment includes a tourniquet, alcohol swabs, needles, tubes, and a tray.
  4. Apply the tourniquet: Apply the tourniquet to the upper arm and ask the patient to make a fist.
  5. Clean the site: Clean the site with an alcohol swab and allow it to dry.
  6. Insert the needle: Insert the needle into the vein at a 15-30 degree angle with the bevel up. Once the needle is in the vein, release the tourniquet.
  7. Collect the blood: Collect the required amount of blood into the appropriate tubes. Invert the tubes gently to mix the sample well. Do not shake vigorously as this may lead to hemolysis of the blood sample.
  8. Remove the needle: Once the required amount of blood has been collected, remove the needle from the vein and apply pressure to the site with a cotton ball or gauze.
  9. Dispose of the equipment: Dispose of the equipment in the appropriate manner.

Reference: Robbins & cotran pathologic basis of diseases, 10th edition Chapter 14, pg 635

question_text: In a venule, which of the following cells are typically located in the centre of the lumen?
explanation:
Explanation:

Red blood cells (RBCs) ccupy the central axial column in the lumen of venules. This arrangement occurs due to laminar blood flow, where RBCs remain in the centre while white blood cells and platelets are pushed toward the vessel wall (margination). RBCs are responsible for transporting oxygen from the lungs to tissues and carrying carbon dioxide back to the lungs for exhalation.

Explanation for Other Options:

Lymphocytes (Option A): Lymphocytes are white blood cells critical for adaptive immunity. B cells produce antibodies, T cells regulate immune responses, and Natural Killer cells target infected or malignant cells. They originate in the bone marrow, circulate in blood and lymph, and are generally found near the endothelium of blood vessels, rather than in the central lumen of venules.

Neutrophils (Option C): Neutrophils are key defenders against bacterial infections, produced in the bone marrow. They rapidly migrate to infection sites and destroy pathogens via phagocytosis. In blood vessels, neutrophils are pushed toward the vessel wall (margination) and are not located in the central axial column.

Platelets (Option D): Platelets are small cytoplasmic fragments derived from megakaryocytes that play a critical role in hemostasis. They aggregate at sites of vascular injury to form clots. In circulating blood, platelets are primarily near the vessel walls, not in the centre of the lumen.

question_text: A 76-year-old Caucasian man presents to his physician because of severe itching following warm baths and showering. These episodes are not associated with visible rash, and the patient reports trying multiple different soaps and shampoos with no change in the symptoms. On examination he appears to be his stated age, ruddy cyanosis of the face is noted, heart and lungs are normal to auscultation. His spleen is slightly enlarged. His serum leukocyte count is 14.3 &times 10^9 cells/L, hemoglobin is 20.1 g/dL, and platelet count is 850 × 10^9 cells/L. Which of the following is likely to be demonstrated on additional testing?
option_a: Positive JAK2 mutation on reverse transcription PCR
option_b: 9,22 translocation on fluorescence in situ hybridization
option_c: Tartate-resistant acid phosphatase activity on peripheral blood film
option_d: Teardrop-shaped erythrocytes on peripheral blood smear
explanation:
• The patient's elevated hemoglobin, history of pruritus with bathing, and ruddy appearance all suggest polycythemia. 95% of all patients with polycythemia vera are positive for the JAK2 mutation.
  • The other tests listed are more consistent with CML, hair cell leukemia, myelofibrosis, and acute promyelocytic leukemia.

question_text: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the emergency room by his family. Over the past two weeks, he has developed marked fatigue, and his parents have noted pinpoint hemorrhages in his eyelids. On examination, the patient appears ill. His vital signs are temperature of 99.6°F, blood pressure of 100/65 mm Hg, and pulse rate of 102 bpm. The white blood cell count is 87,000 cells/μL, with 92% blasts, hemoglobin of 8.6 g/dL, and platelet count of 68,000 cells/ μL. Of the following, which would genetic testing most likely reveal?
explanation:
• The patient has acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The symptoms and signs are consistent with an infiltrative process in the bone marrow, and the differential indicates an acute leukemia.
  • In children, the majority (around 75%) of the acute leukemias are acute lymphoblastic leukemia, so, although other forms of leukemia are possible, the most common would be ALL. t(12;21), which translocates the TEL1 and AML1 genes, is characteristic of acute lymphoblastic leukemia. t(9;22) can be found in ALL, but most commonly in adult ALL.
  • Of the translocations, t(11;14) is found in mantle cell lymphoma, t(14;18) in follicular lymphoma, and t(15;17) in acute myeloid leukemia.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10thedition, page number - 465

question_text: A 50-year-old male presents to his family physician with complaints of fatigue, present for the past 2 months. During that time, he has also lost 20 lbs. without any change in his diet or exercise regimen. His vital signs are temperature of 99.5°F, pulse of 86 bpm, and blood pressure of 125/82 mm Hg. A physical examination reveals splenomegaly. Laboratory testing indicates a white blood cell count of 102,500 cells/μL, hemoglobin of 10.9 g/dL, and Hct of 33%. The blood smear has a prominence of metamyelocytes and myelocytes. If genetic testing is performed, which of the following would most likely be identified?
explanation:
• The patient has signs and symptoms consistent with chronic myelogenous leukemia, which could present with fatigue, weight loss, fever, and splenomegaly. The blood smear is consistent with a leukemia, and the description is that of a chronic myeloid leukemia, with more mature leukemia cells (i.e., not blasts).
  • Of the translocations, the t(9;22) is found in CML. t(8;14) is found in Burkitt’s lymphoma, t(11;14) in mantle cell lymphoma, t(14;18) in follicular lymphoma, and t(15;17) in acute myeloid leukemia.

question_text: A 23-year-old man complains of nasal obstruction, bloody nose, cough, and bloody sputum. A chest X-ray displays cavitated lesions and multiple nodules within both lung fields. Urinalysis reveals 3+ hematuria and red blood cell casts. Laboratory studies show anemia and elevated serum levels of C-ANCA (antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody). Peripheral eosinophils are not increased. A renal biopsy was performed and histopathological image is shown below. Based on the above findings, what is your probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Histopathological images shows crescent which is seen in rapidly proliferative glomerulonephritis.

  • The classic histologic picture is one of enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli. The hypercellularity is caused by
    1. Infiltration by leukocytes, both neutrophils and monocytes;
    2. Proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells.
  • The glomeruli often show focal and segmental necrosis, and variably show diffuse or focal endothelial proliferation, and mesangial proliferation. Segmental glomerular necrosis and distinctive crescents.
  • In classic MPGN, histologic picture is one of enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli. The hypercellularity is caused by
    1. Infiltration by leukocytes, both neutrophils and monocytes;
    2. Proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells.
  • By light microscopy, the glomeruli either appears normal in the early stages of the disease or exhibit uniform, diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall.

question_text: An adult male presents with abdominal distension, chronic diarrhoea, visual complaints, and neurological symptoms. Examination of the peripheral blood smear reveals following characteristic findings. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Based on the patient's clinical features and blood smear showing acanthocytes (spur cells), the most likely diagnosis is Abetalipoproteinemia.

Explanation for other options:

Whipple's disease (Option B) occurs due to Tropheryma whipplei (an actinomycete). It is characterised by foamy macrophages in the small intestinal lamina propria, which contain periodic acid Schiff (PAS)-positive and diastase-resistant granules (partially digested bacteria within lysosomes). While diarrhoea and neurological manifestations are present, protruding abdomen and visual disturbances are less characteristic and peripheral smear findings do not show acanthocytes.

Menetrier's disease (Option C): A rare condition involving hypertrophic gastric folds with protein-losing gastropathy, leading to hypoalbuminemia and oedema. It does not typically cause diarrhoea, visual disturbances, or neurological manifestations, making it unlikely in this case.

Uremia (Option D) results from advanced kidney failure and presents with nonspecific symptoms such as fatigue, nausea, and confusion. While neurological manifestations may occur, diarrhoea and a protruding abdomen are not typical features. Peripheral smear findings do not align with uremia.

question_text: Identify the areas labeled 1, 2 and 3.

question_text: A 33-year-old woman has had several "fainting spells" over the past 6 months. Each time, she has a prodrome of lightheadedness followed by a brief loss of consciousness. After each episode, she awakens and on examination has no loss of motor or sensory function. Physical examination after the current episode shows that she is afebrile, with a pulse of 72/min, respirations of 17/min, and blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg. Imaging studies reveal a 0.5 cm lesion in the head of the pancreas. The microscopic appearance of this lesion is shown in the figure. Which of the following pancreatic disorders is most likely to be present in this patient?
explanation:
The figure shows a circumscribed cellular lesion in the pancreas, most suggestive of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (PanNET). Secretion of insulin by these lesions causes hypoglycemia and the described symptoms. Many of these tumors are less than 1 cm in diameter, making them difficult to detect. Most patients who have an insulinsecreting PanNET have only mild insulin hypersecretion. The laboratory finding of an increased insulin-to-glucose ratio is helpful. Surgical excision is necessary in patients with marked symptoms. Acute pancreatitis is unlikely to increase islet cell release of insulin. Adenocarcinomas of the pancreas are derived from ductal epithelium and have no endocrine function. Fatty replacement of the pancreas can occur with cystic fibrosis, but the number of islets also gradually diminishes. Pseudocysts are complications of pancreatitis that are focal and do not produce insulin hypersecretion.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition, chapter 24, pg 1113

question_text: A young child presents with bleeding gums and bruising for the past two weeks. Bone marrow biopsy and flow cytometry have been performed. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation, along with histopathological and flow cytometry findings, confirms a diagnosis of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) with a B-cell phenotype based on the following results.
  • Histopathological examination reveals lymphoblasts with condensed nuclear chromatin, small nucleoli, and scant agranular cytoplasm.
  • Flow cytometry analysis:
    • Image B: The lymphoblasts (indicated by red dots) expressing terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) and the B-cell marker CD22.
    • Image C: The cells test positive for two other markers, CD10 and CD19, commonly found on pre-B lymphoblasts.

Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL)

  • ALL is an acute-onset blood and bone marrow malignancy of B and T lymphoblasts characterised by the uncontrolled proliferation of abnormal and immature lymphocytes.
  • Clinical features
    • Age: 2-8 years (Fast disease progression), adults: > 50 years.
    • Weight loss, Night sweats
    • Anemia: Easy fatigability and pallor
    • Bleeding: Epistaxis, easy bruising.
    • Leukocytopenia: Recurrent infections
    • Bone Marrow proliferation: Bone pain, sternal tenderness
    • Hepatosplenomegaly, Lymphadenopathy
    • CNS leukemia: Raised ICP, vomiting, and 6th nerve palsy
    • T cell tumors: Mediastinal and testicular mass.

Diagnosis

  • CBC is the first investigation performed while suspecting ALL:
    • Hemoglobin (Hb): Decreased, indicating normocytic normochromic anemia.
    • Hyperleukocytosis: TLC >100,000/µL can lead to leukostasis (more common in AML than ALL) with >20% Blasts.
    • Elderly Presentation: TLC often remains low throughout ALL.
    • Thrombocytopenia may be present.
  • Peripheral smear
    • The smear shows a high percentage of lymphoblasts, which are larger than normal lymphocytes and have a high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio.
    • They often have a scant amount of cytoplasm and may exhibit nucleoli.
  • Bone Marrow aspiration shows blasts >20%.
    • It is also used to classify morphological types into L1, L2, and L3 in the FAB classification system.
  • FISH: Fluorescent in situ hybridisation shows translocation of genes/chromosomes.
    • t(9:22) - ALL associated with the Philadelphia chromosome.
    • t(8:14) - Associated with Burkitt's leukemia
    • t(4:11)
    • t(1:19)
  • Flow cytometry:
    • CD10, also known as common acute lymphoblastic leukaemia antigen (CALLA), is a cell surface marker commonly used in the classification and diagnosis of leukaemias and lymphomas, particularly acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL).
    • B cell type - CD19+, CD79a+
    • T cell type - CD3+ (Option D ruled out)

Explanation of other options:

Acute myeloid leukaemia (Option A): A malignancy of hematopoietic progenitor cells caused by mutations that block differentiation, leading to an accumulation of immature myeloid blasts. These blasts have delicate chromatin, 2-4 nucleoli, and more cytoplasm than lymphoblasts, often containing peroxidase-positive azurophilic granules. Auer rods, needle-like azurophilic inclusions, are commonly present.

CLL (Option B): Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) is marked by lymph node infiltration with small lymphocytes that have condensed chromatin and scant cytoplasm, along with larger activated lymphocytes forming proliferation centers, which are pathognomonic for CLL/SLL. Peripheral blood shows small lymphocytes and smudge cells, and the bone marrow, spleen, and liver are commonly involved to varying extents.

question_text: Patient with generalized fatigue, tiredness. Primary clinical examination is uneventful. Normal TLC and DLC. No immature cells were seen. Superficial discrete lymph nodes enlarged. On biopsy showed effaced architecture, indented nucleus, prominent nucleolus containing atypical cells. CD10 and bcl2 positive.
explanation:
Here the question is based on immunophenotypic markers that are seen in the image below.

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice B: Burkitt's Lymphoma

  • Burkitt's lymphoma also expresses CD10, but it is BCL2 negative.
  • Burkitt's typically has a high mitotic index and a "starry sky" appearance, which is not described in this case.

Choice C: Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma (NHL)

  • Follicular lymphoma is a subtype of NHL, but the question asks for a specific diagnosis.
  • Simply choosing "Non-Hodgkin's" is too broad when follicular lymphoma is clearly indicated by CD10 and BCL2 positivity.

Choice D: Mycosis Fungoides

  • Mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma) presents with skin lesions, Pautrier microabscesses, and cerebriform nuclei, none of which are described here.
  • It is not a CD10+ or BCL2+ lymphoma.

Key Takeaway:

The presence of CD10+ and BCL2+ atypical lymphoid cells with effaced lymph node architecture strongly suggests Follicular Lymphoma (t(14;18) translocation). Follicular cell lymphoma is the only lymphoma that is BCL2 positive.

question_text: An elderly male presents with bilateral cervical lymph node enlargement. Histopathological examination reveals small cleaved cells as well as larger cells with open chromatin. Immunohistochemistry reveals CD10-positive and BCL2-positive cells. Which of the following cytogenetic abnormalities is most commonly associated with this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

An elderly patient presenting with cervical lymphadenopathy along with both small cleaved cells and larger cells, which are CD10 and BCL2 positive, points to a diagnosis of follicular lymphoma, which is associated with t(14;18).

  • Follicular lymphoma is the most common type of indolent non-Hodgkin lymphoma, typically in middle age, with equal prevalence in males and females.
  • It is strongly linked to chromosomal translocations involving BCL2, most notably the t(14;18) translocation in about 90% of cases, which leads to BCL2 overexpression and inhibition of apoptosis.
  • Morphologically, the lymph nodes show a nodular or mixed nodular-diffuse growth pattern.
  • Two main cell types are present: small cleaved cells (centrocytes) with irregular nuclear contours and scant cytoplasm, and larger cells (centroblasts) with open chromatin, nucleoli, and moderate cytoplasm. Centrocytes predominate in most cases.
  • The histopathological findings are shown in the image below.
  • Bone marrow involvement is seen in 85% of cases, typically as paratrabecular lymphoid aggregates, with frequent splenic white pulp and hepatic portal triad infiltration.
  • The immunophenotype closely resembles germinal centre B cells, expressing CD19, CD20, CD10, surface immunoglobulin, and BCL6, but lacking CD5.
  • BCL2 is expressed in over 90% of cases, unlike normal germinal centre B cells, which are BCL2-negative.
  • Clinically, patients often present with painless, generalised lymphadenopathy. Extranodal involvement is uncommon, and the disease usually has a slow, waxing and waning course.

Explanation of other options:

t(11;18) (Option A): Extranodal marginal zone lymphomas (MALTomas) can harbour chromosomal rearrangements, including the t(11;18) translocation, which is relatively characteristic for this subtype and leads to upregulation of signalling proteins that enhance B-cell growth and survival. It causes increased production and activity of BCL10 or MALT1, which are key components of a signalling complex that triggers NF-κB activation, thereby enhancing B-cell proliferation and survival.

t(11;14) (Option C): Mantle cell lymphoma is characterised by the t(11;14) translocation leading to cyclin D1 overexpression and driving progression from the G to S phase of the cell cycle. Microscopically, the tumour typically shows a uniform population of small lymphocytes with irregular to cleaved nuclear contours, condensed chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and scant cytoplasm, lacking large centroblast-like cells and proliferation centres. Immunophenotypically, the neoplastic cells express high levels of cyclin D1, CD19, and CD20, along with surface Ig (usually IgM and IgD with κ or λ light chains), and are CD5 positive but CD23 negative.

t(8;14) (Option D): The commonest translocation seen in Burkitt’s lymphoma is t(8;14), but t(2;8) and t(8;22) are also seen. Burkitt lymphoma is characterised by a diffuse infiltration of medium-sized lymphoid cells and shows a high mitotic rate with numerous apoptotic cells, whose nuclear debris is engulfed by macrophages, producing the classic starry sky appearance.

question_text: A 60-year-old male presents with generalised lymphadenopathy, elevated leukocyte count, and smudge cells on peripheral smear. What is the next best test to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The constellation of findings-widespread lymph node enlargement, raised WBC count, and smudge cells-is highly suggestive of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL).

  • Flow cytometry is the investigation of choice for confirming CLL, as it identifies specific immunophenotypic markers present on malignant lymphocytes.
  • Typical markers in CLL include:
    • CD5+, CD19+, CD20+, CD23+, CD200+
    • CD10 negative

This test helps differentiate CLL from other leukaemias and lymphomas that share overlapping features.

Explanation of other options:

Cytogenetic study(Option A):

  • Techniques like FISH can detect genetic abnormalities in CLL (e.g., del(17p), del(13q)), which have prognostic value.
  • However, they are not the first diagnostic step; they are performed after diagnosis to guide prognosis and treatment.

Bone marrow biopsy(Option B):

  • Useful for assessing bone marrow infiltration or disease staging.
  • It is not required as an initial test when CLL is suspected based on peripheral blood findings

X-ray crystallography(Option D):

  • A method used to study the atomic structure of crystals is completely unrelated to leukaemia diagnosis.

question_text: Parvovirus preferentially involves in which of the following cells:
explanation:
A special form of red cell aplasia occurs in individuals infected with parvovirus B19, which preferentially infects and destroys red cell progenitors. Normal individuals clear parvovirus infections within 1 to 2 weeks; as a result, the aplasia is transient and clinically unimportant. However, in persons with moderate to severe hemolytic anemias, even a brief cessation of erythropoiesis results in rapid worsening of the anemia, producing an aplastic crisis.

question_text: Smudge cells are seen in--
explanation:
• Involved lymph nodes are effaced by sheets of small lymphocytes and by scattered ill-defined foci of larger, actively dividing cells. The predominant cells are small, resting lymphocytes with dark, round nuclei, and scanty cytoplasm.
  • The foci of mitotically active cells are called proliferation centres, which are pathognomonic for CLL/SLL. In addition to the lymph nodes, the bone marrow, spleen, and liver are involved in almost all cases.
  • In most patients there is an absolute lymphocytosis featuring small, mature-looking lymphocytes. These circulating cells are fragile and during the preparation of smears many are disrupted, producing characteristic smudge cells. Variable numbers of larger activated lymphocytes also are usually present in blood smears.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10thedition, page number - 467

question_text: The following picture shows a lymph node biopsy of a 30-year-old male with cervical lymphadenopathy. The diagnosis is:
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation along with the histopathological findings is indicative of Hodgkin lymphoma, characterized by the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells on histopathology.

A distinctive feature of Hodgkin lymphoma is its orderly, contiguous spread, where the disease progresses from one lymph node group to the immediately adjacent group without skipping regions.

Explanation of other options:

Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) (Option A) is a hematologic malignancy marked by the rapid proliferation of abnormal myeloid blasts in the bone marrow and peripheral blood. It is diagnosed when blasts constitute ≥20% of marrow or blood cells and may show Auer rods in myeloblasts.

Human papillomavirus (HPV) (Option C) is a sexually transmitted virus with low-risk strains (6 & 11) causing genital warts, and high-risk strains (16 & 18) associated with cervical carcinoma, vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN), and vulvar carcinoma. Histologically, HPV infection is characterized by koilocytosis, with enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei and perinuclear halos in the superficial epithelial layers.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) (Option D) is a malignancy of mature B-lymphocytes. It is not associated with lytic bone lesions or hypercalcemia. Peripheral blood smears often show smudge cells due to fragile lymphocytes and a uniform population of small, mature-appearing lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm.

question_text: A 30-year-old male complains of fatigue for one year. Examination reveals massive splenomegaly. Blood work shows anemia, total leukocyte count of 150,000/µL, with neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, myeloblasts, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes. The myeloid-to-erythroid ratio is 18:1. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The hallmark features-massive splenomegaly, marked leukocytosis with predominance of neutrophils and immature myeloid cells, basophilia, and elevated myeloid-to-erythroid ratio-indicate CML.

Phases of CML:

  • Chronic phase:<10% blasts, basophils <20%, leukocytosis.
  • Accelerated phase:10-19% blasts, ≥20% basophils, worsening cytopenias.
  • Blast crisis:≥20% blasts; resembles acute leukemia; ~50% transform to AML, others to ALL.

Comparative findings:

Explanation of other options:

ALL (Option A): ≥20% lymphoblasts; cytoplasmic vacuoles.

AML (Option B):≥20% myeloblasts; Auer rods.

CLL (Option D): Smudge cells; homogeneous small lymphocytes.

Key Takeaways:

  • CML hallmark:Philadelphia chromosome (t(9;22)).
  • Splenomegaly + leukocytosis + basophilia.
  • Risk of transformation to AML > ALL.

question_text:
A 35-year-old man presents with spontaneous nosebleeds, bleeding gums, and multiple ecchymoses. Laboratory investigations reveal:
1.Hemoglobin: 8.5 g/dL
2.Platelet count: 12,000/mm3
3.Total leukocyte count: 52,000/mm3 with 83% blasts
Flow cytometry shows CD33 positivity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The acute onset of pancytopenia-related symptoms (bleeding, fatigue, infections) with marked leukocytosis dominated by blasts is classic for Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML).
  • CD33 positivity confirms myeloid lineage of the blasts.
  • AML arises from genetic mutations in hematopoietic stem cells, leading to accumulation of immature myeloblasts in bone marrow and peripheral blood, resulting in marrow failure.
  • Clinical presentation:
    • Anemia: fatigue, pallor
    • Thrombocytopenia: petechiae, ecchymoses, mucosal bleeding
    • Leukopenia with dysfunctional blasts: recurrent infections
    • Gum hypertrophy, chloromas (especially in M4/M5 subtypes)
  • AML is a heterogeneous disease classified by FAB (French-American-British) and WHO criteria.
  • Cytogenetic abnormalities aid prognosis:
    • t(8;21) → M2 subtype
    • t(15;17) → M3 (promyelocytic leukemia, treated with ATRA)
  • Bone marrow: >20% myeloblasts is diagnostic (WHO criteria).
  • Treatment: Induction chemotherapy followed by consolidation or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in eligible patients.

Explanation of Other Options:

Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (Option B):

  • Lymphoblasts are CD33 negative and MPO negative.
  • More common in children and teenagers.
  • Often involves CNS, mediastinum, testes, and bone pain.

Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (Option C):

  • Characterized by smudge cells, CD20+ and CD5+ positivity, CD33 negative.
  • Usually presents in elderly adults with lymphocytosis, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly.

Myelodysplastic Syndrome (Option D):

  • Clonal disorder of hematopoietic stem cells causing dysplasia and ineffective hematopoiesis.
  • Can progress to AML in some patients but presents with cytopenias over months, not acute leukocytosis with blasts >80%.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: An elderly male presents with cervical lymph node enlargement and increased bleeding tendency. Bone marrow examination reveals >25% blasts, and the peripheral smear is as shown below. Which of the following cytogenetic abnormalities is most likely associated with this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given features of cervical lymphadenopathy and bleeding tendency alongside bone marrow with >25% blasts and auer rods on peripheral smear is suggestive of acute promyelocytic leukaemia, which is associated with t(15;17).

  • Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is a malignant disorder of hematopoietic progenitor cells caused by acquired oncogenic mutations that disrupt differentiation, leading to the accumulation of immature myeloid blasts in the bone marrow.
  • This accumulation replaces normal marrow elements, resulting in marrow failure and clinical consequences such as anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia.
  • AML can occur at any age but is more common in older adults, with incidence increasing significantly after age 60.
  • Pathogenesis involves several classes of mutations. The chromosomal abnormalities t(8;21) and inv(16) are the most frequent rearrangements, disrupting the RUNX1 and CBFB genes, respectively.
  • The rearrangements generate chimeric genes that code for fusion proteins, which impair RUNX1/CBFB function and block the maturation of myeloid cells.
  • In acute promyelocytic leukaemia, a t(15;17) translocation creates a PML-RARα fusion protein that arrests granulocyte differentiation, treatable with all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide.
  • Diagnosis requires at least 20% myeloid blasts in the bone marrow, identified morphologically by delicate chromatin, two to four nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm.
  • Auer rods are distinctive needle-like inclusions often seen in AML, especially with t(15;17). (Options A and C ruled out)
  • Immunophenotyping confirms the diagnosis by detecting myeloid-specific antigens.
  • In AML, clinical features usually develop over weeks to months and are due to marrow failure from blast replacement.
  • Patients often present with fatigue from anaemia, spontaneous mucocutaneous bleeding such as petechiae, ecchymoses, and mucosal haemorrhages from thrombocytopenia, and recurrent or severe infections from neutropenia.
  • Fever is common, and bleeding may be pronounced in cases with t(15;17) due to the release of procoagulants.
  • Some patients develop extramedullary involvement such as gingival hypertrophy, skin infiltration (leukaemia cutis), or localised soft tissue masses (myeloid sarcoma).

Explanation of other options:

t(9;22) (Option D): In chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) and certain cases of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, the ABL gene relocates from its usual position on chromosome 9 to chromosome 22, where it merges with the BCR gene. This translocation produces a fusion gene that encodes the BCR-ABL chimeric protein, which possesses continuous tyrosine kinase activity.

question_text: A 53-year-old man has had increasing fatigue for the past 6 months. On physical examination he has a palpable spleen tip. Laboratory studies show a WBC count of 189,000/microliter. The peripheral blood smear shows many mature and immature myeloid cells present. Cytogenetic analysis of cells obtained via bone marrow aspiration reveals a t(9:22) translocation. This translocation leads to formation of a hybrid gene that greatly increases tyrosine kinase activity. Which of the following genes is most likely translocated to cause these findings?
explanation:
• The above history shows organomegaly with increased WBC counts.
  • Peripheral smear with mature, immature myeloid cells and t(9:22) translocation is case of chronic myeloid leukemia.
  • BCR-ABL fusion gene formation is an early, perhaps initiating, event that drives leukemogenesis.
  • The crucial role of BCR-ABL in cancer has been confirmed by the dramatic clinical response of patients with chronic myeloid leukemia to BCR-ABL kinase inhibitors.

Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10th ed, Pg: 207.

question_text: Which of the following is not an immunohistochemical marker for gastrointestinal stromal tumours?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Neuregulin/NRG-1 is not a marker for GIST diagnosis.
  • It is seen in non-TRU type lung adenocarcinoma, including mucinous adenocarcinoma (most common subtype - 38.1%), followed by TRU type lung adenocarcinoma (23.8%) and GI (gastrointestinal) and PB (pancreaticobiliary)(23.8%).

Immunohistochemistry (IHC) markers for GIST

  • DOG1
    • DOG1 is a transmembrane protein and functions as a calcium-activated chloride channel protein.
    • Highly specific and sensitive immunohistochemical marker for GIST; diagnostic of GIST.
    • Most specific marker for GIST and is diagnostic of GIST.
  • KIT (CD117) (Option C ruled out)
    • Most common mutation associated with GIST in adults.
    • KIT or c-kit is a proto-oncogene that encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase.
    • Mutations in KIT are the most frequent genetic alterations in GISTs, found in approximately 70-80% of cases.
  • SDH (Option B ruled out)
    • Succinate Dehydrogenase (SDH) is a mitochondrial enzyme crucial for energy production.
    • Mutations in SDH subunits are found in SDH-deficient GISTs, which lack KIT/PDGFRA mutations.
    • These GISTs are associated with:
      • Carney-Stratakis syndrome (GIST + paraganglioma)
      • Carney triad (GIST + paraganglioma + pulmonary chondroma).
  • PDGFRA (Option A ruled out)
    • Platelet-derived growth factor receptor α (PDGFRA) mutations are most commonly found in gastric GISTs, particularly in the epithelioid variants.
    • They account for approximately 30% to 40% of GISTs that are negative for KIT mutations.
  • CD34: Can sometimes be positive.

Key Takeaways:

IHC Markers of GIST

  • CD117(C-Kit): Most common and highly sensitive.
  • DOG-1: Highly sensitive and specific in C-Kit negative cases.
  • PDGFRA
  • CD34: Non-specific marker of GIST.

Reference:

Targeting Neuregulin 1 (NRG1): A Novel Biomarker for Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer - PubMed

question_text: A patient presented with painless b/l proptosis. What is the next investigation to diagnose it as chloroma?
explanation:
Myeloid (granulocytic) sarcoma, or myeloblastoma are extramedullary blast proliferation.These tumors are called chloromas because some appear green or turn green in dilute acid secondary to expression of MPO. The tumors are usually localized; they often involve bone, periosteum, soft tissues, lymph nodes, or skin. Common sites are the orbit and the paranasal sinuses.

The diagnosis can be made, if Auer rods are detected on blasts in peripheral smear or if myeloid origin is confirmed by cytochemical or immunohistochemical methods. The diagnosis should be suspected, if eosinophilic myelocytes are present in hematoxylin and eosin–stained biopsy sections. Imprint preparations can be helpful.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition, chapter 13, pg 601

question_text: A 5-year-old child was presenting with proptosis. Microscopic examination of the mass has revealed a round cell tumor positive for Desmin immunohistochemical marker. Most likely diagnosis would be:
explanation:
Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma. In the four options provided, all four show morphology of a round cell tumor. However, Desmin positivity is seen only in cases of rhabdomyosarcoma.

  • Three subtypes are alveolar (20%), embryonal (60%), and pleomorphic (20%).
