question_text: A 18-year-boy has experienced headaches, polyuria, and visual problems for the past 5 months. On physical examination, he has bilateral temporal visual field deficits. CT scan of the head shows a large, partially calcified, cystic mass occupying the sellar and suprasellar areas. Removal of the lesion and its histopathological images is shown below. What is your probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Tumor shows palisading epithelium, wet keratin and stellate reticulum which is characteristic of Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma

Craniopharyngiomas are uncommon, usually suprasellar neoplasms; they are typically found in young individuals. They are thought to arise from embryological remnants of the Rathke pouch in the region of the pituitary. These are aggressive neoplasms that infiltrate and destroy the surrounding tissues, making a complete excision difficult. Despite their aggressive behavior, they are composed of benign-appearing squamoid or primitive tooth structures. The increase in prolactin occurs as a “stalk section” effect, and the hypernatremia results from diabetes insipidus caused by the destruction of the hypothalamus, posterior pituitary, or both. A metastasis to this location in a young individual is highly unlikely.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10th Edition, Page Number-1066.

question_text: An 72-year-old man presents with painless swelling below the right ear that has been growing slowly for about a year. Physical examination confirms a cystic lesion. Fine- needle aspiration returns scanty brown fluid, which microscopically consists of a mixture of lymphoid cells and epithelial cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. A biopsy of the mass is shown in the image. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Warthin tumor is a benign neoplasm of the parotid gland, composed of cystic glandular spaces embedded in dense lymphoid tissue. This tumor is the most common monomorphic adenoma. Although the neoplasm is clearly benign, it can be bilateral (15% of cases) or multifocal within the same gland. Warthin tumor is the only tumor of the salivary glands that is more common in men than in women. These lesions generally occur after the age of 30, with most arising after age 50 years. Pleomorphic adenoma (choice c) has a biphasic appearance, which represents an admixture of epithelial and stromal elements. Acinic cell carcinoma (choice a) is an uncommon malignancy. Adenoid cystic carcinoma (choice b) is a slow-growing malignant neoplasm of the salivary gland, which invades locally and tends to recur after surgery.

question_text: A 33-year-old woman has been bothered by a bump on the dorsum of her left wrist for the past 4 months. On physical examination, there is a 1 cm firm but fluctuant subcutaneous nodule over an extensor tendon of the left wrist. The nodule is painful on palpation and movement. Mucoid fluid is aspirated from the nodule. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A ganglion cyst has a thin wall and clear, mucoid content. It arises in the connective tissue of a joint capsule or tendon sheath. The extensor surfaces of the hands and feet are the most common sites, particularly the wrist. Ganglion cysts probably arise after trauma from focal myxoid degeneration of connective tissue to produce a cystic space. They may regress. If not, and if they are painful, they can be excised. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor (villonodular synovitis) is a more diffuse form of giant cell tumor of tendon sheath (a solid mass lesion) and is a proliferation of mononuclear cells resembling synoviocytes. A lipoma is a mass of adipocytes and is not cystic. Nodular fasciitis is a solid reactive fibroblastic proliferation seen in the upper extremities and trunk of young adults, sometimes occurring after trauma. Rheumatoid nodules are firm, solid masses that typically occur in individuals who already have joint involvement with rheumatoid arthritis. A tophus is a solid mass of chalky sodium urate crystals in patients who have a history of gout.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition , chapter 26, pg 1187

question_text: A 44-year-old woman had increasing abdominal enlargement for the past 6 months. She states that she feels like she is pregnant, but results of a pregnancy test are negative. On physical examination, there is abdominal distention with a fluid wave. A pelvic ultrasound scan shows bilateral cystic ovarian masses, 10 cm on the right and 7 cm on the left. The masses are surgically removed. On gross examination, the excised masses are unilocular cysts filled with clear fluid, and papillary projections extend into the central lumen of the cyst. Image of histopathological examination is shown below, based on the above findings what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Microscopic examination shows that the papillae are covered with atypical cuboidal cells that invade underlying stroma.

(a) Endometrioid tumors resemble endometrial carcinomas and may arise in foci of endometriosis.

(b) Cystadenocarcinoma are common ovarian tumors that are often bilateral. The serous type is typically unilocular. As the name indicates, they are cystic in appearance. They may be benign, borderline, or malignant. Benign tumors have a smooth cyst wall with small or absent papillary projections. Borderline tumors have increasing amounts of papillary projections.

(c) Dysgerminomas are solid tumors of germ cell origin. Histological shows lobules of polygonal cells with clear cytoplasm and lymphocytic infiltrate in fibrous septae

(d) Granulosa cell tumors can be solid and cystic and may have Call-Exner bodies with nuclear grooves.

question_text: A 25-year-old woman presents with lower abdominal discomfort. Post-surgical image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis? Biopsy specimen is as shown below.
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis based on the biopsy specimen of the ovary showing cutaneous structures such as hair, is mature cystic teratoma.

Explanation of other options:

Serous cystadenoma (Option A): Serous cystadenomas are often multicystic, with papillary epithelium inside fibrous cyst walls or projecting from the ovarian surface. Benign forms have smooth cyst walls, while borderline tumors show more papillary projections and serous carcinomas display irregular growth, capsule nodularity, and bilateral involvement. Microscopically, they are lined by columnar epithelium, with borderline and malignant forms showing increased papillary complexity, nuclear atypia, and potential stromal infiltration.

Immature teratoma (Option B): Immature teratomas differ from mature ones by containing embryonic or fetal tissues, most commonly primitive neuroepithelial structures.

Endometrioma (Option D): In endometriosis, the ovaries can be significantly altered by large cystic lesions (3-5 cm) filled with dark brown fluid from old haemorrhage, commonly called chocolate cysts or endometriomas.

question_text: Which part of the biliary tree is involved in congenital cystic dilatation that is choledochocele?

question_text:
Which of the following are TRUE for serous cystic neoplasm of pancreas?
i. They usually occur in tail of pancreas
ii. Present with abdominal pain
iii. It is benign neoplasm
iv. Lined by columnar epithelium
option_a: Only i, ii, and iii are correct
option_b: Only i and iii are correct
option_c: Only ii and iv are correct
explanation:
• Serous cystadenomas account for approximately 25% of all pancreatic cystic neoplasms; they are composed of glycogen-rich cuboidal cells surrounding small cysts containing clear, straw coloured fluid.
  • The tumours typically manifest in the seventh decade of life with nonspecific symptoms such as abdominal pain; the female-to-male ratio is 2:1. These tumours are almost uniformly benign, and surgical resection is curative in the vast majority of patients.
  • Most serous cystadenomas carry somatic loss of function mutations of the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) tumour suppressor gene, which you will recall is a negative regulator of hypoxia inducible factor 1 alpha (HIF-1-alpha).

question_text: A 10-year-old male child presented with persistent headache, associated with nausea and vomiting some times. CT scan of the head shows well demarcated oval shaped lesion with cystic change having smooth margin in the cerebellar region. Craniotomy was done, small part of the lesion is removed and send for histopathological examination, the image of which is shown below. Based on the above findings, what is your probable diagnosis.
explanation:
Cerebellar pilocytic astrocytomas usually present during the first two decades of life, with clumsiness, worsening headache, nausea, and vomiting. Most cerebellar and cerebral pilocytic astrocytomas are well demarcated, with a round or oval shape and smooth margins. Calcifications are occasionally present. Heterogeneity as a result of cyst-like areas intermixed with generally intensely enhancing soft tissue components is typical. On microscopy astrocytic tumor of low to moderate cellularity often has a biphasic pattern, with varying proportions of compacted bipolar cells with rosenthal fibers and loose-textured multipolar cells with microcysts. The biphasic pattern is best seen in cerebellar tumors.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition, Chapter – 28 pg 1293

question_text: Most radiosensitive tumour is?
explanation:
TESTICULAR CARCINOMA

The treatment of testicular germ cell neoplasms is a remarkable clinical success story. Although roughly 8000 new cases of testicular cancer occur in the United States yearly, fewer than 400 men are expected to die of the disease. Seminoma, which is extremely radiosensitive and tends to remain localized for long periods, has the best prognosis. More than 95% of patients with early-stage disease can be cured. Among nonseminomatous germ cell tumors, the histologic subtype does not influence the therapy. Approximately 90% of patients achieve complete remission with aggressive chemotherapy and most are cured. The exception is choriocarcinoma, which is associated with a poorer prognosis. With all testicular tumors, recurrences, typically in the form of distant metastases, usually occur within the first 2 years after treatment.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg: 697.

question_text: Which of the following area in a kidney is usually spared in early pyelonephritis?
explanation:
• The characteristic histologic feature of acute pyelonephritis is liquefactive necrosis and abscess formation within the renal parenchyma. In the early stages, pus formation (suppuration) is limited to the tubular lumina, but later abscesses rupture into the interstitial tissue.
  • Large masses of intratubular neutrophils frequently extend within involved nephrons into the collecting ducts, giving rise to characteristic white blood cell casts in the urine.Typically, the glomeruli are not affected.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th edition, Page- 565

question_text: 55-year male patient with persistent high blood pressure with papilledema and headache. What is your histopathology diagnosis from given history and microscopy findings of renal biopsy?
explanation:
• The histology figure shows fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles.
  • The kidney may be normal in size or shrunken, depending on the duration and severity of the hypertensive disease. Small, pinpoint petechial hemorrhages may appear on the cortical surface from rupture of arterioles or glomerular capillaries, giving the kidney a peculiar, flea-bitten appearance. The microscopic changes reflect the pathogenetic events discussed earlier. Damage to the small vessels is manifested as fibrinoid necrosis of the arterioles.
  • The vessel walls show a homogeneous, granular eosinophilic appearance masking underlying detail. In the interlobular arteries and larger arterioles, proliferation of intimal cells after acute injury produces an onion-skin appearance. This name is derived from the concentric arrangement of cells whose origin is believed to be intimal smooth muscle, although this issue has not been finally settled.
  • This lesion, called hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, causes marked narrowing of arterioles and small arteries, to the point of total obliteration. Necrosis also may involve glomeruli ,with microthrombi within the glomeruli as well as necrotic arterioles. Similar lesions are seen in individuals with acute thrombotic microangiopathies, and in patients with scleroderma in renal crisis.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th edition, Page- 570

question_text: A 55-year-old man presented with complaints of hematuria. He is otherwise in excellent health, except for a microcytic, hypochromic anemia. An enlarged right kidney is found on X-ray examination, and CT scan reveals a renal mass of irregular shape, measuring 6 cm in diameter. Nephrectomy was done and sent for histopathological examination, image of which is shown below. Which of the following is the diagnosis?

(a) It is a combination of muscle, fat and blood vessels

(b) Radiological examination must provide primary site of origin and histomorphology compatible with that tumor.

(c) In clear cell carcinoma, the growth pattern varies from solid to trabecular (cordlike) or tubular (resembling tubules). The tumor cells have a rounded or polygonal shape and abundant clear or granular cytoplasm, which contains glycogen and lipids.

(d) Tumor consists of blastemal, epithelial and stromal elements (triphasic) which can be present in variable amounts.

question_text: A 60-year-old man presented with complaints of hematuria. An enlarged right kidney is found on X-ray examination, and CT scan reveals a renal mass of irregular shape, measuring 6 cm in diameter. On nephrectomy tumor is encapsulated, mahogany brown in color and have a central scar and sent for histopathological examination, image of which is shown below. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
explanation:
(a) In clear cell carcinoma, the growth pattern varies from solid to trabecular (cordlike) or tubular (resembling tubules). The tumor cells have a rounded or polygonal shape and abundant clear or granular cytoplasm, which contains glycogen and lipids.

(b) Papillary carcinomas, thought to arise from distal convoluted tubules, can be multifocal and bilateral. They are typically hemorrhagic and cystic, especially when large. The tumor is composed of cuboidal or low columnar cells arranged in papillary cores.

(c) Chromophobe renal carcinoma is made up of pale eosinophilic cells, often with a perinuclear halo, arranged in solid sheets with a concentration of the largest cells around blood vessels.

(d) This is an epithelial neoplasm composed of large eosinophilic cells having small, round, benignappearing nuclei that have large nucleoli.

Reference: Robbins 10th Ed pg. 950

question_text: A 12-year-old male patient presented with puffiness of face, swelling in the feet and hematuria since 3 months. Laboratory studies show elevated serum levels of creatinine and BUN. Urinalysis reveals 3+ proteinuria and presence of RBCs. The renal biopsy was performed and image is shown below. All of the following statements are true regarding the diagnosis; except:
option_a: Histology will show proliferation of mesangial cells and mesangial matrix
option_b: Silver stain will show duplication of basement membrane
option_c: Immunofluorescence shows IgM and C4 depostion in a granular pattern
option_d: Electron microscopy shows sub endothelial deposits
explanation:
• The glomeruli are large and hypercellular. The glomeruli have an accentuated "lobular" appearance due to the proliferating mesangial cells and increased mesangial matrix.This is suggestive of MPGN
  • The GBM is thickened, and often shows a "doublecontour" or "tramtrack" appearance, especially evident in silver or PAS stains. This is caused by "duplication" of the basement membrane (also commonly referred to as splitting), usually as the result of new.
  • By immunofluorescence, IgG and C3 are deposited in a granular pattern, and early complement components (C1q and C4) are often also present, indicative of an immune complex pathogenesis.
  • Type I MPGN is characterized by the presence of discrete subendothelial electron-dense deposits. Mesangial and occasional subepithelial deposits may also be present.

Reference: Robbins 10th Ed pg. 918

question_text: A 25-year-old man presents with headaches, visual disturbances, and hypertension. MRI brain shows a cerebellar hemangioblastoma, and abdominal imaging reveals multiple cysts in the kidneys along with a solid renal mass suggestive of renal cell carcinoma. His father had similar findings and died from a brain tumour in his 40s, Which of the following chromosomal abnormalities is most likely associated with his condition?
explanation:
Explanations:

The given clinical scenario is consistent with a diagnosis of VHL syndrome, which arises due to a deletion of chromosome 3p.

Explanation of other options:

Deletion of Chromosome 13q (Option A): 13q deletions are associated with multiple myeloma and small lymphocytic lymphoma/CLL. The BRCA2 gene is located on chromosome 13q, and mutations can lead to breast cancer.

Deletion of chromosome 17p (Option B): The TP53 gene is located on chromosome 17p, and deletions are associated with small lymphocytic lymphoma and multiple myeloma.

Trisomy of chromosome 12 (Option C): Trisomy of chromosome 12 is associated with small lymphocytic lymphoma/CLL.

question_text: A 20-year-old patient presents with a cerebellar mass and a renal tumour, along with a similar family history. Which of the following is responsible for his findings?
explanation:
Explanation:

VHL is associated with both clear cell Renal cell carcinoma and cerebellar hemangioblastoma.

  • Autosomal dominant disorder of VHL gene on chromosome 3p.

It is associated with

  • Cerebellar Hemangioblastomas: Highly vascular tumours in the central nervous system, especially the cerebellum.
  • Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC): Often clear cell type, multifocal and bilateral
  • Retinal hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytomas, and pancreatic cysts.

Explanation for other options:

NF (Neurofibromatosis) (Option B)

  • Type 1 (NF1): Characterized by cutaneous neurofibromas, cafe-au-lait spots, and optic gliomas.
  • Type 2 (NF2): Associated with bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, and spinal tumours.
  • Neurofibromatosis does not involve renal tumours or cerebellar hemangioblastomas.

TSC (Tuberous Sclerosis Complex) (Option C) is caused by mutations in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes. It is associated with Angiofibromas, cortical tubers, subependymal giant cell astrocytomas, and renal angiomyolipomas.

Li-Fraumeni Syndrome is caused by a mutation in the TP53 gene (Option D): It is associated with multiple sarcomas, breast cancer, leukaemia, and brain tumours.

Reference:

Von Hippel-Lindau Syndrome | Treatment & Management | Point of Care

question_text: A 26-year-old male patient complains of blood in urine. Physical examination revealed raised BP and pitting edema. Laboratory findings like CBC and LFT are normal. question_text: A 17-year-old male patient presented with puffiness of face, swelling in the feet and hematuria since 3 months. Laboratory studies show elevated serum levels of creatinine and BUN. question_text: Commonest renal lesion in SLE(Systemic lupus erythematosus):
explanation:
• Diffuse lupus nephritis is the most common renal lesion in systemic lupus erythematosus(SLE). It is characterized by inflammation and damage to the glomeruli, which are the tiny filters in the kidneys that remove waste products from the blood.
  • Up to 50% of SLE patients have clinically significant renal involvement and the kidney virtually always shows evidence of abnormality if examined by electron microscopy and immunofluorescence.
  • Renal involvement takes a number of forms, all of which are associated with the deposition of immune complexes within the glomeruli. According to the currently accepted classification, six patterns of glomerular disease are recognized.
  • It should be noted that there is overlap within these classes and that lesions may evolve from one class to another over time. Thus, the exact percentage of patients with each of the six classes of lesions is difficult to determine. Suffice it to say that class I is the least common and class IV is the most common pattern.
  • Minimal mesangial lupus nephritis(class I) is very uncommon and is characterized by immune complex deposition in the mesangium, identified by immunofluorescence and by electron microscopy, but without structural changes by light microscopy.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg: 154.

question_text: Onion peeling of renal vessels is seen in:

This lesion occurs in severe hypertension; vessels exhibit concentric, laminated ("onionskin") thickening of the walls with luminal narrowing The laminations consist of SMCs with thickened, reduplicated basement membrane; in malignant hypertension, they are accompanied by fibrinoid deposits and vessel wall necrosis (necrotizing arteriolitis), particularly in the kidney

question_text: A 12-year-old male child presented with facial puffiness along with feet edema since 3 weeks. Physical examination shows pitting edema. The principal lesion is in the visceral epithelial cells, which show a uniform and diffuse effacement of foot processes, these being reduced to a rim of cytoplasm with loss of recognizable intervening slit diaphragms. Immunofluorescence studies shows no Ig or complement deposits.

question_text: A 47-year-old man complains of swelling of his legs and puffiness of face. Physical examination reveals generalized edema and ascites. Laboratory findings revealed normal CBC and LFT. question_text: A 26-year-old male patient complains of blood in urine. Physical examination revealed raised BP and pitting edema. Laboratory findings like CBC and LFT are normal. Renal function test are deranged showing raised creatinine and urea. Urinary investigation shows proteinuria 4+. Renal biopsy was performed, shown below. What is your probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• The classic histologic picture is one of enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli. The hypercellularity is caused by
    1. Infiltration by leukocytes, both neutrophils and monocytes;
    2. Proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells.
  • Crescents are formed by proliferation of glomerular epithelial cells and by migration of monocytes and macrophages into the urinary space. Neutrophils and lymphocytes may be present. The crescents may obliterate the urinary space and compress the glomerular tuft. Fibrin strands are frequently prominent between the cellular layers in the crescents.
  • The glomeruli are normal by light microscopy.
  • By light microscopy, the glomeruli either appear normal in the early stages of the disease or exhibit uniform, diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall.

question_text: A 57-year-old man presented with complaints of hematuria. An enlarged right kidney is found on X-ray examination, and CT scan reveals a renal mass of irregular shape, measuring 6 cm in diameter. Nephrectomy was done and sent for histopathological examination, image of which is shown below. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
explanation:
(a) In clear cell carcinoma, the growth pattern varies from solid to trabecular (cordlike) or tubular (resembling tubules). The tumor cells have a rounded or polygonal shape and abundant clear or granular cytoplasm, which contains glycogen and lipids.

(b) Papillary carcinomas, thought to arise from distal convoluted tubules, can be multifocal and bilateral. They are typically hemorrhagic and cystic, especially when large. The tumor is composed of cuboidal or low columnar cells arranged in papillary cores.

(c) Chromophobe renal carcinoma is made up of pale eosinophilic cells, often with a perinuclear halo, arranged in solid sheets with a concentration of the largest cells around blood vessels.

(d) This is an epithelial neoplasm composed of large eosinophilic cells having small, round, benignappearing nuclei that have large nucleoli.

Reference: Robbins 10th Ed pg. 950

question_text: Which ONE of the following is a commonest childhood Renal tumour?
explanation:

  • Three groups of congenital malformations are associated with an increased risk for Wilms tumour. These are
  • WAGR syndrome (i.e., Wilms tumour, aniridia, genital abnormalities, and mental retardation);
  • Denys-Drash syndrome (DDS),
  • and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS).
  • On microscopic examination, Wilms tumours are characterized by recognizable attempts to recapitulate different stages of nephrogenesis.The classic triphasic combination of blastemal, stromal, and epithelial cell types is observed in most lesions, although the percentage of each component is variable.

question_text: Which malignancy has the strongest association with asbestosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Asbestosis is a chronic pneumoconiosis caused by inhalation of asbestos fibers.

  • The malignancy most strongly associated is malignant mesothelioma, a tumour of pleura or peritoneum.
  • Asbestos also increases the risk of lung carcinoma, laryngeal carcinoma, ovarian carcinoma, colon carcinoma, and other pleural malignancies.
  • In smokers, the risk of bronchogenic carcinoma is synergistically amplified, making lung carcinoma more common than mesothelioma in asbestos workers.

Lung involvement: Unlike other pneumoconioses (which usually affect upper lobes), asbestosis predominantly affects lower lobes.

Common cancers linked with asbestos:

  • Adenocarcinoma (≈45%) → most common bronchogenic carcinoma type.
  • Squamous cell carcinoma → second most common.
  • Mesothelioma → specific marker for asbestos exposure, but less common overall compared to adenocarcinoma.

Explanation of other options:

Anthracosis (Option B): Characterized by black pigmentation of bronchial mucosa due to carbon and silica deposition. It causes bronchial anthracofibrosis (BAF) but is not a malignancy.

Hepatocellular carcinoma (Option C): Primary liver cancer linked to cirrhosis from hepatitis B/C, alcoholism, autoimmune hepatitis, and hemochromatosis-not asbestos.

Renal cell carcinoma (Option D): Originates from proximal tubular cells; associated with flank pain, hematuria, abdominal mass, and smoking, but not with asbestos exposure.

Key Takeaways:

  • Asbestosis → Mesothelioma is the classical association.
  • Most common asbestos-related cancer overall = Lung carcinoma (adenocarcinoma > squamous).
  • Site predilection: Lower lobes of lungs are more affected.

question_text: Patient with h/o long-standing depressive illness came to emergency with acute breathlessness. The X-ray shows diffuse infiltrates with predominance in right middle lobe and right lower lobe. The patient did not survive and the following picture in the lungs was seen on autopsy?
option_a: Severe necrosis with fungal hyphae, severe fungal pneumonia
explanation:
Aspiration pneumonia occurs in markedly debilitated patients or those who aspirate gastric contents either while unconscious (e.g., after a stroke) or during repeated vomiting.

These patients have abnormal gag and swallowing reflexes that predispose to aspiration. The resultant pneumonia is partly chemical due to the irritating effects of gastric acid and partly bacterial (from the oral flora). Typically, more than one organism is recovered on culture, aerobes being more common than anaerobes. This type of pneumonia is often necrotizing, pursues a fulminant clinical course, and is a frequent cause of death. In patients who survive, lung abscess is a common complication. Micro aspiration, in contrast, occurs frequently in almost all people, especially those with gastroesophageal reflux disease. It usually results in small, poorly formed non-necrotizing granulomas with multinucleated foreign body giant cell reaction. It is usually inconsequential, but may exacerbate other pre-existing lung diseases such as asthma, interstitial fibrosis, and lung rejection.

Reference: Robin's basic pathology 10th edition, 711

question_text: A 50-year-old woman complained of severe headaches and dizziness. The patient has a history of repeated urinary tract infections. The blood pressure is 180/110 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show elevated levels of BUN (38 mg/dL) and creatinine (2.8 mg/dL). A CT scan of the lower abdomen reveals small, irregularly shaped kidneys with deep coarse scars. Nephrectomy was done and histopathological examination features are shown below. Which of the following is the appropriate diagnosis?
explanation:
(a) Acute pyelonephritis is not characterized by scarred and shrunken kidneys.

(b & d) These are not related to bacterial infections.

(c) Patients with chronic pyelonephritis suffer episodic manifestations of urinary tract infection or acute pyelonephritis, such as recurrent fever and flank pain. Urinalysis demonstrates leukocytes, and imaging studies reveal cortical scarring. The microscopic appearance of chronic pyelonephritis is nonspecific. Histopathological shows periglomerular fibrosis, tubular dilation, and atrophy. Many tubules contain eosinophilic hyaline casts resembling the colloid of thyroid follicles (so-called hybridization). The interstitium is scarred and contains a chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate. Except for acute pyelonephritis, the other choices.

question_text: A female neonate is noted at birth to have a gross deformity of her lower back. Examination of the subcutaneous lesion reveals disorganized neural tissue with entrapment of nerve roots. What is the appropriate diagnosis?
explanation:
Neural tube defects (dysraphic anomalies) reflect impaired closure of the dorsal aspect of the vertebral column. These abnormalities are classified according the extent of the defect, ranging in severity from spina bifida occulta to meningocele, meningomyelocele, and rachischisis.

Spina bifida (choice d) is restricted to the vertebral arches and is usually asymptomatic.

Meningocele (choice a) permits protrusion of the meninges as a fluid-filled sac.

Meningomyelocele (choice b) exposes the spinal canal and causes the nerve roots to be entrapped.

Rachischisis (choice c) is an extreme defect, often without a recognizable spinal cord.

question_text: A 48-year-old male presents to his primary care physician for a rash that started 1 week prior to his visit. Erythematous lesions with necrotic centers can be seen in cellulitis; however, central clearing of the lesion would never be seen in cellulitis. The late manifestation of arthritis and cranial nerve palsy are extremely suggestive of Lyme disease. Neither a brain abscess nor a brain metastasis would cause cranial nerve VII palsy. With no other systemic symptoms, and given the fact that Lyme disease is much more common than Whipple’s disease, is incorrect. Such skin changes are not usually associated with Gaucher’s disease.
  • It is caused by infection with the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, which is transmitted by deer ticks of the Ixodes ricinus complex.
  • In its classic form, Lyme disease progressively involves multiple organ systems through three clinical phases. The initial infection of the skin, or early localized stage, is followed by an early disseminated stage involving skin, cranial nerves, heart, and meninges. If left untreated, arthritis, especially of the knee, occurs weeks to months after infection.

question_text: Identify the arrow marked structure in Urine routine microscopy?
explanation:
Here are common types of crystals that may be found in urine:

  1. Uric Acid Crystals:
    • These crystals typically form in acidic urine (urine pH < 5.5).
    • They can vary in size and shape, appearing as barrels, rosettes, rhomboids, needles, or hexagonal plates.
  2. Cystine Crystals:
    • Cystine crystals are monomorphic, colorless hexagonal plates resembling benzene rings.
    • They occur in acidic urine (urine pH < 6.0) and are associated with a genetic defect called cystinuria, affecting renal cystine transport.
  3. Triple Phosphate (Struvite) Crystals:
    • These crystals have a characteristic "coffin-lid" shape.
    • Composed of magnesium ammonium phosphate, they are typically seen in alkaline urine (urine pH > 7.0).
    • Struvite crystals are associated with urinary tract infections caused by urea-splitting bacteria (e.g., Proteus mirabilis) and are often found in infected calculi (struvite stones).
  4. Calcium Oxalate Crystals:
    • These crystals are usually found in acidic urine.
    • They can occur as either bihydrated or monohydrated calcium oxalate.
    • Bihydrate crystals appear as colorless bipyramids of various sizes

question_text: A 40-year-old female presents with new-onset seizures. A CT-guided brain biopsy reveals psammoma bodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Meningioma arises from arachnoid cap cells of the meninges, not from glial cells.

  • Histopathological Features:
    • Psammoma bodies: Concentric lamellated calcifications
    • Whorled pattern of tumor cells
    • Spindle-shaped cells with indistinct cytoplasm
  • Clinical Features:
    • Typically slow-growing and benign
    • Seizures, headaches, or focal neurological deficits depending on location
  • KeyPoints:
    • Most commonly located along the convexities of the cerebral hemispheres or falx cerebri
  • WHO Grade I: Benign; higher grades may show atypia, mitoses

Explanation of Other Options:

Astrocytoma (Option A):

  • Tumor of astrocytes (glial origin)
  • GFAP-positive
  • Histology: Densely packed elongated cells with round-to-oval nuclei and prominent nucleoli
  • Most common primary brain tumor in children

Medulloblastoma (Option B):

  • Embryonal tumor from undifferentiated neuroepithelial cells
  • Arises in the cerebellum, usually in children
  • Highly malignant
  • Histology: Sheets of small round blue cells, Homer-Wright rosettes

Ependymoma (Option D):

  • Tumor of ependymal cells lining ventricles or spinal cord
  • Histology: Perivascular pseudorosettes and true ependymal rosettes
  • Commonly located in the fourth ventricle in children or spinal cord in adults

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Astrocytoma is the most common primary brain tumour in children.
  • Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant tumour in children.

question_text: A 49-year-old female presented with pain in the shoulder which is progressive in nature, associated with shoulder activity. X-rays confirms mass lesion the scapula and excision of the lesion done. Gross examination revealed glistening lesion. Histopathological examination revealed as shown in the image below. Based on above findings, what is your probable diagnosis.
explanation:
Conventional chondrosarcomas are large bulky tumors made up of nodules of glistening gray-white, translucent cartilage, but the matrix is often gelatinous or myxoid and can ooze from the cut surface. Histologically, neoplastic cartilage infiltrates the marrow space and surrounds pre-existing bony trabeculae. Chondrosarcomas vary in cellularity, degree of cytologic atypia, and mitotic activity and, on this basis, are graded from 1 to 3

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition chapter 26, pg 1187

question_text: Which of the following tumour suppression gene mutation is associated with endometrial carcinoma?
explanation:
Important tumor suppressor called PTEN is a negative inhibitor of PI3 kinase and is frequently mutated in carcinomas, certain leukemias and other cancers as well.

Mutations in mismatch repair genes and the tumor suppressor gene PTEN are early events in the stepwise development of endometrioid carcinoma. Women with germline mutations in PTEN(Cowden Syndrome) and germline alterations in DNA mismatch repair genes(Lynch Syndrome) are at high risk for this cancer. TP53 mutations occur but are relatively uncommon and are late events in the genesis of this tumor type.

The PTEN gene provides instructions for making an enzyme that is found in almost all tissues in the body. The enzyme acts as a tumor suppressor, which means that it helps regulate cell division by keeping cells from growing and dividing(proliferating) too rapidly or in an uncontrolled way.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg: 207, 724.

question_text: What is the characteristic feature of Oligodendroglioma?
explanation:
The diagnostic features of Oligodendroglioma are:

  • fried egg tumour cells (Perinuclear halo surrounding the nucleus)

Oligodendroglioma. Tumor nuclei are round, with cleared cytoplasm forming halos and vasculature composed of thin - walled capillaries.

question_text: Which is not a risk factor of endometrial carcinoma -
explanation: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Smoking Endometrial carcinoma Endometrial carcinoma is the most common invasive cancer of the female genital tract and accounts for 7% of all invasive cancer in women. The peak incidence is in the 55- to 65-year-old woman. Clinicopathological studies & molecular analysis support its classification into two major broad categories. Type-I Carcinoma Most common type. Majority are well differentiated & mimic proliferative endometetrial glands. They are associated with- obesity, diabetes, hypertension, infertility and unopposed estrogen stimulation. Tamoxifen also increases the risk of endometrial cancer. Endometrial hyperplasia is a precursor to endometroid carcinoma. Mutation in PTEN tumor suppressor gene have been seen in 30- 80% of endometeriod carcinoma & 20% patients with endometrial hyperplasia. Additional molecular changes that are common are microsatellite instability & mutations in KRAS & beta catenin oncogenes. Type-H Carcinoma These occur in women a decade later than type I carcinoma. These usually arise in setting of endometrial atropy. They are poorly differentiated. The most common subtype is serous carcinoma, clear cell type & malignant mixed mullerian tumor. The most frequent alteration described is mutation in p53 tumor suppressor gene.

question_text: Hysterectomy from a 35-year-old female showed the following gross and histological features. What could be your possible diagnosis?
explanation:
Leiomyomas are sharply circumscribed, discrete, round, firm, gray-white tumors varying in size from small, barely visible nodules to massive tumors that fill the pelvis.

Except in rare instances, they are found within the myometrium of the corpus. Leiomyomas are typically composed of bundles of smooth muscle cells that resemble the uninvolved myometrium. Usually, the individual muscle cells are uniform in size and shape and have the characteristic oval nucleus and long, slender bipolar cytoplasmic processes. Mitotic figures are scarce.

Reference: Robbins 9th ed p 1020

question_text: A 45-year-old female presents with a 2-year history of progressive unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and ataxia. An MRI imaging of the brain reveals a well-defined tumour located in the cerebellopontine angle (CPA). A surgical resection is performed, and subsequent histopathological examination of the tumour reveals Antoni A and B areas. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given clinical vignette of a patient with progressive unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, ataxia, with imaging revealing cerebellopontine angle tumour and histopathological findings of Antoni A and B areas is consistent with a diagnosis of schwannoma.

  • Schwannomas are benign tumours usually originating from peripheral nerves. They are linked to inactivating mutations in the NF2 gene on chromosome 22, with loss of the NF2 gene product, merlin, seen in all cases.
  • Morphologically, schwannomas are encapsulated, well-defined masses loosely attached to nerves, allowing removal without loss of nerve function.
  • Grossly, they are firm and grey, composed of alternating dense (Antoni A) and loose (Antoni B) areas as shown below.
  • Antoni A areas have eosinophilic spindle cells in intersecting fascicles with nuclear palisading, forming structures called Verocay bodies.
  • Antoni B areas have sparse cells in a myxoid extracellular matrix, sometimes with microcysts.
  • These tumours show S-100 immunoreactivity and may undergo degenerative changes such as nuclear pleomorphism, xanthomatous change, vascular hyalinization, cystic change, and necrosis.
  • Clinically, they produce symptoms from compression of nerves or nearby structures. Intracranially, they often occur at the cerebellopontine angle on the vestibular branch of the eighth nerve, causing tinnitus and hearing loss and are commonly termed acoustic neuroma, though this name is misleading.
  • They can also affect the trigeminal branches, dorsal roots, or present as extradural masses on large nerves or soft tissue without nerve association. Surgical excision is curative.

Explanation of other options:

Meningioma (Option A): Meningiomas are typically slow-growing tumours that may cause vague, nonlocalizing symptoms or focal neurological deficits. Hormonal influence,s such as progesterone receptors, may lead to accelerated growth during pregnancy. Histologically, meningiomas present in various patterns such as meningothelial, fibroblastic, transitional, and psammomatous. The following image shows numerous psammoma bodies in a meningioma specimen.

On imaging, a common feature is the dural tail, which appears as a thickened, enhancing extension of the dura projecting from the main lesion.

Ependymoma (Option B): Ependymomas in the posterior fossa commonly present with hydrocephalus due to progressive blockage of the fourth ventricle, while CSF dissemination is uncommon. Histologically, they consist of cells with fibrillary processes and round to oval nuclei, often forming ependymal canals or perivascular pseudorosettes, as shown below.

Vestibular neuritis (Option D): Vestibular neuritis presents with sudden, persistent vertigo accompanied by nausea, vomiting, oscillopsia, and imbalance due to asymmetric vestibular input, with symptoms continuing even when the head is still.

question_text: A 55-year-old female presents with complaints of persistent headaches. A CT scan of the head reveals a mass lesion. HPE findings are given below, showing psammoma bodies. Based on these findings, what is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Histopathological examination (HPE) shows whorled patterns of spindle cells and psammoma bodies, which are characteristic of meningiomas.

Psammoma bodies are microscopic, concentric, lamellated calcified structures found in various lesions. They are thought to arise from dystrophic calcification. They are seen in Papillary Carcinoma of Thyroid, Prolactinoma, Serous Ovarian Carcinoma, Somatostatinoma, Meningioma and Mesothelioma

Meningiomas are common intracranial tumours arising from the meninges and are typically extra-axial. They are slow-growing, often presenting with headaches, seizures, or neurological deficits due to compression of adjacent brain structures.

Explanation of Other Options:

Glioblastoma (GBM) (Option A): Highly malignant, rapidly growing, with necrosis and pseudopalisading tumour cells, but does not typically show psammoma bodies.

Astrocytoma (Option B): A type of glioma without psammoma bodies, commonly showing fibrillary processes.

Medulloblastoma (Option D): More common in children, arises in the cerebellum, and typically shows small round blue cells with Homer-Wright rosettes, but not psammoma bodies.

Key Takeaway:

Meningiomas are the most common primary brain tumours in adults and often contain psammoma bodies, which are calcified concentric lamellated structures. References: Robbins and Contran, 10th Edition, Page 1300

question_text: A 27-year-old female has vulvar pruritus along with a thick, whitish, odorless, globular vaginal discharge for the past 2 weeks. On pelvic examination, the cervix appears erythematous, but there are no erosions or masses. A Pap smear shows budding cells and pseudohyphae (as shown below). No dysplastic cells are present. Which of the following infectious agents is most likely to produce these findings?
explanation:
The presence of the budding cells with pseudohyphae indicates a fungal infection with Candida. Candidal (monilial) vaginitis is common; this organism is present in about 5–10% of women. Recurrent episodes of vaginal candidiasis may be associated with non-albicans species. The inflammation tends to be superficial, and there is typically no invasion of underlying tissues. Chlamydia is a bacterial agent can produce cervicitis. Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a gram-negative diplococcus, is the causative agent of gonorrhea. Infection with Trichomonas vaginalis can produce a purulent vaginal discharge, but the organisms are protozoa and do not produce hyphae.

question_text: 35 year old female presents with weak pulses in upper limbs, BP 90/60 mm Hg, retinal haemorrhages +nt. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis that primarily affects the aorta and its major branches, leading to narrowing (stenosis), occlusion, or aneurysm formation.

Key Features in the Question:

  1. Weak Pulses in Upper Limbs → Suggests subclavian artery involvement, which is a hallmark of Takayasu arteritis.
  2. Low Blood Pressure (90/60 mm Hg) → Due to vascular stenosis and ischemia.
  3. Retinal Hemorrhages → Due to ocular ischemia caused by reduced blood supply to the retinal arteries.

Incorrect choices explanation:

  • (Choice A) Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN)
    • Affects medium-sized arteries, but spares the lungs.
    • Presents with systemic vasculitis symptoms (renal involvement, skin nodules, neuropathy, GI symptoms), but does not cause pulselessness.
    • No granulomas in histology.
  • (Choice B) Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA)
    • Small-vessel vasculitis, associated with p-ANCA.
    • Features include rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN), pulmonary involvement (hemoptysis), and palpable purpura.
    • No large vessel involvement or pulselessness.
  • (Choice D) Henoch-Schonlein Purpura (HSP)
    • IgA-mediated small vessel vasculitis, mainly affecting children.
    • Features palpable purpura, abdominal pain, arthritis, and glomerulonephritis, not large vessel disease.
    • Does not cause pulselessness or retinal hemorrhages.

Key takeaway:

This patient's pulseless upper limb, low BP, and retinal hemorrhages strongly suggest Takayasu arteritis.

question_text: 40-year-old female presented with neck swelling. Gross and histology is shown below. What is your diagnosis?
explanation:
Sporadic medullary thyroid carcinomas present as a solitary nodule. In contrast, bilaterality and multicentricity are common in familial cases. Larger lesions often contain areas of necrosis and hemorrhage and may extend through the capsule of the thyroid. The tumor tissue is firm, pale gray to tan, and infiltrative. Microscopically, medullary carcinomas are composed of polygonal to spindle-shaped cells, which may form nests, trabeculae, and even follicles. Small, more anaplastic cells are present in some tumors and may be the predominant cell type. Acellular amyloid deposits derived from calcitonin polypeptides are present in the stroma in many cases

question_text: An elderly male presents with progressive, painless testicular swelling. Gross examination of the testis shows a multinodular, homogeneous, gray-white mass without haemorrhage or necrosis. Histopathological examination is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis based on the given features of painless testicular swelling with gross examination revealing a homogeneous mass and histopathology revealing lymphocytic fibrous cords separating poorly defined lobules of cells is seminoma.

  • Seminoma is the most frequent type of germ cell tumour (GCT), representing about half of all cases, with peak occurrence in the fourth decade.
  • These tumours typically form large masses, sometimes reaching up to ten times the normal testis size, with a homogeneous, gray-white, lobulated surface that usually lacks haemorrhage or necrosis.
  • The tunica albuginea is generally intact, though spread to the epididymis, spermatic cord, or scrotal sac may occur.
  • Histologically, seminomas are composed of sheets of uniform cells separated into lobules by fine fibrous septa with lymphocytic infiltration, and some may have ill-defined granulomas as part of a host response.
  • Classic seminoma cells are round to polyhedral, with a distinct membrane, clear or watery cytoplasm, and a large central nucleus containing one or two prominent nucleoli, often with glycogen deposits.
  • Immunohistochemically, tumour cells are usually KIT and OCT3/4 positive, podoplanin positive, and cytokeratin negative. Around 15% contain syncytiotrophoblasts, leading to elevated serum hCG levels, though generally less than in choriocarcinoma.

Explanation of other options:

Yolk sac tumour (Option A): Yolk sac tumour, also called endodermal sinus tumour, is the most common testicular tumour in infants and children under 3 years old. Microscopically, these tumours typically display a lace-like network of medium-sized cuboidal, flattened, or spindled cells with less cytologic atypia compared to embryonal carcinoma. About half of the cases show Schiller-Duval bodies, which are structures resembling primitive glomeruli with a mesodermal core, central capillary, and visceral and parietal cell layers as shown below.

Embryonal carcinoma (Option C): Embryonal carcinomas are locally aggressive tumours that often invade through the tunica albuginea into the epididymis or spermatic cord. On gross examination, they present a variegated appearance due to areas of haemorrhage or necrosis. Microscopically, the tumour cells grow in alveolar or tubular patterns, sometimes forming papillary folds, while undifferentiated areas may consist of sheets of cells with cleft-like spaces. The cells are large, anaplastic, with hyperchromatic nuclei, prominent nucleoli, indistinct cell borders, and marked pleomorphism.

Leydig cell tumour (Option D): Leydig cell tumours are well-circumscribed nodules, typically less than 5 cm in diameter, with a distinctive golden-brown, homogeneous cut surface. Microscopically, the tumour cells resemble normal Leydig cells, being large with round or polygonal outlines, abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, and a central round nucleus. The cytoplasm often contains lipid droplets, vacuoles, or lipofuscin pigment, and some tumours display characteristic rod-shaped Reinke crystalloids shown below.

question_text: A 15-year-old male child presents in casualty with respiratory distress. He gave family history allergy to pollen. He complains that during this distress period he feels chest tightness, cough with sputum and wheezing. He uses accessory muscle during distress. His CBC shows eosinophilia. explanation:
(b) Asthma is a chronic lung disease caused by increased responsiveness of the airways to a variety of stimuli. Patients typically have paroxysms of wheezing, dyspnea, and cough. Acute episodes of asthma may alternate with asymptomatic periods or they may be superimposed on a background of chronic airway obstruction. The consensus hypothesis attributes bronchial hyperresponsiveness in asthma to an inflammatory reaction to diverse stimuli, either extrinsic (e.g., pollen) or intrinsic (e.g., exercise). Extrinsic asthma is typically a childhood disease, whereas intrinsic asthma usually begins in adults.

question_text:
A 44-year-old male patient presented with headaches, with occasionally change in behavior. There is occurrence of seizure infrequently. CT scan performed shows isodense well demarcated mass lesion located in cortex with perifocal edema. Craniotomy was done and tissue removed sent for histopathological examination, the images of which are attached below.

What is your probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Oligodendrogliomas arise preferentially in the white matter and cortex of the cerebral hemispheres. The frontal lobe is the most common location (involved in >50% of all patients). Approximately two thirds of patients present with seizures. Other common presenting symptoms include headache and other signs of increased intracranial pressure, focal neurological deficits, and cognitive or mental changes. On CT oligodendrogliomas usually present as hypodense or isodense well-demarcated mass lesions, typically located in the cortex and subcortical white matter. Calcification is common but not diagnostic. The lesion is usually well demarcated and shows little perifocal edema. Oligodendrogliomas are diffusely infiltrating gliomas of moderate cellularity that in classic cases are composed of monomorphic cells with uniform round nuclei and variable perinuclear haloes on paraffin sections (a honeycomb or fried egg appearance). Additional features include microcalcifications, mucoid/ cystic degeneration, and a dense network of delicate branching capillaries. Mitotic activity is either absent or low.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran pathologic basis of disease, 10th edition, page-1295-1296

question_text: A 42-year-old male is being evaluated by his family physician. Initial laboratory results indicated an AST of 78 U/L and an ALT of 64 U/L. The laboratory results were repeated one month later, and the AST and ALT were still elevated. A creatine kinase was normal. Additional test performed and results were as follows: anti-HCV, HBsAg, ceruloplasmin, and SPEP, which were all normal. Results of a third round of tests were serum iron of 201 μg/dL, ferritin of 289 ng/mL, and transferrin saturation of 53%. The patient is not on any medication, and he reportedly drinks about 1 to 2 beers per week socially with friends. Of the following, what test would most likely confirm his diagnosis?
explanation:
• Hemochromatosis is a cause of elevated AST and ALT.
  • With additional laboratory testing, elevated serum iron, elevated ferritin, and increased transferrin saturation would be identified, and the diagnosis of hemochromatosis confirmed via genetic analysis.
  • The hfe gene has two common mutations, c282y and h63d. Genetic testing can reveal whether you have these changes in your hfe gene. If you inherit two altered genes, you may develop hemochromatosis. You also can pass the altered gene on to your children.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg-656

question_text: An 18-year-old man presented with a 3-week history of heaviness in the right testis and it's gradually increasing. question_text: H/o male child presenting with Flexner Wintersteiner rosettes, his eye examination shows white reflex given. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
The presence of Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes along with white reflex (leukocoria) strongly suggests retinoblastoma, the most common malignant intraocular tumor in children.

Incorrect choices explanation:

Choice A: Medulloblastoma

  • Medulloblastoma is a cerebellar tumor and does not cause leukocoria.
  • Homer-Wright rosettes, not Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes, are seen in medulloblastoma.

Choice C: Rhabdomyosarcoma

  • Rhabdomyosarcoma can affect the orbit, but it does not produce leukocoria or Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes.
  • Presents with a rapidly growing orbital mass, not a white reflex.

Choice D: Coat's Disease

  • Coat's disease is a non-malignant retinal disorder that can also cause leukocoria, mimicking retinoblastoma.
  • It involves abnormal retinal vessels with exudative retinal detachment but lacks Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes.

Key takeaway:

Leukocoria (White Reflex in the Eye) → Due to tumor mass in the retina.

Strabismus (Misalignment of the Eyes) → Due to retinal involvement affecting vision.

Flexner-Wintersteiner Rosettes → Histopathological hallmark of retinoblastoma, showing tumor cells arranged in a circular pattern with a central lumen.

Mutation in the RB1 Gene on Chromosome 13 → Inactivates the retinoblastoma tumor suppressor gene.

question_text: A 52-year-old male presents to his family physician with complaints of vague abdominal pain and a sensation of fullness. A CT scan of the abdomen reveals a mass in the right upper quadrant. The patient is scheduled for resection, and a pathologist examining the tumor identifies it as being derived from bile ducts. Of the following, which is a characteristic of this tumor?
option_a: It rarely occurs in association with cirrhosis.
option_c: It frequently produces an elevation of α-fetoprotein
option_d: One complication of ulcerative colitis is a significant risk factor for the tumor
explanation:
• The tumor derived from bile ducts is a cholangiocarcinoma, which commonly occurs in cirrhotic livers, often in combination with hepatocellular carcinoma (A).
  • The tumor has a poor prognosis (B).
  • Hepatocellular carcinomas are most frequently associated with an elevation of α-fetoproteins; in fact, patients with cirrhosis of the liver, a risk factor for the development of hepatocellular carcinoma, can be followed with serial α-fetoproteins to monitor for the possible development of the tumor (although ultrasound imaging is preferred) (C).
  • Primary sclerosis cholangitis, which occurs in a large proportion of patients with ulcerative colitis, is a significant risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma, along with Opisthorchis sinensis infection (D).

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg-669

question_text: A 42-year-old male patient complaints of presence of postauricular swelling since 3 months. He explains that swelling is gradually increasing in size and it's becoming painful now. After proper radiological investigation surgeon removed the swelling present in the parotid gland and send for histopathological examination (image shown below). Based on the above findings, what is your probable diagnosis?
explanation:
(a) In Pleomorphic adenoma epithelial elements resembling ductal cells or myoepithelial cells are arranged as ducts, acini, irregular tubules, strands, or sheets of cells. These elements are typically dispersed within a background of loose myxoid and hyaline tissue containing islands of cartilage and, rarely, foci of bone.

(b) Transection reveals a pale gray surface punctuated by narrow cystic or cleft like spaces filled with mucinous or serous secretions and frequently narrowed by polypoid projections of lymphoepithelial elements. The lining is composed of a double layer of oncocytic cells; the innermost layer is columnar, while cuboidal cells occupy.

(c) The tumor cells are organized in a cribriform growth pattern that resembles swiss cheese. The spaces between the tumor cells are often filled with hyaline material thought to represent excess basement membrane.

(d) Basal cell carcinoma will show peripheral palisading with cleft like space formation.

question_text: A 23-year-old male patient presented with persistent headache associated with nausea and vomiting. On clinical examination it is found to have raised intracranial pressure due to lesion in posterior fossa. On gadolinium enhanced MRI shows well circumscribed mass with mild enhancement. After craniotomy tissue is taken for diagnosis and sent for histopathological examination, image of which is shown below. What is your probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Ependymomas can develop in patients of any age, with reported patient ages ranging from birth to 81 years. Ependymomas may occur along the ventricular system or spinal canal, in the cerebral hemispheres, or at extra CNS sites. Overall, 60% of the tumors develop in the posterior fossa, 30% in the supratentorial compartment. The clinical manifestations depend on tumor localization. Ependymomas of the posterior fossa can present with signs and symptoms of hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure, such as headache, nausea, vomiting, and dizziness. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI shows well-circumscribed masses with various degrees of contrast enhancement. Ventricular obstruction or brain stem displacement and hydrocephalus are common accompanying features.

Classic ependymoma is a well-delineated glioma with monomorphic cells characterized by a variable density and round to oval nuclei with speckled nuclear chromatin. The key histological features are perivascular anucleate zones (pseudorosettes) and (true) ependymal rosettes. The pseudorosettes are composed of tumor cells radially arranged around blood vessels, creating perivascular anucleate zones of fine fibrillary processes. The ependymal rosettes and tubular canals are composed of bland cuboidal or columnar tumor cells arranged around a central lumen.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition, Chapter - 28 pg 1293

question_text: Post surgery image of a tumor in scrotum is shown below along with its histology. What could be your possible diagnosis?
explanation:
Seminomas produce bulky masses, sometimes ten times the size of the normal testis. The typical seminoma has a homogeneous, gray-white, lobulated cut surface, usually devoid of hemorrhage or necrosis. Generally the tunica albuginea is not penetrated, but occasionally extension to the epididymis, spermatic cord, or scrotal sac occurs.

The lesion is composed of sheets of uniform cells divided into poorly demarcated lobules by delicate fibrous septa containing a lymphocytic infiltrate in some tumors, ill-defined granulomas also are present, presumably as part of a host response to the neoplasm.

The classic seminoma cell is round to polyhedral and has a distinct cell membrane; clear or watery-appearing cytoplasm; and a large, central nucleus with one or two prominent nucleoli.

The cytoplasm contains varying amounts of glycogen. By immunohistochemistry, the tumor cells are typically positive for KIT, OCT3/4, and podoplanin and negative for cytokeratin. Approximately 15% of seminomas contain syncytiotrophoblasts. In this subset of patients, serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) levels are elevated, though not to the extent seen in patients with choriocarcinoma.

Reference: Robin's basic pathology 10th edition, pg 970-971

question_text: 55 year old male died on autopsy. He was found to have mass in atria. Most common primary tumor of heart is:
explanation:
Myxomas are the most common primary tumor of the adult heart These are benign neoplasms arising from primitive multipotent mesenchymal cells. Although sporadic myxomas do not show consistent genetic alterations, familial syndromes associated with myxomas have activating mutations in the GNAS1 gene, (in association with McCune-Albright syndrome) or null mutations in PRKAR1A, encoding a regulatory subunit of a cyclic-AMP-dependent protein kinase (Carney complex). About 90% of myxomas arise in the atria, with a left-to-right ratio of approximately 4:1.

Reference: Robin's basic pathology 10th edition, 579

question_text: A middle-aged adult undergoes orchiectomy. Looking at the gross and the histological findings, which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A middle-aged adult undergoing orchiectomy with specific gross and histopathological findings suggests a testicular germ cell tumor (GCT). Among the options provided, seminoma is the most common and likely diagnosis in this age group.

Incorrect Choices explanation :

  • (Choice A) Lymphoma
    • Most common testicular tumor in men >60 years, but not in middle-aged adults.
    • Histology: Diffuse sheets of lymphoid cells; positive for CD20.
    • Often bilateral and associated with systemic B symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats).
  • (Choice C) Yolk Sac Tumor
    • Most common testicular tumor in infants and children, rare in adults.
    • Histology: Schiller-Duval bodies (resembles glomeruli).
    • AFP (Alpha-fetoprotein) is elevated (highly specific).
    • Grossly, it shows a yellow, mucinous appearance.
  • (Choice D) Teratoma
    • Composed of multiple tissue types (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm).
    • Grossly heterogeneous, with cysts and cartilage/bone-like structures.
    • Can be benign in children but malignant in adults.
    • No uniform cells like seminoma.

Key takeaway:

  • Most common testicular tumor in middle-aged adults (30-40 years).
  • Gross findings:
    • Well-circumscribed, homogeneous, gray-white mass, without necrosis or hemorrhage.
  • Histological findings:
    • Large uniform cells with clear cytoplasm (glycogen-rich).
    • Lymphocytic infiltration in the stroma.
    • Positive for immunohistochemical markers PLAP, OCT4, and c-KIT (CD117).

question_text: A 54-year-old male patient presented with history of hypertension since long time. These days he is having high blood pressure along with palpitations, headache, sweating and occasional tremor. Inspite of medication symptoms persist. He underwent whole body CT scan and well circumscribed lesion is identified in the adrenal medulla for which he underwent surgery. Histopathological examination (image shown below) of the lesion will show all of the findings, except:
option_a: Cells typically show zellballen pattern of arrangement
option_b: Cells varies from polygonal to spindle shaped cells
option_c: Cytoplasm of the cells is fine granular contains granules of catecholamine
option_d: The nuclei shows pleomorphism with prominent nucleoli
explanation:
The histologic pattern in pheochromocytoma is quite variable. The tumors are composed of clusters of polygonal to spindle-shaped chromaffin cells or chief cells that are surrounded by supporting sustentacular cells, creating small nests or alveoli (zellballen) that are supplied by a rich vascular network. Uncommonly, the dominant cell type is a spindle or small cell; various patterns can be found in any one tumor. The cytoplasm has a finely granular appearance, best demonstrated with silver stains, due to the presence of granules containing catecholamines. The nuclei are usually round to ovoid, with a stippled "salt-and-pepper" chromatin that is characteristic of neuroendocrine tumors. Electron microscopy reveals variable numbers of membrane-bound, electron-dense secretory granules.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition, chapter 24, pg 1127

question_text: A 22-year-old female patient have undergone excision of mass as it is gradually increasing in size and USG examination shows BIRADS 2 (benign) nature-on mammogram. option_b: The epithelium shows intracanalicular and pericanalicular pattern
option_c: Stroma shows myxoid change and edema
option_d: Glands are lined by single layer of epithelium with nucleomegaly and prominent nucleoli
explanation:
(a) The tumors are well circumscribed, rubbery, grayish white nodules that bulge above the surrounding tissue and often contain slit-like spaces lined by epithelium.

(b) The epithelium may be surrounded by stroma (pericanalicular pattern) or compressed and distorted by it (intracanalicular pattern).

(c) The delicate and often myxoid stroma resembles normal intralobular stroma.

(d) Lining of ductal cells by single layer of epithelium suggest the possibility of malignancy.

Reference: Robbins 10th Ed, pg. 1062

question_text: A 32-year-old HIV-positive male presents with dry cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows "crushed ping-pong ball" appearance on Giemsa stain. Which of the following is the most likely organism?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely organism based on the clinical features of dry cough, dyspnea, and hypoxia along with 'crushed ping-pong ball' appearance on Giemsa stain is Pneumocystis jirovecii.

Explanation of other options:

Cryptococcus neoformans (Option A): Cryptococcus exists in yeast form within humans, lacking hyphal or pseudohyphal structures. Its hallmark is a thick gelatinous capsule (5-10 μm) that stains strongly with periodic acid-Schiff and mucicarmine. It can also be delineated using India ink staining as shown below. While lung infection is often mild or silent, the organism can spread to the CNS, and certain species like C. gattii may form coin-like pulmonary granulomas.

Histoplasma capsulatum (Option B): Histoplasma capsulatum grows as mold below 37°C, producing slow-growing colonies with hyaline septate hyphae that generate small microconidia (2-5 μm) and larger thick-walled macroconidia (8-16 μm) with surface projections. At 37°C, in tissue or enriched medium, it transitions into small oval yeast cells (about 2 × 4 μm), which are the form seen in human infections.

Mycobacterium avium complex (Option D): Mycobacterium avium complex often causes pulmonary or disseminated infections, particularly in untreated AIDS patients and other immunosuppressed individuals. It is not typically associated with crushed ping pong ball appearance.

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6784444/

question_text: A 23-year-old male is being evaluated by his family physician. He has no past medical history and appears to be well-nourished. Initial laboratory results indicated an AST of 72 U/L and an ALT of 73 U/L. The laboratory results were repeated in one month, and the AST and ALT were still elevated. A creatine kinase was 44 U/L. Additional tests and the results are as follows: anti-HCV, HBsAg, and SPEP, which were all normal. An ultrasound of the liver reveals no abnormality. The serum ceruloplasmin is 17 mg/dL, and serum copper is 57 μg/dL. The patient is not on any medication, and he reportedly drinks about 1 to 2 beers per week socially with friends. Of the following, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• The clinical scenario, given the elevated liver enzymes and decreased serum ceruloplasmin and serum copper, is consistent with Wilson’s disease.
  • Wilson disease is a genetic disorder that prevents the body from removing extra copper, causing copper to build up in the liver, brain, eyes, and other organs. Without treatment, high copper levels can cause life-threatening organ damage.

question_text: A 65-year-old male patient who is coal miner is admitted with respiratory distress. The patient admits that he smokes one pack of cigarettes a day for 40 years. On physical examination revealed barrel-shaped chest and use accessory muscles for inspiration. A chest X-ray is compatible with nodular opacity in upper zone of lung. A transbronchial lung biopsy was taken and histopathological image of which is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Carbon deposits are dark black in color and are readily visible grossly and microscopically. Anthracosis is the most innocuous coal-induced pulmonary lesion in coal miners and is also seen to some degree in urban dwellers and tobacco smokers. Coal macules consist of carbonladen macrophages; nodules also contain a delicate network of collagen fibers. Although these lesions are scattered throughout the lung, the upper lobes and upper zones of the lower lobes are more heavily involved. They are located primarily adjacent to respiratory bronchioles, the site of initial dust accumulation. In due course dilation of adjacent alveoli occurs, sometimes giving rise to centrilobular emphysema.

question_text: A 59-year-old male patient having smoking history presented in casualty for respiratory distress, productive cough with occasional hemoptysis. He had lost weight and had clubbing. Chest X-ray shows mass in the right apex of lung. A biopsy was performed and histopathological image of which is shown below. Based on the above findings, what is your probable diagnosis?
explanation:
(a) Histologically, squamous cell carcinoma is characterized by the presence of keratinization and/or intercellular bridges. Keratinization may take the form of squamous pearls or individual cells with markedly eosinophilic cytoplasm. These features are prominent in well-differentiated tumors, are easily seen but not extensive in moderately differentiated tumors, and are focally seen in poorly differentiated tumors.

(b) Adenocarcinoma is an invasive malignant epithelial tumor with glandular differentiation or mucin production by the tumor cells. Adenocarcinomas grow in various patterns, including acinar, lepidic, papillary, micropapillary, and solid.

(c) Small cell carcinoma is comprised of relatively small cells with scant cytoplasm, ill-defined cell borders, finely granular nuclear chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli.

(d) Uniform cells with round nucleus and salt and pepper chromatin.

Reference: Robbins 10th Ed, pg 718

question_text: A 25-year-old male patient presented to the surgeon for the complaints of rectal bleeding since 3 months which is on and off. On colonoscopy, he noticed as small polyp, measures 1.5 cm in maximum dimension. Polypectomy was done and sent for histopathological examination, image of which is shown below. explanation:
(a) Most juvenile polyps are less than 3 cm in diameter. They are typically pedunculated, smooth-surfaced, reddish lesions with characteristic cystic spaces. Microscopic examination shows these cysts to be dilated glands filled with mucin and inflammatory debris.

(b) Histologic examination demonstrates a characteristic arborizing network of connective tissue, smooth muscle, lamina propria, and glands lined by normalappearing intestinal epithelium.

(c) Microscopically, tubular adenomas exhibit closely packed epithelial tubules, which may be uniform or irregular with excessive branching.

(d) Histologically glands are line by malignant epithelial cells.

question_text: A 12-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents, who noticed a mass on his left testicle. Physical examination reveals increase in size of left testis as compared to right and it cannot be transilluminated, and biopsy shows a haphazard arrangement of benign differentiated tissues, including squamous epithelium, glandular epithelium, cartilage, and neural tissue. The left testicle was removed surgically, and the patient is symptom free 5 years later. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
(a) Histologically, the cells grow in alveolar or tubular patterns, sometimes with papillary folds. More undifferentiated lesions may display sheets of cells. The neoplastic cells have an epithelial appearance, are large and anaplastic, and have hyperchromatic nuclei with prominent nucleoli. The cell borders are usually indistinct, and there is considerable pleomorphism.

(b) Teratomas are the most common testicular tumor in the age group between 4 and 12 years. They are believed to be derived from primordial germ cells. Benign teratomas in the prepubertal testes are composed of mature somatic tissues representing the three embryonic germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm).

(c) The lesion is composed of sheets of uniform cells divided into poorly demarcated lobules by delicate fibrous septa containing a lymphocytic infiltrate.

(d) Yolk sac tumors are typically composed of a lacelike (reticular) network of medium-sized cuboidal, flattened, or spindled cells, which generally show less cytologic atypia

question_text: Apoptotic bodies are composed of which of the following?
explanation:
Explanation:

Apoptotic bodies are membrane-bound fragments that contain cytoplasm, organelles, and nuclear material. They are formed during apoptosis, a form of programmed cell death regulated by caspases.

Apoptosis:

  • Definition: Caspase-dependent programmed cell death that removes damaged or unnecessary cells without causing inflammation.
  • Purpose: Eliminates cells injured beyond repair while minimising tissue damage.
  • Mechanism:
    • Initiation phase: Caspases 8, 9, and 10 become active, triggering a cascade of downstream caspases.
    • Execution phase: Caspases 3, 6, and 7 dismantle cellular components, fragmenting the cell into apoptotic bodies.
  • Morphological Features:
    • Cell shrinkage
    • Chromatin condensation
    • Formation of cytoplasmic blebs and apoptotic bodies (contain cytoplasm, organelles, and sometimes nuclear fragments)
    • Phagocytosis of apoptotic bodies by macrophages
  • Histopathology:
    • Apoptotic cells appear as round or oval masses with intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm and condensed nuclear chromatin.
  • Example: Epidermal cell undergoing apoptosis shows reduction in size, bright eosinophilic cytoplasm, and a condensed nucleus.

Types of Apoptosis:

Apoptotic bodies are not single organelles; they are cell fragments containing cytoplasm, organelles, and nuclear material, facilitating safe removal of cells by phagocytes.

question_text:

Which of the following correctly describes patient's condition clinically?

question_text: A 42-year-old male patient presented with complaints of nausea fatigability and yellowish discoloration sclera. He gave history that he is taking alcohol in large quantities since long time. On proper clinical evaluation, serum bilirubin level is raised. Liver biopsy was performed and diagnosis of alcoholic hepatitis was made. Which of the following histological features can be seen in this diagnosis?
explanation:
The morphologic findings in alcoholic hepatitis include the following:

(a) Ballooned hepatocytes. These are injured, swollen hepatocytes with cleared-out cytoplasm and cytoskeletal damage, which when extensive, results in formation of Mallory hyaline.

(b) Lobular lymphocytic infiltrates are common, and portal lymphocytic infiltrates also may occur.

(c) Perivenular/pericellular fibrosis. Steatohepatitis is often accompanied by fibrosis.

question_text: A 36-year-old, alcoholic woman presents with a 1-week history of yellow skin and sclerae. She has suffered persistent headaches. Her vital signs are normal. Physical examination reveals jaundice. Laboratory studies disclose markedly elevated levels of AST and ALT (956 and 1,400 U/L, respectively). A few days later, she develops hepatic encephalopathy and renal failure. A liver biopsy shows prominent centrilobular necrosis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
(a) Drug toxicity should be suspected in all cases of acute hepatitis. In this case, centrilobular necrosis suggests acetaminophen toxicity. The toxic dose of acetaminophen after a single acute ingestion is in the range of 150 mg/kg in children and 7 g in adults. Acetaminophen is rapidly absorbed from the stomach and small intestine and conjugated in the liver to nontoxic agents, which then are eliminated in the urine. In cases of acute overdose, normal pathways of acetaminophen metabolism become saturated. Excess acetaminophen is then metabolized in the liver via the mixed function oxidase P450 system, yielding oxidative metabolites that cause predictable, hepatocellular necrosis. (b, c, d) The centrilobular zones are particularly affected (centrilobular necrosis). Centrilobular necrosis is not seen in the other choices.

  • Reye syndrome (choice d) occurs in children.

Fatty liver of pregnancy (choice b) features microvesicular steatosis

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition Chapter 18, pg 826

question_text: A 49-year-old woman presents with a 1 month history of yellow discoloration of her eyes, abdominal pain, malaise, weight loss, and low-grade fever (38.4°C, 101°F). (d) Mallory body seen but other features of alcoholic liver disease are not seen.
