question_text: Antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) positivity is most strongly associated with which of the following conditions?
explanation:
Explanation:

Among the given options, anti-mitochondrial antibodies are most strongly associated with primary biliary cholangitis.

  • Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is an autoimmune disease marked by chronic inflammatory destruction of small- and medium-sized intrahepatic bile ducts, sparing large intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts.
  • It predominantly affects women (9:1 ratio), with peak incidence between ages 40-50.
  • The disease likely results from T lymphocyte-mediated injury to small interlobular bile ducts, possibly triggered by environmental factors in genetically susceptible individuals, leading to bile salt retention, hepatocellular injury, and eventual cirrhosis.
  • Antimitochondrial antibodies against the E2 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex are present in 90-95% of cases and are highly characteristic, though not directly linked to pathogenesis. Other autoantibodies may also occur.
  • Morphologically, PBC is defined by lymphocytic infiltration and epithelial injury of small bile ducts, often with poorly formed granulomas and the distinctive florid duct lesion as shown below, progressing to ductopenia and periportal changes such as feathery degeneration.
  • Clinically, patients may present with fatigue, pruritus, hypercholesterolemia, jaundice, xanthelasmas, steatorrhea, and vitamin D-related bone disease, with frequent association with other autoimmune conditions.
  • Diagnosis is supported by elevated alkaline phosphatase, presence of antimitochondrial antibodies, and characteristic histology.
  • The disease progresses slowly, but some develop end-stage liver disease over 15-20 years.
  • Oral ursodeoxycholic acid slows progression in most but not all patients.
  • In advanced cases, liver transplantation offers a better prognosis in terms of survival. PBC also carries an increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.

Explanation of other options:

Autoimmune hepatitis (Option A): Type 1autoimmune hepatitis, which is more common, is typically marked by the presence of antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and anti-smooth muscle actin (SMA) antibodies. Additional antibodies may include those against soluble liver antigen/liver-pancreas antigen (SLA/LPA) and, less commonly, anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA), which are more characteristic of primary biliary cholangitis. Type 2 is more frequently seen in children and is characterised by anti-liver kidney microsome-1 (LKM-1) antibodies directed against CYP2D6, as well as anti-liver cytosol-1 (ACL-1) antibodies. In both types, serum IgG levels are often elevated, which can aid in diagnosis.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (Option C): Alpha-1 antitrypsin (α1AT) deficiency is an autosomal recessive protein-folding disorder characterised by markedly reduced circulating α1AT, leading to unopposed neutrophil elastase activity and resulting in pulmonary emphysema, as well as liver disease from hepatocellular accumulation of misfolded protein.

Wilson disease (Option D): Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by ATP7B gene mutations, leading to defective copper transport into bile and reduced incorporation into ceruloplasmin, resulting in toxic copper accumulation in organs such as the liver, brain, and eyes. Clinical manifestations vary and may include hepatic injury, neurologic symptoms, psychiatric disturbances, and Kayser-Fleischer rings.

question_text: A 42-year-old female presented in OPD for routine examination. She complains of anorexia, fatigue ability nausea, pruritus, icterus and occasional abdominal pain. LFT reveals AST 350 U/L and ALT 400 U/L while S bilirubin is 3.1 mg/dL. Serological analysis shows positivity for antimitochondrial antibody. Liver biopsy performed and the image of which is shown below. All of the following are the histological features of the disease; except:
explanation:
Antimitochondrial antibodies directed against the E2 component of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC-E2) are the most characteristic finding in primary biliary cholangitis (PBC).

(a) The hallmark of PBC is lymphocytic infiltration.

(b) Periductal fibrosis leading to onion skin like appearance is seen in primary sclerosing cholangitis.

(c) Stasis of bile salts leads to swelling of periportal hepatocytes, which have clear cytoplasm with granular strands (feathery degeneration) and may develop Mallory hyaline.

(d) The histologic picture of lymphocytic and/or granulomatous bile duct destruction (florid duct lesion) is highly characteristic of PBC.

Reference: Robbins 10th Ed, pg 857

question_text: A 41-year-old female has been followed by a physician for several years. Originally, she presented to her primary care physician with episodes of itching. Today she is being seen for fatigue. On physical examination, her physician notes that her conjunctivae are yellow. Other than mild hypothyroidism requiring hormone replacement, she has no other significant past medical history. She has no family history of liver disease. Of the following, what is her most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
• Primary biliary cirrhosis is most common in middle aged females, and patients will often present with pruritus due to cholestasis, which can evolve to cirrhosis of the liver (D).
  • Jaundice is a sign of liver failure, and thus, among the choices, α-1-antitrypsin and Galactosemia could cause fatigue, but they are not commonly associated with pruritus; also, Galactosemia would affect younger ages (A, B).
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis is associated with ulcerative colitis (C).
  • Primary biliary cholangitis, previously called primary biliary cirrhosis, is a chronic disease in which the bile ducts in your liver are slowly destroyed. Bile is a fluid made in your liver. It aids with digestion and helps you absorb certain vitamins.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg-664

question_text: A 48-year-old man having progressive fatigue, pruritus, and icterus for 3 months. On physical examination, he now has generalized jaundice. The abdomen is not distended; on palpation, there is no abdominal pain and there are no masses. Laboratory studies show a serum alkaline phosphatase level of 285 U/L, AST 350 U/L and ALT 400 U/L while S bilirubin is 3.1 mg/dL. After cholangiography liver biopsy was performed and histopathological image is shown below. Based on the above findings, what is your probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Histopathological image shows periductal fibrosis:

(a) The histologic picture of lymphocytic and/or granulomatous bile duct destruction (florid duct lesion) is highly characteristic of PBC.

(b) The inflammatory injury can result in circumferential "onion skin" fibrosis (periductal fibrosis/sclerosis) around an increasingly atrophic duct lumen, eventually leading to obliteration by a "tombstone" scar.

(c) It will show variable sized nodules and fibrosis.

(d) These lesions are part of the spectrum of developmental ductal plate malformations, which result from persistence of the fetal periportal ductal plates and will show variable sized and haphazardly placed ducts.

Reference: Robbins 10th Ed, pg 858

question_text: Which factor acts as morphogen in embryonic development and acts as mitogenic effects on hepatocytes and most epithelium including biliary, lung, kidney, breast, and skin.
explanation:
Hepatocyte Growth Factor (HGF). HGF (also known as scatter factor) has mitogenic effects on hepatocytes and most epithelium including biliary, lung, kidney, breast, and skin. HGF acts as a morphogen in embryonic development (i.e., influences the pattern of tissue differentiation), promotes cell migration (hence the designation scatter factor), and enhances hepatocyte survival. HGF is produced by fibroblasts and most mesenchymal cells, endothelial cells, and non-hepatocyte liver cells.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition, Chapter - 1 pg 23

question_text: Which ONE of the following is the commonest type of bladder tumour?
explanation:
• Two distinct precursor lesions of invasive urothelial carcinoma are recognized. The most common is a non invasive papillary tumour.

question_text: A patient had a cystoscopy that revealed several yellowish-white plaques in the bladder trigone. The provided histopathology image is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of yellow-white plaques in the bladder trigone on cystoscopy, along with histology showing Michaelis-Gutmann bodies, is indicative of malakoplakia.

  • Malakoplakia is an uncommon inflammatory disorder that frequently occurs in immunocompromised individuals, such as patients on long-term immunosuppressive therapy after organ transplantation.

Explanation of other options:

Interstitial cystitis (Option A): Interstitial cystitis is a long-term disorder marked by bladder pain, urgency, and frequent urination, usually lacking distinct histological markers such as Michaelis-Gutmann bodies. On cystoscopy, it typically presents with Hunner's ulcers or reduced bladder capacity, rather than yellow-white plaques.

Polypoid cystitis (Option C): Polypoid cystitis is a non-cancerous inflammatory condition characterized by the formation of inflammatory polyps, but it lacks Michaelis-Gutmann bodies.

Acute cystitis (Option D): Acute cystitis, a frequent urinary tract infection, typically presents with urgency, frequency, and painful urination but does not produce yellow-white plaques or Michaelis-Gutmann bodies.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK564348/

question_text: A 4-year-old boy presented with painful urination, obstructive symptoms, and severe urgency and straining. Cystoscope examination reveals presence of polypoidal mass in the bladder. Excision of the mass was done and sent for histopathological examination. What is the most likely diagnosis based on the histopathological examination of the bladder biopsy?
explanation:
This is embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, botryoid type. The polypoid masses are typical of the botryoid variant of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma. Underneath the urothelial surface is a dense band of small clusters of round cells with scattered rhabdomyoblasts referred to as cambium layer. By immunohistochemistry, the tumors are positive for myogenin, Myo D1, Desmin, and Actin. The prognosis is favorable compared with the deeply invasive variants of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition, Chapter - 22 pg 962

question_text: A 40-year-old female present with dull ache pain in the epigastric region associated with nausea and vomiting since 1 year. Total bilirubin is 4.4 mg/dL and alkaline phosphatase is also raised. USG examination reveals thickening of gall bladder wall. After cholecystectomy, histopathological examination reveals the image of which attached below. Based on above findings, what is your probable diagnosis?

(a) Gallbladder cancers are mainly adenocarcinomas and are most often detected in the fundus. They may produce a firm, poorly circumscribed mass or may diffusely infiltrate the wall of gallbladder, simulating the gross appearance of chronic cholecystitis. Microscopically, they are usually characterized by the presence of glands embedded in desmoplastic stroma, but in some cases cytologic atypia and stromal response are minimal; in these instances, identification of perineural and vascular invasion help to establish the diagnosis.

(b, c, d) These will not show glands lined by malignant epithelial cells.

question_text: A 65-year-old man presents with a painless, slowly growing, ulcerated, pearly papule-like mass with rolled-out edges at the medial canthus of his eye. On histopathological examination, the lesion shows the presence of keratin pearls and nuclear palisading. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

An ulcer on the medial canthus with rolled-out margins is a classic presentation of Basal Cell Carcinoma. This is confirmed by a microscopic description showing nesting cells with peripheral palisading.

Explanation of Other Options:

Sebaceous carcinoma (Option C): An aggressive tumour commonly seen in the eyelids, often presenting with yellowish nodules, loss of eyelash growth, and a tendency to mimic inflammatory conditions (chronic blepharitis).

Merkel cell carcinoma (Option D): A rare, aggressive neuroendocrine tumour appearing as a rapidly growing, red or violaceous nodule on sun-exposed areas, with small round blue cells and neuroendocrine markers (CK20, synaptophysin, chromogranin A).

Key Takeaway:

A painless, ulcerated, pearly mass with rolled-out edges at the medial canthus suggests basal cell carcinoma (BCC). The presence of nuclear palisading and basaloid tumour nests on histopathology further confirms the diagnosis. Early detection and surgical excision (Mohs micrographic surgery) offer an excellent prognosis.

question_text: A farmer presents with a lesion on the shoulder. Based on the histopathological image shown below, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of keratin pearls on histopathology is diagnostic of Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC). SCC is a malignant tumour arising from epidermal keratinocytes and represents the second most common skin cancer after BCC.

  • Predisposing factors: Prolonged UV exposure, chronic immunosuppression (e.g., HIV, transplant recipients), and premalignant conditions such as xeroderma pigmentosum, albinism, lichen planus, and discoid lupus erythematosus.
  • Clinical features: Indurated papules, nodules, or plaques with crusting or scaling, usually on sun-exposed sites. It grows locally and has a lower risk of metastasis compared to many other skin cancers.
  • Histology: Shows sheets of malignant squamous cells with intercellular bridges and keratin pearls (concentric layers of keratinised cells).
  • Treatment: Wide local surgical excision with adequate margins is the standard approach; advanced disease may require radiotherapy or chemotherapy.

Explanation for other options:

Basal Cell Carcinoma (option B): BCC is the most common skin cancer, usually presenting as a pearly, translucent papule or nodule with surface telangiectasias, often on sun-exposed facial skin. Histologically, it shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and characteristic clefting between tumour nests and surrounding stroma, not keratin pearls.

Molluscum contagiosum (option C): This is a viral infection caused by a poxvirus, leading to small, umbilicated, flesh-colored papules, commonly in children or immunocompromised adults. Histology shows Henderson-Patterson bodies (large intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies) and cup-shaped epidermal hyperplasia, rather than malignant keratinocytes.

Verrucous carcinoma (option D): A low-grade variant of SCC, typically found in sites of chronic irritation such as the oral cavity, anogenital region, or plantar surface of the foot. It appears as a slow-growing, warty, exophytic mass. Histology demonstrates thick keratinised epithelium with broad, pushing borders, minimal cytologic atypia, and absence of keratin pearls typical of conventional SCC.

question_text: A 68-year-old male patient presented to the OPD with complaints of difficulty in food intake which is gradually increasing since 6 months. Endoscopy was performed shows a polypoidal mass protruding into the lumen in middle third of esophagus. Punch biopsy from the mass was taken and histopathological examination was performed, image of which is shown below. Based on the above findings, what is your probable diagnosis?
explanation:
(a) Adenocarcinoma shows glands lined by atypical (malignant) cells with infiltration in the lamina propria.

(b) Squamous cell carcinomas occur in the middle third of the esophagus. Over months to years they grow into tumor masses that may be polypoid, or exophytic, and protrude into and obstruct the lumen. Most squamous cell carcinomas are moderately to well differentiated and have squamoid appearance.

(c) It will show spindle shaped cells, which is absent here.

(d) It will shows diffuse infiltration of atypical lymphocytes in the lamina propria.

question_text: Identify the histopathological image
explanation:
Explanation:

The histopathological slide shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and a stromal retraction artefact, which are classic features of Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC), also called Rodent Ulcer.

  • Epidemiology: BCC is the most common skin cancer, usually developing in sun-exposed areas such as the face, nose, and around the eyes.
  • Pathogenesis
  • Growth: It is slow-growing, locally invasive, but very rarely metastasises.
  • Origin: It arises from pluripotent basal cells in the epidermis or adnexal structures.
  • Clinical presentation:
    • Pearly papules with surface telangiectasia.
    • May ulcerate, producing the classic rodent ulcer.
    • Progressive local invasion may involve the bone and sinuses in neglected cases.
  • Histopathology: Clusters of basaloid cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, arranged in a palisading pattern, with a distinctive retraction cleft between stroma and tumour nests.
  • Treatment:
    • Medical: Topical imiquimod, 5-FU, intralesional interferon-α2b.
    • Targeted: Hedgehog pathway inhibitors (e.g., vismodegib).
    • Surgical: Mohs micrographic surgery, especially for recurrent or cosmetically sensitive lesions.

Explanation for other options:

Squamous Cell Carcinoma (option B): SCC originates from epidermal keratinocytes and shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges on histology. The cells are larger with more abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, unlike the smaller, darker basaloid cells in BCC.

Adenocarcinoma (option C): Adenocarcinoma arises from glandular epithelium and demonstrates gland-like structures or mucin production. It is not a typical skin cancer and differs markedly from BCC histology.

Malignant Melanoma (option D): Melanoma is a malignant tumour of melanocytes, showing atypical pigmented melanocytes arranged as nests or single cells at the dermo-epidermal junction and within the dermis. Melanin pigment is often visible within tumour cells, which is absent in BCC.

question_text: A 63-year-old female with an 80-pack-per year smoking history has been complaining of weakness and constipation. She also has abdominal pain and episodes of seizure. Laboratory testing reveals a total calcium of 13.0 mg/dL. On chest X-ray, she has a probable mass in the left upper lobe of the lung near the hilum. Of the following, what would a biopsy of the mass most likely reveal?
option_b: Small neoplastic cells with a high nuclear to cytoplasm ratio
explanation:
The patient has symptoms consistent with hypercalcemia: weakness, constipation, abdominal pain, and psychiatric symptoms. Seizures can also occur. Squamous cell carcinoma, which has keratin pearls, can produce a parathyroid-hormone-like protein that will result in hypercalcemia (C). Adenocarcinoma (A) and small cell carcinoma (B) are not usually associated with PTH production. The mass is not a pulmonary sarcoidosis (D).

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg-539

question_text: A 48-year-old male patient presented to the OPD with complaints of increasing difficulty swallowing during the past 4 months. Physical examination is unremarkable. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy shows areas of erythematous mucosa 3 cm. A biopsy is taken from the erythematous lesion and histopathology reveals squamous epithelium with columnar metaplasia typical of Barrett esophagus. Which of the following complications is most likely to occur as a consequence of this patient's condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Barrett esophagus is characterized by intestinal-type columnar metaplasia replacing normal squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus.
  • It is a complication of chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).
  • Patients with Barrett esophagus have a significantly increased risk of developing esophageal adenocarcinoma compared to the general population.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • A) Achalasia:
    • Failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax → proximal esophageal dilation.
    • Not a complication of Barrett esophagus.
  • C) Mallory-Weiss syndrome:
    • Vertical mucosal lacerations at the gastroesophageal junction due to severe vomiting/retching.
    • Unrelated to Barrett esophagus.
  • D) Squamous cell carcinoma:
    • Typically arises in the mid-esophagus.
    • Associated with smoking and alcohol consumption, not Barrett esophagus.

Key Takeaway:

  • Barrett esophagus → predisposes to adenocarcinoma of the esophagus.
  • Recognizing this link is crucial for early surveillance and management.

question_text: A 36-year-old obese woman has been experiencing heartburn from gastric reflux for the past 5 years after eating large meals. She undergoes upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and a biopsy specimen of the distal esophagus is obtained. Which of the following stains shown in the figure can help in making the diagnosis?
explanation:
Inflammation from reflux of gastric acid has resulted in replacement of normal esophageal squamous epithelium by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells. Such conversion of one adult cell type into another cell type is called metaplasia and it occurs when stimuli reprogram stem cells. These goblet cells contain acidic mucin picked by alcian blue.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10th Edition, Page Number-34.

question_text: A 69-year-old woman presents with difficulty swallowing and weight loss over the past few months. Barium swallow and other radiological investigation revealed irregular narrowing of the lower third of the esophagus. A biopsy was taken and histopathological image of which is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Endoscopic surveillance for adenocarcinoma is now commonly done in patients with Barrett esophagus, particularly those with dysplasia. Tumors tend to grow into the lumen of the esophagus. The affected region of the esophagus is typically indurated and ulcerated, causing pain and bleeding.

question_text: A 40-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of burning epigastric pain that usually occurs between meals. The pain can be relieved with antacids or food. The patient also reports a recent history of tarry stools. She denies taking aspirin or NSAIDs. Gastroscopy reveals a bleeding mucosal defect in the antrum measuring 1.5 cm in diameter. An endoscopic biopsy is taken from the antrum is shown below. Based on the clinical findings and histopathological image features are suggestive of:
explanation:
(a) Achlorhydria is incorrect because the formation of peptic ulcers requires at least some gastric acid secretion.

(d) Peptic ulcer disease refers to breaks in the mucosa of the stomach and small intestine, principally the proximal duodenum, which are produced by the action of gastric secretions. The pathogenesis of peptic ulcer disease is believed to involve an underlying chronic gastritis caused by H. pylori. This pathogen has been isolated from the gastric antrum of virtually all patients with duodenal ulcers and from about 75% of those with gastric ulcers. H. pylori gastritis is the most common type of gastritis in the United States and is characterized by prominent chronic inflammation of the antrum and body of the stomach. The inflammatory infiltrate includes large numbers of plasma cells, often in clusters or sheets, within the superficial lamina propria. These are accompanied by increased numbers of lymphocytes, macrophages, and neutrophils within the lamina propria. Neutrophils infiltrate across the basement membrane and accumulate in the lumens of gastric glands, or pits, to create pit abscesses. In addition to peptic ulcer disease, H. pylori gastritis is a risk factor for development of gastric adenocarcinoma and lymphoma. Eradication of H. pylori infection is curative of peptic ulcer disease in most patients.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basics of Diseases 10th edition, Chapter 17, pg773

question_text: A 65-year-old male patient having smoking history presented with shortness of breath and hemoptysis since 4 months. He is also complaining of productive cough and chest pain. Chest X-ray performed shows small mass in the right lung in the periphery. A transbronchial lung biopsy was performed, histopathological image of which is shown below. explanation:
(a) Histologically, squamous cell carcinoma is characterized by the presence of keratinization and/or intercellular bridges. Keratinization may take the form of squamous pearls or individual cells with markedly eosinophilic cytoplasm.

(b) Adenocarcinoma is an invasive malignant epithelial tumor with glandular differentiation or mucin production by the tumor cells. Adenocarcinomas grow in various patterns, including acinar, lepidic, papillary, micropapillary, and solid.

(c) Small cell carcinoma is comprised of relatively small cells with scant cytoplasm, ill-defined cell borders, finely granular nuclear chromatin and inconspicuous nucleoli.

question_text: TTF-1 immunohistochemical marker is associated with which of the following cancers?

question_text: A patient is brought to the emergency room following a seizure. Serum Na+ level is 128 mEq/L. The urine osmolarity is higher than serum osmolarity. Chest X-Ray reveals a centrally located lung mass. On biopsy it shows salt and pepper appearance. Which tumour is most likely present in view of the clinicopathological profile?
explanation:
Until recently, carcinomas of the lung were classified into two broad groups: small cell lung cancer (SCLC) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), the latter including adenocarcinoma, squamous and large cell carcinoma, and large cell neuroendocrine carcinomas. Small cell lung carcinomas (SCLCs) generally appear as pale gray, centrally located masses that extend into the lung parenchyma. These cancers are composed of relatively small tumor cells with a round to fusiform shape, scant cytoplasm, and finely granular chromatin with a salt and pepper appearance.

question_text: A 4-year-old baby incidentally detected to have undescended testis on USG. Now, parents are willing to remove the testes from intra-abdominal location. Now, what are the possible histological changes that can be expected in such testes

The histologic changes in the malpositioned testis begin as early as 2 years of age. Early on, thickening of the basement membrane of the spermatic tubules is seen. Subsequent loss of spermatogonia leaves the tubules with only Sertoli cells. The scarred tubules may appear as dense cords of hyaline connective tissue associated with a concomitant increase in interstitial stroma. Leydig cells are spared and therefore, appear relatively prominent.

question_text: Small intestinal biopsy reveals PAS positive macrophages in the lamina propria as shown in the figure. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Whipple's disease is a rare bacterial infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that primarily affects the small intestine. The disease leads to malabsorption, weight loss, diarrhea, and systemic symptoms.

Why is Whipple's Disease the Correct Answer?

  • Small intestinal biopsy shows PAS-positive macrophages in the lamina propria, which contain non-acid-fast, Gram-positive bacilli.
  • Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) positivity indicates the presence of glycoprotein-rich bacterial debris within macrophages.
  • The hallmark histopathology is foamy macrophages in the lamina propria.
  • Systemic symptoms such as arthritis, neurological involvement (dementia, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia), and cardiac manifestations are common.

Incorrect choices explanation :

  • (Choice A) Gluten-Sensitive Enteropathy (Celiac Disease)
    • Celiac disease presents with villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia rather than PAS-positive macrophages.
    • Anti-tTG and Anti-EMA antibodies are diagnostic, and symptoms improve with a gluten-free diet.
  • (Choice C) Abetalipoproteinemia
    • A rare disorder with defective chylomicron formation, leading to fat malabsorption and acanthocytosis (spiky RBCs).
    • Small intestinal biopsy shows lipid accumulation in enterocytes, not PAS-positive macrophages.
  • (Choice D) Giardiasis
    • Caused by Giardia lamblia, leading to chronic diarrhea and malabsorption.
    • Characterized by pear-shaped trophozoites with flagella, seen in stool microscopy or duodenal biopsy, but not PAS-positive macrophages.

Key takeaway of Whipple's Disease

The presence of PAS-positive macrophages in the lamina propria is a hallmark finding of Whipple's disease.

question_text: Which of the following is not associated with coeliac disease?
explanation:
Explanation:

HLA DQ6 and HLA DQ11 are not linked to Celiac Disease.

Celiac Disease

  • Also known as Gluten-sensitive Enteropathy or Celiac Sprue
  • Its an autoimmune disorder triggered by ingesting gluten-containing foods in genetically susceptible individuals.
  • The alcohol-soluble fraction of gluten, gliadin, contains most of the disease-producing components.
  • It is influenced by HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8.

Pathogenesis

Serum markers

  • IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase (tTG): Most sensitive (Option A ruled out)
  • Anti-endomysial antibodies (EMA)-most specific
  • IgG antibodies against gliadin (component of gluten) (Option B ruled out)

Histology

  • Specimen: Biopsy of the second part of the duodenum or proximal jejunum.
  • Findings:
    • Increased intraepithelial CD8+ T lymphocytes (intraepithelial lymphocytosis),
    • Crypt hyperplasia (increased mitosis)
    • Villous atrophy (reduced mucosal surface area, causing malabsorption)
    • Inflammatory cells infiltration

Fig: HPE showing A) Normal intestinal epithelium B) Celiac disease

Explanation of other options:

Modified Marsh classification (Option C): This is used to evaluate and grade the severity of damage to the small intestine in patients with Celiac disease. It categorises the damage based on histopathological findings in biopsy samples.

question_text: A patient presents with itchy, blistering skin lesions known as dermatitis herpetiformis. Which of the following intestinal disorders is most associated with this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

Celiac Disease, also called gluten-sensitive enteropathy or celiac sprue, is an autoimmune disorder triggered by ingestion of gluten in genetically susceptible individuals, often with HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 haplotypes.

Pathogenesis:

Ingestion of gluten leads to an immune-mediated attack on the small intestinal mucosa, causing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis, which results in malabsorption of nutrients.

Clinical Features:

  • Adults: Often between 30-60 years, more common in females. Can be silent or latent. Symptoms include chronic diarrhoea, bloating, fatigue, iron/vitamin deficiency anaemia, and dermatitis herpetiformis.
  • Children: Equal in both sexes, presenting with malabsorption, irritability, abdominal distension, diarrhoea, failure to thrive, weight loss, and extraintestinal manifestations like arthritis, delayed puberty, or short stature.
  • Pathogenesis

Serological Markers:

  • IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase (tTG) - most sensitive
  • Anti-endomysial antibodies (EMA) - most specific
  • IgG antibodies against gliadin

Histology:

  • Increased intraepithelial CD8+ T cells
  • Crypt hyperplasia
  • Villous atrophy
  • Inflammatory infiltration

Explanation for Other Options:

Ulcerative colitis (Option A): A chronic inflammatory bowel disease affecting the colon and rectum, causing ulceration of the mucosal lining. Patients typically present with bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain, cramping, and weight loss. It is autoimmune in origin and involves continuous lesions, not associated with dermatitis herpetiformis.

Whipple's disease (Option B): A rare bacterial infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that primarily affects the small intestine, leading to malabsorption, diarrhoea, and weight loss. It can also involve the joints, heart, CNS, and lungs.

Crohn's disease (Option D): A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, with transmural inflammation and skip lesions. Symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and weight loss.

question_text:
Assertion: Lung and small intestine show red infarcts
Reason: Lung and small intestine have dual circulation which allows blood to flow from an unobstructed parallel supply into the necrotic zone.
option_a: If both statements are true and causally related
option_b: If both statements are true but not causally related
option_c: If the first statement is true and second is false
option_d: If the first statement is false and second is true
explanation:
Red infarcts occur (1) as a result of venous occlusions (such as in ovarian torsion); (2) in loose tissues (e.g., lung) where blood can collect in infarcted zones;(3) in tissues with dual circulations such as lung and small intestine, where partial, albeit inadequate perfusion by collateral arterial supplies is typical; (4) in previously congested tissues (as a consequence of sluggish venous outflow); and (5) when flow is reestablished after infarction has occurred (e.g., after angioplasty of an arterial obstruction).

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg-114-115

Option c is true- major clinical features include hemoptysis, hematuria and proteinuria, bowel pain or bleeding, muscle pain or weakness, and palpable cutaneous purpura. Skin findings are as follows:

question_text: A 36-year-old man presents with fever and painful joints for 2 weeks. Physical examination shows skin pigmentation, glossitis, angular cheilitis, and generalized lymphadenopathy. The patient has lost 9 kg (20 lb) over the past 6 months. He reports that his stools are pale and foul smelling. Blood cultures are negative. The patient is started on antibiotic therapy and exhibits remarkable clinical improvement. Biopsy of the small intestine is taken and histopathological image is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Biopsy of the small intestine shows marked distortion of the intestinal villi and numerous foamy macrophages suggestive of Whipple disease. It's a rare infectious disorder of the small intestine in which malabsorption is the most prominent feature. The disorder typically features infiltration of the small bowel mucosa by macrophages that are packed with small, rod-shaped bacilli (Tropheryma whipplei). Infiltrate of macrophages containing bacilli may be found in other organs, including regional lymph nodes and the heart. The other choices do not feature these distinctive aggregates of foamy macrophages.

question_text: A 6-year-old child presents with multiple small, firm, skin-colored papules on the trunk and face. Each lesion is dome-shaped with a central umbilication. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis in this child who has presented with multiple small, firm, skin-coloured dome-shaped papules with central umbilication is molluscum contagiosum.

Explanation of other options:

Chickenpox (Option A): Chickenpox rash typically appears about two weeks after infection, starting on the torso and spreading to the head and limbs in successive waves. The lesions evolve quickly from red macules to fluid-filled vesicles resembling'dew drops on a rose petal,' which later rupture, crust, and usually heal without scarring unless secondarily infected. Microscopy shows intraepithelial vesicles with intranuclear inclusions in keratinocytes.

Verruca vulgaris (Option C): Verruca vulgaris, the most common wart, usually appears on the hands and periungual areas as rough, gray-white to tan papules with a coarse surface as shown below. Histologically, they show epidermal hyperplasia with papillomatous growth and koilocytosis, marked by vacuolated keratinocytes with halos around nuclei. These changes are characteristic of HPV infection.

Impetigo (Option D): Impetigo begins as red macules that quickly develop into small pustules. When these pustules rupture, they leave shallow erosions that dry into the classic honey-colored crusts. Microscopically, there is a build-up of neutrophils beneath the stratum corneum, forming subcorneal pustules filled with serum and inflammatory cells.

question_text: Which of the following conditions is associated with pulmonary haemorrhage and is typically positive for perinuclear ANCA (P-ANCA)?
explanation:
Explanation:

Microscopic polyangiitis is a type of small-vessel vasculitis associated with P-ANCA (perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies).

Explanation for other options:

Monckeberg's sclerosis (Option A) is a form of medial calcific sclerosis where calcium deposits in the walls of medium and small arteries, leading to arterial stiffness. It does not cause inflammation, or pulmonary haemorrhage or doesn't show P-ANCA positivity.

Wegener's granulomatosis (Option C) can cause pulmonary haemorrhage, but it is typically associated with C-ANCA (anti-PR3 antibodies), not P-ANCA.

Polyarteritis nodosa (Option D) involves medium-sized arteries and is not typically associated with pulmonary involvement or P-ANCA positivity. It predominantly affects organs like the kidneys, skin, and gastrointestinal tract, but spares the lungs.

question_text: Section of lung showing what?
explanation:
This is a "miliary pattern" of granulomas because there are a multitude of small tan granulomas about 2-4 mm in size, scattered throughout the lung parenchyma. The miliary pattern gets its name from the resemblance of the granulomas to millet seeds.

  • Miliary TB can occur when TB lung lesions erode pulmonary veins or when extrapulmonary TB lesions erode systemic veins.

question_text: A middle-aged immunocompromised male came with fever and breathlessness. HRCT showed a middle lobe lesion with infiltration in the lung as shown in image. Most likely diagnosis is:
explanation:
The history of immune compromise is provided in the history.

  • In the given image, many cells with intranuclear inclusions, suggestive of cytomegalovirus, are seen.
  • Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia is also known as bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia. It is a disease of unknown etiology characterized by polypoid plugs of loose organizing connective tissue (Masson bodies) within alveolar ducts, alveoli, and often bronchioles. The connective tissue in this is all of the same age, with normal lung architecture and without interstitial fibrosis or honeycomb lung. In tuberculosis of lung, there are well-defined epithelioid cell granulomas which are not seen in the given microphotograph.

The cells can be round, oval, or spindle shaped, with prominent nuclear molding. The tumor cells are smaller than three times the diameter of a small resting lymphocyte (approximately 25 mm)

question_text: Identify the given histopathological image of lung carcinoma.
explanation:
Explanation:

The histopathology image showing glandular structures indicates lung adenocarcinoma, where neoplastic epithelial cells form well-differentiated tumours in a glandular pattern. It is the most common subtype in non-smokers.

Explanation of other options:

Large cell carcinoma (Option D): Large cell carcinoma is an undifferentiated lung cancer with large nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and moderate cytoplasm. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, lacking markers for adenocarcinoma (TTF-1, Napsin A) or squamous cell carcinoma (p40, p63).

question_text: An elderly male with a history of smoking presents with chronic cough, marked weight loss, and fatigue. Laboratory tests show elevated serum calcium levels. Lung biopsy reveals large atypical cells with hyperchromatic nuclei. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

An elderly male smoker with chronic cough, weight loss, fatigue, and elevated serum calcium likely has squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.

  • This cancer is associated with paraneoplastic hypercalcemia due to PTHrP secretion. The biopsy showing large atypical cells with hyperchromasia supports this diagnosis.
  • Smoking significantly increases the risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the lung as it has a strong association, resulting in chromosomal deletions involving tumour suppressor loci involving 3p,9p and

Squamous cell carcinoma:

Squamous Cell Carcinoma is typically found in the central regions of the lungs (Not peripheral), often originating in the major bronchi near the hilum. It can cause symptoms by obstructing the airways. Histopathologically, it is characterised by keratin pearls, intercellular bridges, and nests of malignant squamous cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm.

Location of lung carcinomas:

  • Central: Squamous cell carcinoma, Small cell carcinoma, and Bronchial carcinoids.
  • Peripheral: Adenocarcinoma and Large-cell carcinoma.

question_text: A 58 years old shivang complaints of chronic cough, hoarseness of voice and classic pleural effusion. On examination, a small mass was found at periphery and the histomorphology is as given below. What is the probable type of lung tumour?
explanation:
Adenocarcinomas are usually peripherally located, but also may occur closer to the hilum. In general, adenocarcinomas grow slowly and form smaller masses than do the other subtypes, but they tend to metastasize widely at an early stage. They may assume a variety of growth patterns, including acinar (gland-forming); papillary; mucinous which is often multifocal and may manifest as pneumonia-like consolidation); and solid types. The solid variant often requires demonstration of intracellular mucin by special stains to establish its adenocarcinomatous differentiation.

Adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS) (formerly bronchioloalveolar carcinoma), often involves peripheral parts of the lung as a single nodule.The key features of AIS are diameter of 3 cm or less, growth along preexisting structures, and preservation of alveolar architecture. The tumor cells, which may be nonmucinous, mucinous, or mixed, grow in a monolayer along the alveolar septa, which serve as a scaffold. By definition, AIS does not demonstrate destruction of alveolar architecture or stromal invasion with desmoplasia, features that would merit the diagnosis of invasive adenocarcinoma.

Squamous cell carcinomas are more common in men than in women and are closely correlated with a smoking history; they tend to arise centrally in major bronchi and eventually spread to local hilar nodes, but they disseminate outside the thorax later than do other histologic types. Large lesions may undergo central necrosis, giving rise to cavitation.

Large cell carcinomas are undifferentiated malignant epithelial tumors that lack the cytologic features of neuroendocrine carcinoma and show no evidence of glandular or squamous differentiation. The cells typically have large nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and moderate amounts of cytoplasm.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg-539

question_text: A 25-year-old woman with a mass in the left lobe of the liver underwent lobectomy. This left lobe was sent for histopathological examination and image of which is shown below. All statements about this lesion are true; except:

(a) It is seen more commonly in young adults.

(b) It is rarely associated with cirrhosis or alphafetoprotein elevation. However, in children, classic hepatocellular carcinoma still predominates.

(c & d) These have a better prognosis and characteristic histopathological findings of large tumor cells with eosinophilic granular cytoplasm separated by thick bands of hyalinized collagen are suggestive of fibrolamellar variant of hepatocellular carcinoma.

question_text: A 34-year-old woman presented with coughing, dyspnea, flushing, diarrhea, hypotension, hematemesis for 3 months. Bronchoscopy shows large intraductal mass. Histopathology of the mass is given below. Mitosis was 5/hpf and is chromogranin positive. What is your diagnosis?

question_text: A 40-year-old woman presented to the clinic with a 4 cm mass in the upper outer quadrant. Biopsy bland nuclei and mucin infiltrating the stroma. Which of the following is your diagnosis?
explanation:

  • Colloid carcinoma has better prognosis than the usual infiltrating duct carcinoma.

question_text: Which amongst the following is a highly vascular neoplasm that occurs as a mural nodule associated with a large, fluid-filled cyst?

• Hemangioblastoma, the principal neurologic manifestation of the disease, is a highly vascular neoplasm that occurs as a mural nodule associated with a large, fluid-filled cyst.

  • On microscopic examination, the lesion consists of numerous capillary-sized or some what larger thin-walled vessels separated by intervening stromal cells with a vacuolated, lightly PAS-positive, lipid-rich cytoplasm.
  • These stromal cells express inhibin, a member of the TGF-β family, which serves as a useful diagnostic marker.

question_text: A 55-year-old woman presents with easy fatiguability and shortness of breath. question_text: What is/are use's of DNA Microarrays?

question_text: A 22-year-old woman presents with a large right ovarian mass. Histopathology confirms the tumour contains elements derived from all three germ layers. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Teratomas are tumours derived from all three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm), commonly seen in ovaries of young women. These tumours may contain hair, teeth, or muscle.

Types of Teratomas:

  • Immature Teratoma:
    • Bulky, solid ovarian tumour with immature neuroepithelium, cartilage, bone, muscle.
    • Rapidly growing, may spread beyond ovary.
    • High malignant potential.
    • Microscopy: small blue cells (immature neural tissue).
  • Mature Teratoma (Dermoid cyst):
    • Benign ovarian tumour, bilateral in 10-15% of cases.
    • Contains hair, skin, teeth.
    • Gross: unilocular cyst with hair/sebaceous material.
    • Histology: squamous epithelium + sebaceous glands.
    • Rare malignant transformation (e.g., squamous cell carcinoma).
  • Monodermal Teratoma:
    • Predominantly a single tissue type.
    • Examples: Struma ovarii(thyroid tissue), carcinoid tumour.

Explanation of other options:

Dysgerminoma (Option A): Germ cell tumour secreting β-hCG; does not contain all three germ layers.

Thecoma (Option C): Rare benign stromal tumour, common in peri/postmenopausal women.

Theca lutein cyst (Option D): Benign hCG-driven cyst, not a true neoplasm.

Key Takeaways:

  • Teratomas = all 3 germ layers.
  • Mature = benign, Immature = malignant potential, Monodermal = single tissue.

question_text: A patient presents with a hand lesion, and the histopathology of the lesion is provided. Which of the following statements is incorrect?
option_a: It originates from the peripheral nerve
option_b: Verrocay bodies are seen in light microscopy
option_d: It is malignant and often metastasizes
explanation:
Explanation:

The described scenario, featuring a lesion in the hand and histopathological findings of tissue with areas of dense cellularity and loose myxoid regions, suggests a diagnosis of Schwannoma.

Schwannoma

  • Schwannomas are benign tumours exhibiting Schwann cell differentiation and originate directly from peripheral nerves. (Option A ruled out)
  • It is associated with NF2 mutations on chromosome 22, producing (Option C ruled out); (NF - Neurofibromatosis)
  • Most common location: Cerebellopontine angle
  • Microscopically, they are comprised of:
    • Antoni A area: Dense eosinophilic areas containing spindle cells are arranged into intersecting fascicles, leading to nuclei palisading. The resulting structures with central "nuclear-free zones" are called Verocay bodies. (Option B ruled out)
    • Antoni B area: Loose, hypocellular areas where a myxoid extracellular matrix spreads apart the spindle cells.
  • It typically shows immunoreactivity to S-100.
  • Clinical features:
    • Cause symptoms by local compression of the involved nerve or adjacent structures (e.g., brainstem or spinal cord).
    • Mostly occurs at the cerebellopontine angle (attached to the vestibular branch of the 8th nerve).
    • Presents with tinnitus and hearing loss
    • Sensory nerves are involved (trigeminal nerve and dorsal roots).
    • They can arise in association with large nerve trunks or as soft tissue lesions (extradural)
  • Management: Surgical removal is curative.

question_text: All the following are microscopic features of acute pulmonary congestion EXCEPT:

question_text: A male patient with ARDS shows poor response to oxygen therapy. What is the primary role of interleukin-8 (IL-8) in the pathogenesis of ARDS?
explanation:
Explanation:

Interleukin-8 (IL-8) is a potent chemokine that recruits neutrophils to the site of inflammation in the lungs in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS).

Explanation for other options:

Endothelial Cell Activation (Option A), mediated by IL-1 and TNF-α, leads to increased vascular permeability and upregulation of adhesion molecules. This facilitates leukocyte adhesion and migration, an essential step in the inflammatory response.

Macrophage Activation (Option C) is influenced by IL-4 and IL-10. IL-4 promotes the M2 anti-inflammatory phenotype, supporting tissue repair and resolution of inflammation. IL-10 suppresses pro-inflammatory cytokine production, modulating macrophages to dampen inflammatory responses.

Promotion of Surfactant Production (Option D) is indirectly supported by IL-6 by influencing surfactant protein expression, though it is not the primary cytokine for this role.

question_text: Which of the following is a post-mortem finding in the lung after the death of a patient from COVID-19 after a week?
option_d: Pulmonary artery hypertrophy with increased resistance
explanation:
Explanation:

In severe COVID-19, one of the hallmark post-mortem features after about a week is a thick layer of fibrin within alveoli.

  • This reflects the severe inflammatory and pro-thrombotic state, with fibrin deposition and hyaline membrane formation contributing to diffuse alveolar damage (DAD), the morphological basis of ARDS.

Explanation for Other Options:

Fresh and old intra-alveolar haemorrhage (Option A): Haemorrhage may be seen in acute/early stages of lung injury, but after a week, fibrin deposition and hyaline membranes dominate the pathology rather than ongoing haemorrhage.

Perivascular cuffing (Option C): Refers to lymphocytic accumulation around vessels, a feature of viral pneumonias in early disease, but it is not the defining finding in later stages of COVID-19 lung pathology.

Pulmonary artery hypertrophy with increased resistance (Option D): Seen in chronic pulmonary hypertension and long-standing lung diseases. This is a chronic remodelling feature, not an acute/subacute post-mortem finding in COVID-19.

Key point:

After about one week of COVID-19 illness, the lungs typically show hyaline membranes, alveolar fibrin deposition, and diffuse alveolar damage, the microscopic correlate of ARDS.

Reference:

Autopsy findings in COVID-19-related deaths: a literature review

question_text: Gray hepatization of lungs lasts for how many days?
explanation:

question_text: A 61-year-old man had leg swelling with grade 2 pitting edema upto the knees, prominent jugular venous distention to the level of the mandible and increasing levels of serum AST and ALT. question_text: A 48-year-old man presented with high-grade fever and acute respiratory distress. A chest X-ray revealed diffuse bilateral infiltrates, and ABG analysis showed severe hypoxemia. A transbronchial lung biopsy was performed, with the histopathological findings shown below. Based on these clinical and pathological findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation of acute respiratory failure with bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and hypoxemia is diagnostic of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS). The histopathological correlate of ARDS is Diffuse Alveolar Damage (DAD), which is seen in the image.

The image shows the characteristic features of the exudative phase of DAD, including:

  • Hyaline membranes: Waxy, eosinophilic (pink) membranes lining the alveolar ducts and spaces. These are composed of fibrin-rich edema fluid mixed with necrotic epithelial cell debris.
  • Interstitial and alveolar edema with an associated inflammatory infiltrate.

Explanation of Other Options:

Emphysema (Option B): The histology of emphysema is characterized by the destruction of alveolar walls, leading to permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole. Hyaline membranes are not a feature.

Asthma (Option C): Asthma is an airway disease. Histopathology would show inflammation of the bronchi (predominantly eosinophils), smooth muscle hypertrophy, thickening of the basement membrane, and mucus plugging, not alveolar hyaline membranes.

Tuberculosis (Option D): The classic histopathological finding in tuberculosis is a caseating granuloma, which is a collection of epithelioid macrophages, Langhans giant cells, and lymphocytes surrounding a central area of amorphous, eosinophilic necrosis. This is not seen in the image.

Key Takeaways:

  • Diffuse Alveolar Damage (DAD) is the pathologic pattern underlying the clinical syndrome of ARDS.
  • The hallmark of the acute, exudative phase of DAD is the presence of alveolar hyaline membranes.
  • ARDS/DAD can be caused by numerous insults, including sepsis, pneumonia, trauma, and aspiration.

question_text: A 48-year-old male patient presented with high grade fever along with respiratory distress. He was admitted in the hospital, X-ray was done which revealed diffuse bilateral infiltrates, laboratory investigations revealed neutrophilic leukocytosis and ABG analysis shows hypoxemia. When patient is stabilized, a transbronchial lung biopsy was performed, histopathological image of which is shown below. Based on the above findings, what is your probable diagnosis?
explanation:
(a) Histopathological image of a transbronchial lung biopsy specimen on microscopic examination shows hyaline membranes lining distended alveolar ducts and sacs. Hence diagnosis is diffuse alveolar damage.

(b) Patient will have long smoking history and respiratory difficulties which will be gradually increasing.

(c) Lung will be overinflated and main findings in bronchi and bronchioles.

(d) Many granulomas will be seen.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition Chapter-15, pg 688

question_text: A 49-year-old female admitted in hospital with 50% burn. Laboratory investigations performed show neutrophilic leukocytosis with mild left shift along with raised procalcitonin (PCT) and positive blood culture. During the course of treatment, she develops respiratory difficulties and high grade fever, with chills and productive cough. Chest X-ray shows bilateral diffuse pulmonary consolidation. A transbronchial biopsy was planned and histopathological image of lung shown below. Which stage of pneumonia is present?
explanation:
(a) In the first stage of congestion, the lung is heavy, boggy, and red. It is characterized by vascular engorgement, intra-alveolar edema fluid containing a few neutrophils, and the presence of bacteria, which may be numerous.

(b) In the next stage of red hepatization, there is massive confluent exudation, as neutrophils, red cells, and fibrin fill the alveolar spaces. On gross examination, the lobe is red, firm, and airless, with a liver-like consistency, hence the name hepatization.

(c) The third stage of gray hepatization is marked by progressive disintegration of red cells and the persistence of a fibrinosuppurative exudates, resulting in a color change to grayish-brown.

(d) In the final stage of resolution, the exudate within the alveolar spaces is broken down by enzymatic digestion to produce granular, semifluid debris that is resorbed, ingested by macrophages, expectorated, or organized by fibroblasts growing into it.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition Chapter-15, Pg 675

question_text: Identify the stage of pathological lesion of given autopsy lung specimen of 42-year female patient with history lower respiratory tract infection, fever and productive cough for last one month.
explanation:
In lobar pneumonia, four stages of the inflammatory response are as follow:

  • In the first stage of congestion, the lung is heavy, boggy, and red. It is characterized by vascular engorgement, intraalveolar fluid with few neutrophils, and often the presence of numerous bacteria.
  • The stage of red hepatization that follows is characterized by massive confluent exudation, as neutrophils, red cells, and fibrin fill the alveolar spaces. On gross examination, the lobe is red, firm, and airless, with a liver-like consistency, hence the term hepatization.
  • The stage of gray hepatization that follows is marked by progressive disintegration of red cells and the persistence of a fibrinosuppurative exudate, resulting in a colour change to grayish-brown. In the final stage of resolution, the exudate within the alveolar spaces is broken down by enzymatic digestion to produce granular, semifluid debris that is resorbed, ingested by macrophages, expectorated, or organized by fibroblasts growing into it.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg-522

question_text: The following is a picture of the crystalloids seen in the sputum of an individual suffering from Bronchial asthma. What is the origin of these crystalloids?
explanation:
The most striking finding is occlusion of bronchi and bronchioles by thick, tenacious mucous plugs containing whorls of shed epithelium (Curschmann spirals). Numerous eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals (crystalloids made up of the eosinophil protein galectin-10) also are present.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg-505

question_text: A 52-year-old patient presents with respiratory distress, and he is diagnosed with pan-acinar emphysema. Which deficiency is responsible for his condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

Deficiency of Alpha-1 antitrypsin leads to panacinar emphysema along with liver cirrhosis.

  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a genetic condition characterised by low levels or dysfunctional alpha-1 antitrypsin protein.
  • It is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the alpha-1 antitrypsin gene located on Chromosome 14.
  • Normal individuals have the PiMM genotype, while those with the disease have the PiZZ genotype.
  • This results in significantly reduced levels of functional alpha-1 antitrypsin protein.
  • Carriers possess the PiMZ genotype.
  • The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to panacinar emphysema and the liver, causing cirrhosis due to abnormal protein accumulation.

The image below shows centriacinar emphysema.

The image below shows paraseptal emphysema.


Type 1 alveolar cells (Option A) are squamous cells responsible for gas exchange in the alveoli. Dysfunction or loss of these cells can impair gas exchange, but does not cause emphysema or structural destruction of alveoli.

Type 2 alveolar cells (Option C) produce surfactant and play a role in alveolar repair. Their dysfunction leads to surfactant deficiency, contributing to conditions like neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, not emphysema.

Albumin (Option D) is a plasma protein involved in maintaining oncotic pressure and the transport of substances. It has no role in the structural integrity of alveoli or the pathogenesis of emphysema.

Learning Objective:

A-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency:

  • Gene on Chromosome 14
    • PiMM: Normal
    • PiZZ: Diseased
    • PiMZ: Carrier
  • Organs affected :
    • Lungs: Pan-acinar emphysema
    • Liver: Cirrhosis

question_text: Which of the following show Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency?
explanation:
Emphysema is characterized by permanent enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of their walls without significant fibrosis.

question_text: Tamm-Horsfall protein is a major component of which of the following?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Tamm-Horsfall proteinis synthesized in the ascending loop of Henle and is the most abundant protein in normal urine.
  • It plays a role in tubular functionand helps prevent urinary tract infections.
  • It is the main constituent of hyaline casts, which are the most common type of urinary casts.

Explanation of other options:

Mural thrombi (Option A): Blood clots adhering to the vessel or heart walls; unrelated to Tamm-Horsfall protein.

Curschmann spirals (Option B): Mucus plugs seen in sputum from asthma or other obstructive pulmonary diseases.

Bence-Jones proteins (Option D): Free immunoglobulin light chains in urine, associated with multiple myeloma, not a normal renal protein.

question_text: A 36-year-old male is brought to the emergency room by his roommate. While driving around, he began to cough and developed shortness of breath and wheezing. His roommate reports that he has had multiple attacks like this in the past. When he was coughing, he did not cough anything up. question_text: A 30-year-old male presented with history of dyspnea, cough and sputum production. The patient died of respiratory failure. Gross image of lung is shown below. What is the likely etiology?
explanation:
This image shows Panacinar (panlobular) emphysema.

Panacinar emphysema is associated with α1-antitrypsin deficiency and is exacerbated by smoking. In this type the acini are uniformly enlarged from the level of the respiratory bronchiole to the terminal blind alveoli.

In contrast to centriacinar emphysema, panacinar emphysema tends to occur more commonly in the lower zones and in the anterior margins of the lung, and it is usually most severe at the bases.

Reference: Robin's basic pathology 10th edition, 679

question_text: A 43-year-old female develops a chronic cough and dyspnea on exertion over the course of a few years. A lung biopsy reveals areas of honeycomb change, areas with fibroblastic foci, and areas of normal lung parenchyma. What is probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• Usual interstitial pneumonitis is one form of restrictive lung disease, which can present with a slowly developing chronic cough and dyspnea on exertion.
  • The characteristic histologic features are temporally heterogeneous changes-both honeycomb change and fibroblastic foci, and areas of unaffected lung interspersed between areas of affected lung (i.e., patchy distribution).
  • NSIP is temporally homogenous, and the pulmonary parenchyma is diffusely affected.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg-507

question_text: A 68-year-old female villager patient having long-standing history of taking bidi and hookah since childhood. She has respiratory difficulties these days which usually gradually increasing since 4 months. Chest X-ray and CT scan show a mass in the periphery of left lung. Transbronchial lung biopsy was performed and the histopathological image of which is shown below. Regarding histopathological findings of tumor, all of these are true; except:
option_a: Tumor comprising small cells with scant cytoplasm
option_b: Tumor cells have fine granular nuclear chromatin, with nuclear molding
option_c: Tumor cells show marked nuclear pleomorphism with prominent nucleoli
explanation:
Small cell carcinoma is comprised of relatively small cells with scant cytoplasm, ill-defined cell borders, finely granular nuclear chromatin (salt and pepper pattern), and absent or inconspicuous nucleoli. The cells are round, oval, or spindle-shaped, and nuclear molding is prominent. Basophilic staining of vascular walls due to encrustation by DNA from necrotic tumor cells (Azzopardi effect) is frequently present.

Reference: Robbins 10th Ed, pg 719

question_text: A 56-year-old male presented with lesion at the lung apex. He was working in asbestos factory for last 20 years. The lung biopsy was seen under electron microscope which revealed the following. What is your diagnosis?

question_text: Procalcitonin is used as a marker for:
explanation:
Measurement of procalcitonin can be used as a marker of severe sepsis caused by bacteria and generally grades well with the degree of sepsis.

question_text: A 38-year-old man complains of sudden attacks of dizziness, blurred vision, and excruciating headaches of 4 months in duration. During one of these attacks, his blood pressure was 180/120 mm Hg. The patient's father had been treated for thyroid cancer about 15 years ago. Laboratory studies show normal serum levels of aldosterone, renin, and angiotensin. A 24-hour urinalysis reveals increased metanephrines. Episodic hypertension in this patient is most likely caused by a tumor in which of the following endocrine organs?
explanation:
Pheochromocytoma is a rare tumor of chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla that secretes catecholamines. Such tumors also originate in extra-adrenal sites, in which case they are termed paragangliomas. The clinical features associated with pheochromocytoma are caused by the release of catecholamines. Patients with pheochromocytoma come to medical attention because of (1) asymptomatic hypertension discovered on a routine physical examination, (2) symptomatic hypertension that is resistant to antihypertensive therapy; (3) malignant hypertension (e.g., encephalopathy, papilledema, proteinuria), (4) myocardial infarction or aortic dissection, or (5) convulsions. The other choices do not include tumors that lead to episodic hypertension.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition, chapter 24, pg 1127

question_text: A patient presents with truncal obesity, abdominal striae, and poor wound healing. What is the likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Explanation:

A patient presenting with truncal obesity, abdominal striae, and poor wound healing is suggestive of Cushing's syndrome, a disorder characterized by chronic hypercortisolism leading to these clinical features.


Management:

  • Surgery is the preferred treatment for most cases.
  • Selective transsphenoidal surgery to remove the pituitary adenoma is the preferred initial treatment for Cushing's disease caused by a pituitary adenoma.
  • Medical Therapy:
    • Used to control cortisol levels pre-operatively or in cases where surgery is not feasible (like refractory hyperkalemic hypertension, acute psychosis, undetected ectopic metastasis)
    • Metyrapone and ketoconazole: Inhibit cortisol synthesis.
    • Osilodrostat: A potent 11β-hydroxylase inhibitor.
    • Mitotane: An adrenolytic agent often used for ACC.
    • Etomidate: Blocks 11β-hydroxylase, administered intravenously.
    • Pasireotide: A somatostatin receptor agonist used for Cushing's disease when surgery is not successful.
  • Post-Surgical Management:
    • Hydrocortisone replacement (HPA axis suppression).
  • Long-term Monitoring
    • Essential to detect recurrence and manage potential complications.

Explanation of other options:

Addison's disease (Option B): Addison's disease (Option B) is primary adrenal cortical insufficiency characterised by glucocorticoid deficiency. Clinical features include weight loss, anorexia, malaise, weakness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea or constipation, postural hypotension, shock, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, and hypercalcemia.

Hypoestrogenism (Option C): Hypoestrogenism refers to low estrogen levels in the body. Common manifestations include irregular or absent menstruation, hot flashes, night sweats, mood changes, and reduced bone density.

Increased growth hormone (Option D): Increased growth hormone levels result in acromegaly in adults or gigantism in children, usually due to pituitary tumours secreting excess GH.

question_text: Which of the following is the primary function of inhibin?
explanation:
Explanation:

Inhibin is a hormone secreted mainly by:

  • Granulosa cells in the ovary (females)
  • Sertoli cells in the testes (males)

Its principal function is to suppress Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) secretion from the anterior pituitary. This regulation helps control the growth and maturation of ovarian follicles in females and sperm production in males.

  • Inhibin B: Predominantly secreted before ovulation
  • Inhibin A: Predominantly secreted after ovulation

Explanation for Other Options:

Stimulates the secretion of FSH (Option A): Inhibin does not increase FSH levels; it acts to suppress them once follicular or sperm development reaches adequate levels.

Inhibition of PRL (Option C):nhibin does not regulate prolactin (PRL). PRL secretion is mainly controlled by dopamine and other hypothalamic factors. Thus, inhibin neither inhibits nor stimulates PRL production.

Stimulation of PRL (Option D): Inhibin does not regulate prolactin (PRL). PRL secretion is mainly controlled by dopamine and other hypothalamic factors. Thus, inhibin neither inhibits nor stimulates PRL production.

question_text: An 8-year-old child presents with progressive vision loss, and an MRI was done, which showed a suprasellar mass. Histopathology of the mass showed the findings of palisading epithelium and wet keratin. Which among the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Craniopharyngiomas are slow-growing tumours arising from remnants of Rathke's pouch, most often located in the suprasellar region with or without intrasellar extension.
  • They show a bimodal age distribution: One peak in childhood (5-15 years) and another in adults over 65.
  • It typically presents with headaches, visual disturbances, or, in children, growth retardation due to pituitary hypofunction and GH deficiency.
  • Typically measuring 3-4 cm, they are often cystic, sometimes multiloculated, and may encroach on the optic chiasm or cranial nerves, with two histologic subtypes: adamantinomatous (common in children) and papillary (common in adults).
  • The adamantinomatous variant features nests or cords of squamous epithelium in a spongy reticulum, peripheral palisading, wet keratin as shown below, and frequent dystrophic calcification.
  • The cysts may be filled with cholesterol-rich fluid, linked to CTNNB1 mutations activating Wnt signalling.
  • The papillary variant consists of solid squamous epithelium without wet keratin, occasional calcifications, and is associated with BRAF V600E mutations, which have therapeutic implications.
  • Lesions under 5 cm generally have excellent recurrence-free survival, whereas larger tumours may be more invasive.
  • Malignant transformation into squamous carcinoma is rare and typically follows irradiation.

Explanation of other options:

Pituitary adenoma (Option B): Pituitary adenomas are typically soft, well-circumscribed tumours that may remain confined to the sella turcica or expand to erode surrounding bone and compress nearby structures, with larger lesions sometimes infiltrating adjacent tissues. Histologically, they consist of uniform polygonal cells arranged in sheets or cords with sparse supporting connective tissue, giving a soft, gelatinous consistency, and show low mitotic activity unless aggressive. Clinically, they cause symptoms through hormone hypersecretion or local mass effects, which may include visual field defects, signs of raised intracranial pressure, and hypopituitarism.

Rathke's cleft cyst (Option C): These cysts are lined by ciliated cuboidal epithelium, containing occasional goblet cells and anterior pituitary cells, and can accumulate protein-rich fluid, leading to expansion that compresses the normal gland. It can lead to hypopituitarism.

Meningioma (Option D): Meningiomas are typically rubbery, rounded dural masses that compress the brain and often contain psammomatous calcifications. Clinically, they are slow-growing, causing vague or focal neurological symptoms from brain compression, commonly arising in locations such as the parasagittal region, convexities, olfactory groove, and sella turcica. They are rare in children, more frequent in women, and may grow faster during pregnancy due to hormone receptor expression.

question_text:
A 25-year-old female presents with the acute onset of cessation of lactation. She delivered her first child several months ago and has been breastfeeding since then. She reports that she has not menstruated since the delivery.
She also says that lately she has been tired and has been "feeling cold" all of the time. Laboratory workup reveals a
deficiency of ACTH and other anterior pituitary hormones. What is the most likely cause of this patient's signs and
symptoms?
explanation:
Hypopituitarism results from destructive processes that involve the adenohypophysis (anterior pituitary). These processes may be acute (sudden) or chronic. Sheehan's syndrome, also known as postpartum pituitary necrosis, results from the sudden infarction of the anterior lobe of the pituitary. This can occur with obstetric complications, such as hemorrhage or shock. The pituitary gland normally doubles in size during pregnancy; hypovolemia during delivery decreases blood flow and may result in infarction of the anterior pituitary. Sheehan's syndrome produces symptoms of hypopituitarism. The initial sign is cessation of lactation, which may be followed by secondary amenorrhea due to the loss of gonadotropins. Other signs of hypopituitarism include hypothyroidism and decreased functioning of the adrenal gland. Acute destruction of the pituitary is also associated with DIC and thrombosis of the cavernous sinus. Chronic causes of hypopituitarism include nonsecretory chromophobe pituitary adenomas, empty sella syndrome, and suprasellar (hypothalamic) tumors. The term pituitary apoplexy refers to spontaneous hemorrhage into a pituitary tumor, while the empty sella syndrome is caused by a defective diaphragma sellae, which permits CSF from the third ventricle to enter the sella. It may also be secondary to infarction or necrosis. A CT scan reveals the sella to be enlarged or to appear empty.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition , chapter 24, pg 1066

question_text: A 32-year-old woman has cyclic abdominal pain that coincides with her menses. Attempts to become pregnant have failed over the past 5 years. There are no abnormal findings on physical examination. Laparoscopic examination shows numerous hemorrhagic 0.2-0.5 cm lesions over the peritoneal surfaces of the uterus and ovaries. Which of the following ovarian lesions is most likely to be associated with her findings?
explanation:
Endometriosis is a condition in which functional endometrial glands are found outside the uterus. Common sites include ovaries, uterine ligaments, rectovaginal septum, and pelvic peritoneum. These endometrial glands can respond to ovarian hormones so that cyclic abdominal pain coincides with menstruation. Recurrent hemorrhages may incite scarring and the formation of fibrous adhesions in the pelvic region. This may cause distortion of the ovaries and fallopian tubes and may lead to infertility. One common variation is formation of an endometrioma, or chocolate cyst, which represents a focus of endometriosis that becomes an expanding cystic lesion as its center becomes filled with chocolate-brown sludge from the recurrent hemorrhage. The remaining choices are not associated with endometriosis, although endometrioid tumors may form in foci of endometriosis.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition, Chapter - 22 pg 1004

question_text: All the following condition can be diagnosed by FNAC; except:

Careful evaluation of the integrity of the capsule is therefore, critical in distinguishing follicular adenomas from follicular carcinomas, which demonstrate capsular and/or vascular invasion. This can be demonstrated by biopsy of the gland and not FNAC which will demonstrate only the morphology of the tumor cells and not the entire gland histology.

question_text: Needle biopsy of prostate shows acinar adenocarcinoma. Predominantly in cribriform pattern followed by cells with central necrosis. What is the grade it belongs to?

Changes in 2019 Gleason score

Discontinued Gleason grades 1 and 2

  • Gleason grade 4: Key finding is coalescent or fused glands with > 1 lumen and absence of intervening stroma between adjacent glands. Patterns included are
    • Cribriform

  • Grade 5 has 2 patterns:

question_text: Which of the following cancers are most commonly associated with RET gene mutation?
explanation:
Explanation:

Among the given options, medullary carcinoma of thyroid is most commonly associated with RET gene mutation.

Explanation of other options:

Follicular carcinoma of thyroid (Option B): The gene mutations associated with follicular carcinoma of the thyroid are RAS point mutations, PAX8-PPARG fusion gene, PIK3CA mutations and PTEN mutations.

Renal cell cancer (Option C): Renal cell carcinoma involves distinct genetic changes depending on the subtype. Clear cell carcinoma is most often linked to VHL gene inactivation on chromosome 3p, while papillary carcinoma shows trisomy 7, trisomy 17, and MET mutations. Chromophobe carcinoma has multiple chromosome losses, Xp11 translocation carcinoma is defined by TFE3 translocations, and collecting duct carcinoma shows various chromosomal losses and deletions.

Anaplastic carcinoma of thyroid (Option D): The gene mutations associated with anaplastic (undifferentiated) thyroid carcinoma are TP53 (tumor suppressor gene), CTNNB1 (encodes β-catenin), and TERT (encodes the catalytic component of telomerase)

question_text: A patient presents with a midline neck swelling. Biopsy of the lesion demonstrates "orphan Annie's eye" nuclei as seen in the provided image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of orphan Annie's eye nuclei, optically clear nuclei resembling ground glass, is characteristic of Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC).

  • Papillary carcinoma is the most common type of thyroid cancer.
  • It typically presents as an anterior neck nodule with cervical lymphadenopathy.
  • Spread is via lymphatics.
  • Associated genetic alterations: BRAF mutations, RET/PTC rearrangements.

Histopathological features of PTC:

  • True papillae with fibrovascular core
  • Orphan Annie's eye nuclei (optically clear)
  • Intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions (INCI)
  • Nuclear grooves ("coffee-bean" nuclei)
  • Psammoma bodies (dystrophic calcifications)

Related important points and concepts:

  • PTC has the best prognosis among thyroid cancers.
  • More common in younger females.
  • Risk factors: radiation exposure in childhood.

Explanation of other options:

Follicular carcinoma (Option A): Malignant tumour of follicular cells, usually in older individuals. Spreads hematogenously and lacks nuclear features of PTC.

Toxic nodular goiter (Option C): A hormonally active goiter (Plummer disease). Causes hyperthyroidism but lacks malignant histology.

Medullary carcinoma (Option D): Neuroendocrine tumour of C cells producing calcitonin. May cause amyloid deposition in the stroma. Does not show orphan Annie's nuclei.

Key Takeaways:

  • Papillary carcinoma thyroid → most common thyroid malignancy.
  • Classic nuclear features: Orphan Annie eye nuclei, INCI, nuclear grooves, psammoma bodies.
  • Best prognosis among thyroid cancers.
