Explanation:

Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy and typically presents as a painless thyroid nodule, often with cervical lymphadenopathy.

    • Tends to spread via lymphatics rather than hematogenous routes

  • Characterised by follicular architecture, not nuclear features of papillary carcinoma
  • Tends to metastasize via blood vessels (hematogenous spread)

Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (Option C):

  • Highly aggressive, undifferentiated tumor
  • Histology shows marked pleomorphism, giant cells, spindle cells
  • Poor prognosis

question_text: A 28-year-old woman presents with neck swelling. USG neck performed shows a nodule in the left lobe of thyroid. Thyroid function tests are within normal limits. Ultrasound guided fine needle aspiration cytology reveals malignant cells. The tumor is excised and examined by light microscopy (shown in the image). What is the appropriate pathologic diagnosis?
explanation:
Thyroid lesion shows branching papillae lined by epithelial cells with clear nuclei and fibrovascular core.

(a) Anaplastic carcinomas demonstrate variable morphology, including (1) large, pleomorphic giant cells, including occasional osteoclast-like multinucleate giant cells; (2) spindle cells with a sarcomatous appearance; and (3) mixed spindle and giant cells.

(b) Microscopically, most follicular carcinomas are composed of fairly uniform cells forming small follicles containing colloid, quite reminiscent of normal thyroid with capsular and vascular invasion.

(c) Medullary carcinomas are composed of polygonal to spindle-shaped cells, which may form nests, trabeculae, and even follicles.

(d) Branching papillae having a fibrovascular stalk covered by a single to multiple layers of cuboidal epithelial cells. In most neoplasms, the epithelium covering the papillae consists of well-differentiated, uniform, orderly cuboidal cells.

Reference: Robbins 10th Ed pg. 1088

question_text: A 45-year-old patient presents with a solitary thyroid nodule. Histopathological examination of the thyroid mass shows pink, eosinophilic extracellular material. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The histopathological hallmark of MTC is pink, eosinophilic extracellular material, which represents amyloid deposits derived from calcitonin. Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid (MTC) arises from parafollicular C cells and is unique among thyroid malignancies due to the presence of amyloid deposition in the stroma.

A Congo red stain confirms the presence of amyloid, showing apple-green birefringence under polarised light. Medullary carcinoma is associated with RET mutations and can occur sporadically or as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndromes (MEN 2A and 2B).

Explanation of Other Options:

Papillary carcinoma (Option A) is characterised by Orphan Annie eye nuclei, nuclear grooves, and psammoma bodies, but it does not contain amyloid deposits.

Follicular carcinoma (Option B) shows capsular and vascular invasion with follicular structures, but lacks eosinophilic extracellular amyloid.

Anaplastic carcinoma (Option C) is an undifferentiated, highly aggressive tumour with pleomorphic giant cells and spindle cells, but it does not exhibit amyloid deposition.

Key Takeaway:

The presence of pink, eosinophilic extracellular material in a thyroid tumour suggests amyloid deposition, which is highly characteristic of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC).

Confirmatory tests include Congo red staining (showing apple-green birefringence), serum calcitonin levels (elevated in MTC), and RET proto-oncogene mutation analysis, particularly in hereditary cases associated with MEN 2A and 2B.

question_text: A patient presents with a midline neck swelling. Histology showed amyloid deposition, and immunohistochemistry is positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin, and TTF-1. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Based on the features of histopathological examination showing amyloid deposition in a midline neck swelling and immunohistochemistry revealing synaptophysin, chromogranin, and TTF-1 positivity, the most likely diagnosis is medullary thyroid cancer.

  • Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid is a neuroendocrine tumour derived from parafollicular C cells.
  • These tumours secrete calcitonin, which is important for diagnosis and follow-up, and can also produce other hormones like serotonin, ACTH, and VIP.
  • Most are sporadic, while the rest are associated with MEN-2A or MEN-2B syndromes due to activating RET proto-oncogene mutations.
  • MEN-associated cases occur in younger patients, sometimes in the first decade, whereas sporadic cases typically appear in adulthood, peaking in the 40s and 50s.
  • Sporadic tumours usually present as solitary nodules, while familial cases often show bilaterality and multicentricity.
  • Grossly, they are firm, pale grey to tan, and infiltrative, sometimes with necrosis and haemorrhage.
  • Microscopically, they are composed of polygonal to spindle-shaped cells arranged in nests, trabeculae, or follicles, with anaplastic cells in some tumours.
  • Amyloid deposits from calcitonin peptides are common, and calcitonin can be demonstrated in both the cytoplasm and stromal amyloid, as shown below.
  • Ultrastructurally, they contain membrane-bound electron-dense granules typical of neuroendocrine tumours, and immunohistochemical testing shows positivity for markers of endocrine granules, including synaptophysin and chromogranin A.
  • Nuclear staining for thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF-1) is commonly observed in cancers of the lung and thyroid.

Explanation of other options:

Papillary thyroid cancer (Option A): Papillary thyroid carcinoma may have ill-defined margins and can involve adjacent parenchyma, sometimes with areas of fibrosis, calcification, or cystic change. The cut surface may display papillary foci. Papillary microcarcinoma refers to lesions under 1 cm but otherwise identical histologically. Microscopically, they show branching papillae with fibrovascular cores lined by cuboidal epithelial cells, varying from uniform to markedly anaplastic. Nuclei characteristically have finely dispersed chromatin and a clear, empty appearance known as ground-glass or Orphan Annie eye nuclei, which are shown below, with possible nuclear grooves or pseudoinclusions. Psammoma bodies, which are concentrically calcified structures, are often present within papillary cores, strongly indicating papillary carcinoma.

Follicular thyroid cancer (Option C): Follicular carcinoma of the thyroid usually appears as a single nodule, which may be either well-circumscribed or widely infiltrative. Microscopically, most tumours consist of uniform cells forming small follicles with colloid, as shown below, resembling normal thyroid, though some have less apparent follicular differentiation with nests or sheets of cells lacking colloid. In some cases, cells contain abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm, known as the Hürthle cell or oncocytic variant. Thyroglobulin is commonly used to monitor recurrence.

Anaplastic thyroid cancer (Option D): Poorly differentiated thyroid carcinomas consist of cells with minimal follicular differentiation, arranged in insular or trabecular patterns, often with intratumoral necrosis and frequent mitoses. Anaplastic carcinomas show variable morphology, including large pleomorphic giant cells, spindle cells with a sarcomatoid appearance, or a mix of both, and may retain foci of papillary or follicular differentiation, indicating origin from a well-differentiated carcinoma. These tumours express epithelial markers like cytokeratin but are typically negative for thyroid differentiation markers such as thyroglobulin.

question_text: A patient presents with a neck swelling causing compression of the trachea and oesophagus. Histopathological examination reveals cell nests with pink extracellular amyloid stroma. What is the cellular origin of this tumour?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The presence of neck swelling, amyloid stroma, and a nesting pattern of tumor cells strongly suggests Medullary Carcinoma of the Thyroid.
  • It arises from parafollicular C cells (also called C cells) and often presents as a solitary thyroid nodule.

Medullary carcinoma thyroid

  • Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) is a neuroendocrine tumor originating from the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid.
  • It represents approximately 5% of all thyroid neoplasms.
  • Genetics:
    • The most common associated mutation is in the RET proto-oncogene.
    • MCT can occur sporadically or as part of familial syndromes, particularly Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) type 2.
  • Tumor Markers:
    • Calcitonin: A specific and sensitive marker for MCT.
    • Carcinoembryonic Antigen (CEA): Used as an additional marker, especially in cases where calcitonin levels are not elevated.
  • Histopathology:
    • Amyloid deposits: Derived from calcitonin.
    • Nesting pattern: Tumor cells are arranged in nests with characteristic amyloid stroma.

  • Under polarizing microscopy, Congo red-stained amyloid exhibits apple-green birefringence.

Explanation of other options:

Hurthle cells (Option B), Askanazy cells (Option D): Hurthle cells also called Askanazy, oncocytic, or oxyphilic cells, these are large thyroid cells with dense, eosinophilic cytoplasm. They are typically seen in Hashimoto's thyroiditis, which also shows extensive lymphocytic infiltration with well-formed germinal centres. Hurthle cells are not associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma.


Follicular cells (Option C): Follicular cells give rise to papillary, follicular, and anaplastic thyroid carcinomas but not medullary carcinoma. They have a round nucleus and basophilic cytoplasm, and their primary function is to synthesise thyroid hormones.

question_text: 25-year-old female presented with swelling in front of neck. TSH levels were elevated. Biopsy showed lymphocytic infiltration and Hurthle cells. Which of the following is the possible diagnosis?

question_text: RET proto-oncogene is associated with:
explanation:
The RET proto-oncogene is a key genetic driver in Medullary Thyroid Cancer (MTC). Germline mutations in RET are associated with familial MTC and Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) syndromes, while somatic mutations in RET are found in sporadic cases of MTC.

Incorrect choices explanation :

  • (Choice B) Follicular Thyroid Cancer (FTC)
    • Not associated with RET mutations.
    • Instead, RAS mutations and PAX8-PPARγ translocations are common.
    • Arises from follicular cells and spreads hematogenously.
  • (Choice C) Papillary Thyroid Cancer (PTC)
    • RET/PTC rearrangement (NOT RET mutations) is seen in PTC.
    • PTC is also linked with BRAF mutations (most common).
    • Characterized by Orphan Annie-eye nuclei, nuclear grooves, and psammoma bodies.
  • (Choice D) Anaplastic Thyroid Cancer (ATC)
    • Highly aggressive thyroid malignancy.
    • No significant association with RET mutations.
    • Instead, it is associated with TP53 mutations, TERT promoter mutations, and dedifferentiation of PTC or FTC.

Key takeaway:

  • MTC arises from parafollicular C cells, which produce calcitonin.
  • Activating mutations in the RET proto-oncogene lead to uncontrolled cell proliferation.
  • RET mutations are present in:
    • Familial MTC (FMTC)
    • Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) Type 2A & 2B
    • Sporadic MTC (~50% cases show RET mutations)

The RET proto-oncogene is strongly associated with Medullary Thyroid Cancer (MTC),

question_text: A 38-year-old male patient presented for routine examination. He was advised for routine test and for single cervical lymph node enlargement detected on ultrasound. A solitary nodule was also identified in the thyroid. His thyroid function tests are normal and FNAC from cervical lymph nodes shows reactive lymphoid hyperplasia. Scintigraphy shows cold masses (suspected malignancy). Thyroidectomy was done and histopathological image is shown below. All these features can be seen in this lesion; except:
explanation:
(a) Nuclei with finely dispersed chromatin and optically clear or empty appearance, giving rise to the designation ground-glass or Orphan Annie eye nuclei.

(b) In addition, invaginations of the nuclear membrane may give the appearance of nuclear inclusions ("pseudo-inclusions") or grooves.

(c) Concentrically calcified structure termed psammoma bodies are often present, usually within the cores of papillae.

(d) Cells with abundant granular, eosinophilic cytoplasm (Hurthle cell or oncocytic) seen in variant of follicular carcinoma.

Reference: Robbins 10th Ed pg. 1088

question_text: A 24-year-old male presented with a swelling on anterior aspect of neck. On examination, the swelling was firm and moved with deglutination. Biopsy from the lesion has been shown. What is the typical finding and diagnosis?
option_a: Orphan Annie eye nuclei; Follicular Ca thyroid
option_b: Orphan Annie eye nuclei; Papillary Ca thyroid
option_c: Hurthle cell change; Follicular Ca thyroid
option_d: Hurthle cell change; Papillary Ca thyroid
explanation:
• High power shows nuclei of papillary carcinoma cells contain finely dispersed chromatin, which imparts an optically clear or empty appearance, giving rise to the ground glass or Orphan Annie eye nuclei. In addition, invaginations of the cytoplasm may give the appearance of intranuclear inclusions ("pseudoinclusions') or intranuclear grooves. The diagnosis of papillary carcinoma can be made based on these nuclear features, even in the absence of papillary architecture.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition, chapter 24, pg 1086

question_text: A middle-aged woman presents with dry eyes and dry mouth. Laboratory tests reveal positive anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) antibodies. What is the most likely underlying pathological mechanism?
option_a: Destruction of exocrine glands by neutrophils
option_c: Lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of salivary and lacrimal glands
option_d: Deposition of amyloid in salivary glands
explanation:
Explanation:

The given clinical vignette of dry eyes and dry mouth, along with anti-Ro and anti-La positivity is suggestive of Sjogren’s syndrome, characterised by lymphocytic infiltration and destruction of salivary and lacrimal glands.

  • Sjogren syndrome is a chronic autoimmune disease characterised by immune-mediated destruction of the lacrimal and salivary glands, leading to dry eyes (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth (xerostomia).
  • It can occur as a primary form (sicca syndrome) or secondary to other autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, polymyositis, and scleroderma.
  • Pathogenesis involves lymphocytic infiltration and fibrosis of the glands as shown below, with predominantly activated CD4+ T cells, plasma cells, and some B cells. (Options A, B, and D ruled out)
  • Rheumatoid factor is present in most cases and is also associated with ANA positivity..
  • Antibodies against SS-A (Ro) and SS-B (La) are detectable in up to 90% of patients and are important serologic markers.
  • Morphologically, major targets are the lacrimal and salivary glands, but other exocrine glands (respiratory, gastrointestinal, vaginal) may be affected.
  • Early changes show periductal and perivascular lymphoid infiltration. Later, there is ductal epithelial hyperplasia, acinar atrophy, fibrosis, hyalinization, and fat replacement, with possible lymphoid follicles and germinal centres.
  • Clinically, it occurs most often in women aged 50-60 years, with keratoconjunctivitis causing burning, itching, and blurred vision. Xerostomia causes difficulty swallowing solid foods, decreased taste, oral dryness, fissuring, and parotid enlargement in half of patients.
  • The combination of lacrimal and salivary gland enlargement was once termed Mikulicz disease, now referred to as Mikulicz syndrome, which may result from various causes, including sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease, lymphoma, or other tumours.
  • Chronic lymphocytic inflammation carries a risk of developing marginal zone lymphoma.

question_text: A 40-year-old female presents with swelling in her neck that she first noticed 4 months ago. She also complains of intermittent watery diarrhea over the same time period. Physical examination reveals a nontender and nodular lesion in the left lobe of the thyroid. The patient's mother died of thyroid cancer 8 years ago. The thyroid nodule is found to be "cold" by radioiodine scintiscan. Patient underwent total thyroidectomy due to possibility of tumorigenesis. Histopathological image of the patient is shown below. Laboratory studies would likely show elevated blood levels of which of the following hormones in this patient?
explanation:
(a) Histopathological examination reveals amyloid deposition seen predominantly in medullary carcinoma of thyroid. Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) is derived from C cells of the thyroid, which secrete the calcium-lowering hormone calcitonin.

(b & c) (cortisol and PTH) are not thyroid hormones.

(d) TSH (choice e) is normal because the remaining thyroid produces adequate thyroid hormone.

Reference: Robbins 10th Ed pg. 1091

question_text: What is the gene commonly involved in carcinoma histology shown below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The histopathology shown in the image shows Orphan Annie's eye nucleus (seen in papillary thyroid cancer) associated with the BRAF V600 gene.

Papillary thyroid cancer is the most common type of thyroid cancer and is characterised by lymphatic spread.

  • It often presents with a nodule in the anterior neck and lymphadenopathy.
  • Associated with BRAF mutations and RET-PTC fusion.
  • It has the best prognosis among thyroid malignancies.
  • HPE shows
    • True papillae: Fingerlike projections with fibrovascular cores.
    • Orphan Annie eye nuclei: Optically clear nucleus produced due to artefact.
    • Intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions (INCI).
    • Nuclear groove or coffee bean nucleus.
    • Presence of psammoma bodies - Dystrophic calcifications.

Explanation for other options:

RAS (Option A) mutations are commonly found in

  • Follicular thyroid carcinoma
  • Follicular adenomas.
  • Colorectal cancer
  • Pancreatic cancer
  • Lung adenocarcinoma.

RET (Option B) mutation is seen in

  • Medullary thyroid carcinoma (as part of MEN2 syndromes)
  • Papillary thyroid carcinoma (via RET/PTC rearrangements)

P53 (Option D) mutation is seen in Breast, lung, and colon carcinomas.

Learning Objective:

BRAF V600E mutation seen in:

  • Langerhans cell histiocytosis
  • Hairy cell leukemia
  • Papillary carcinoma thyroid
  • Juvenile pilocytic astrocytoma
  • Colon cancer
  • Melanoma

question_text: A 60-year-old man with a history of hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and coronary artery disease presented to ER complaining of approximately 1-2 weeks of neck pains radiating to his chest. The pains were associated with movement, particularly when he moved his head and neck. Other than his presenting symptoms, his review of symptoms was negative. His blood pressure was 126/67 mm HG and his pulse was 88 beats/min. Chest CT revealed no significant cardiac or pulmonary disease. However, a large ill-defined 4 cm right thyroid nodule was noted, associated with tracheal deviation at the thoracic inlet. TSH was normal at 1.18 mIU/ml. Hemithyroidectomy done and H&E stain was positive for nest of tumor cells and calcitonin shown below. RET proto-oncogene is associated with the most probable diagnosis discussed above:
explanation:
The patient presents with a large thyroid nodule (4 cm) causing tracheal deviation, normal TSH levels, and histological findings of tumor nests and calcitonin positivity. These features are highly suggestive of Medullary Thyroid Cancer (MTC), which originates from parafollicular C cells of the thyroid and is known for calcitonin production. Additionally, the association with the RET proto-oncogene further supports the diagnosis.

Why Medullary Thyroid Cancer (MTC)?

  • Derived from Parafollicular C cells, which secrete calcitonin.
  • Calcitonin positivity on immunohistochemistry (IHC) is a hallmark feature.
  • RET proto-oncogene mutations are commonly involved, especially in familial MTC or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) 2A/2B syndromes.
  • Histopathology: Tumor cells appear in nests, trabeculae, or sheets with amyloid deposits (from calcitonin).

Incorrect choices explanation :

  • (Choice B) Follicular Thyroid Cancer (FTC)
    • Typically presents as a solitary, encapsulated nodule, often invading blood vessels.
    • Does not produce calcitonin.
    • RET mutations are not associated; instead, RAS and PAX8-PPARγ mutations are seen.
  • (Choice C) Papillary Thyroid Cancer (PTC)
    • Most common thyroid cancer, but characterized by Orphan Annie-eye nuclei, nuclear grooves, and psammoma bodies.
    • Associated with BRAF and RET/PTC rearrangements, not typically with RET proto-oncogene mutations.
  • (Choice D) Anaplastic Thyroid Cancer (ATC)
    • Extremely aggressive, presents with rapidly growing thyroid mass and airway invasion.
    • No calcitonin production and RET mutations are not typical.
    • Poorly differentiated, often showing pleomorphic giant cells and spindle cells on histology.

Key takeaway:

The presence of calcitonin positivity, nest-like tumor cells, and RET proto-oncogene involvement confirms Medullary Thyroid Cancer (MTC)

question_text: Breast biopsy shows the following histopathological image. The tumour cells show PAS positivity. What is your most likely diagnosis
explanation:
The histopathological image demonstrates large, pale-staining cells with abundant clear cytoplasm scattered singly or in clusters within the epidermis. These cells are known as Paget cells, characteristic of Paget's disease of the breast.

Incorrect choices explanation:

  • (Choice B) Ductal carcinoma: Typically presents as invasive clusters or nests of tumor cells within breast stroma, not epidermis.
  • (Choice C) Inflammatory carcinoma: Clinical presentation includes erythema and edema ("peau d'orange") of breast skin. Histologically, dermal lymphatics are blocked by carcinoma cells, not epidermal infiltration.
  • (Choice D) Lobular carcinoma: Usually characterized by small cells infiltrating the stroma in a single-file pattern, not epidermal involvement.

Thus, the correct diagnosis is Paget's disease (Choice A).

Key takeaway:

  • Large cells with clear cytoplasm (Paget cells) interspersed among keratinocytes.
  • PAS positivity is a hallmark, reflecting intracellular mucopolysaccharides within Paget cells.

Clinical correlation typically shows an eczematous lesion involving the nipple and areola

question_text: After mastectomy, breast reconstruction is done by
explanation: Answer- B. latissimus dorsi If the skin at the mastectomy site is poor (e.g. following radiotherapy) or if a larger volume of tissue is required, a musculocutaneous flap can be constructed either from the latissimusdorsi muscle (an LD flap) or using the transversusabdominis muscle (a TRAM flap as). The latter gives an excellent cosmetic result in experienced hands but is a lengthy procedure and requires careful patient selection.

question_text: A 60-year-old female presents with a slow-growing, painless mass in her left breast. On physical examination, the mass is soft, well-circumscribed, and mobile. A biopsy is performed, and histopathology reveals the following. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Histopathology shows tumour cells floating in pools of mucin, which is a hallmark feature of Mucinous Carcinoma. This subtype of invasive carcinoma has a good prognosis, with a lower likelihood of lymph node metastasis compared to other invasive breast cancers.

Mucinous carcinoma of the breast, also known as colloid carcinoma, is a rare, slow-growing malignant breast tumour characterised by abundant extracellular mucin. It typically presents in postmenopausal women as a soft, well-circumscribed, and mobile mass, similar to a benign lesion.

Explanation of Other Options:

Medullary carcinoma (Option A): Presents as a well-circumscribed mass, but histologically, it shows sheets of pleomorphic cells with lymphoplasmacytic infiltration and lacks extracellular mucin.

Lobular carcinoma (Option B): Classically infiltrates in a single-file pattern, due to loss of E-cadherin, and does not form well-circumscribed, mucin-rich masses.

Invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) (Option D): The most common breast malignancy, presenting as a firm, irregular, and infiltrative mass, usually with desmoplastic stroma, unlike the soft nature of mucinous carcinoma.

Key Takeaway:

A slow-growing, soft, well-circumscribed breast mass in an older woman with histopathological findings of tumour cells in pools of extracellular mucin strongly suggests mucinous carcinoma of the breast. This subtype has a better prognosis than invasive ductal carcinoma and is less likely to metastasise.

question_text: A 35-year-old woman presents with a lump located in the upper outer quadrant of her breast. Histopathological examination of the mass shows tumour cells with a signet ring-like appearance. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Colloid carcinoma, also called mucinous carcinoma, is a subtype of infiltrating ductal carcinoma. It is recognised microscopically by abundant extracellular mucin with tumour cells arranged in clusters or islands. The cells may also contain intracellular mucin that pushes the nucleus to the periphery, producing a signet ring cell appearance.

Clinically, it usually appears as a soft, sometimes mobile mass that can mimic a benign lesion. It occurs more often in older women and generally carries an excellent prognosis.

  • Gross features: Pale gelatinous / jelly-like consistency, soft and rubbery texture.
  • Microscopy: Tumour cells floating in pools of extracellular mucin, with occasional intracellular mucin forming signet rings.
  • FNAC finding: Presence of "chicken wire"blood vessels.
  • Location: Most frequently seen in the upper outer quadrant.

Explanation of other options:

Papillary carcinoma (Option B): Rare, ~0.5% of breast cancers, typically seen in postmenopausal women (60-80 years). Presents with bloody nipple discharge or a palpable mass. Favourable prognosis.

Medullary carcinoma (Option C): Appears as a well-circumscribed, grey-tan, lobulated tumour often with haemorrhage or necrosis. Commonly ~2-3 cm. May present with axillary lymphadenopathy.

Phyllodes tumour (Option D): Fibroepithelial tumour (benign to malignant spectrum). Large, nodular, firm mass with lobulated cut surface and cleft-like spaces containing serous or jelly-like fluid.

Key Takeaways:

  • Colloid carcinoma = mucinous carcinoma.
  • Histology hallmark: Signet ring cells + extracellular mucin pools.
  • Prognosis is generally favourable.

Reference:

question_text: A 32-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of painful subareolar swelling in her right breast for the past 6 months. On examination, there is a tender, indurated lump beneath the areola with mild erythema. She is a chronic smoker. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis based on the clinical features of painful subareolar swelling in her right breast in a chronic smoker is periductal mastitis.

Explanation of other options:

Fibroadenoma (Option B): Fibroadenomas are well-circumscribed, rubbery breast tumors that can range from very small to large masses, often appearing as palpable nodules in young women or as mammographic densities or calcifications in older women. Clinically, they are most common in women in their 20s-30s, may be multiple and bilateral, enlarge during pregnancy, and regress after menopause. The given clinical features are more consistent with a diagnosis of periductal mastitis.

Fat necrosis of breast (Option C): Appears as a painless lump, skin retraction/thickening, or calcifications on mammogram.

Duct ectasia (Option D): Duct ectasia usually appears as a periareolar lump, often accompanied by thick, white nipple discharge and sometimes skin retraction, though pain and redness are rare. It typically develops in women in their 50s or 60s, most often those who have had multiple pregnancies, and unlike squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts, it is not linked to smoking.

question_text: A woman presents with a firm and irregular lump in the upper outer quadrant of her breast. The histopathological slide of the mass sample is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis for a firm, irregular lump in the upper outer quadrant of the breast with an Indian file pattern on histology is Invasive Lobular Carcinoma (ILC).

Invasive Lobular Carcinoma (ILC)

  • Genetic Basis:Commonly associated with CDH1 gene mutation, leading to loss of E-cadherin, an adhesion molecule. This mutation is also seen in signet ring gastric adenocarcinoma.
  • Clinical Features:Frequently bilateral and multicentric. When one breast is affected, the other should always be evaluated.
  • Histopathology:
    • Cells are dyscohesivedue to loss of adhesion.
    • Classic Indian file pattern- tumour cells arranged in single rows.
    • Minimal desmoplasiaand fibrosis.
    • Targetoid spread- tumour cells encircle uninvolved ducts.
    • Pagetoid spread- tumour cells infiltrate the ducts.
    • Some variants may show signet ring cellswith mucin.
  • Metastasis:Can spread to unusual sites such as the peritoneum and leptomeninges (leading to carcinomatous meningitis).
  • Prognosis:Generally favourable compared to other invasive breast carcinomas.

Explanation of Other Options:

Phyllodes Tumour (Option A): A stromal tumour of breast connective tissue. Presents as a firm, smooth, well-defined lump. Histology shows increased stromal cellularity and leaf-like (phyllodes) architecture.

Inflammatory Breast Carcinoma (Option B): Rapidly progressive with skin thickening, oedema, and peau d'orange appearance.

Fibroadenoma (Option D): The most common benign breast tumour in young women (15-35 years). Presents as a mobile, well-circumscribed, non-tender lump. Histology reveals a fibrous capsule with proliferating stroma compressing glandular elements.

question_text: A 52-year-old woman feels a lump in her right breast. Her physician palpates an irregular 3 cm mass that is not movable because it appears fixed to the overlying skin, which is retracted. A mastectomy is performed and the pathologist on sectioning the breast finds a 3 x 3.5 cm ovoid mass that does not have discrete borders, but appears to infiltrate into the surrounding fibrofatty breast stroma. The mass is firm, white and has a fibrous consistency. Which of the following features is most likely demonstrated by the gross appearance of this mass?
explanation:
• Malignant potential is revealed only by invasion into adjacent tissues or metastasis.
  • The stroma carrying the blood supply is crucial to the growth of tumours but does not aid in the separation of benign from malignant ones.
  • The amount of stromal connective tissue does, however, determine the consistency of a neoplasm.
  • Certain cancers induce a dense, abundant fibrous stroma(desmoplasia), making them hard, so-called "scirrhous tumors".
  • Desmoplasia is the result of increased synthesis of extracellular matrix proteins and collagen by stromal cells. It is considered to be a reaction and response of the host tissue against invasive cancer cells.[5] The biological relevance of the desmoplastic response to cancer is still unclear.

Reference: Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 10th ed, Pg: 193.

question_text: A 21-year-old female presents to the surgical clinic with a small, incidentally detected mass in her left breast. On examination, the lump is soft, non-tender, and highly mobile. It is occasionally painful around her menstrual periods. A mammogram is reported as BI-RADS 3. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation for tissue sampling, providing rapid results?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture of a young woman with a soft, non-tender, highly mobile "breast mouse" that is hormonally sensitive is classic for a fibroadenoma. The standard evaluation for a breast lump is the "triple assessment," which includes clinical examination, imaging, and tissue sampling.

Given the high probability of a benign lesion in this young patient (supported by the BI-RADS 3 classification), Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC) is a very appropriate initial step. It is a minimally invasive, rapid, and cost-effective outpatient procedure that provides a cytological diagnosis, often within 2-3 days, to help confirm the benign nature of the mass.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Core Needle Biopsy (Option B): This is now considered the gold standard for tissue diagnosis because it provides a histological sample, which preserves the tissue architecture and is more accurate than cytology. While it is the definitive test for suspicious lesions, the less invasive FNAC is a reasonable and common first-line choice for a classic, likely benign fibroadenoma in a very young patient.
  • (Option C) Immunohistochemistry (IHC) & (Option D) Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH): These are not primary diagnostic tests. They are specialized ancillary studies performed on biopsy or excision specimens to further characterize a tumor, particularly a malignancy (e.g., to determine hormone receptor or HER2 status).

Key Takeaways:

  • A fibroadenoma is the most common benign breast tumor in young women.
  • The "Triple Assessment" (clinical exam, imaging, pathology) is the standard of care for any breast lump.
  • FNAC is a rapid cytological test suitable for confirming clinically and radiologically benign lesion.
  • Core biopsy provides a definitive histological diagnosis and is the gold standard for suspicious lesions.

question_text: Identify the disease associated with the following image provided
explanation:
Explanation:

The given image shows a 'crumpled tissue paper' appearance, a characteristic finding of Gaucher's disease.

Gaucher disease:

  • It is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in the GBA gene, which encodes the enzyme glucocerebrosidase.
  • Accumulation of glucocerebroside (glucosylceramide) within lysosomes of macrophages, forming characteristic Gaucher cells.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Hematologic: Pancytopenia
    • Skeletal: Bone crisis, severe bone pain.
    • Neurological: Parkinsonism, cognitive impairment, neuropathy
  • Investigations:
    • Bone marrow examination: Shows Gaucher cells with a characteristic wrinkled tissue paper appearance. Gaucher cells are macrophages that accumulate with glucocerebroside.
    • Enzyme assay: Demonstrates reduced activity of glucocerebrosidase in leukocytes or fibroblasts.
    • Long bone X-rays may show the Erlenmeyer flask deformity.

Explanation for other options:

Tay-Sachs disease (Option B) is caused by a deficiency of hexosaminidase A, leading to the accumulation of GM2 gangliosides in neurons. It presents with progressive neurodegeneration, developmental delay, cherry-red spot on the macula, but no Gaucher cells in the bone marrow.

Sandhoff's disease (Option C) occurs due to a hexosaminidase A and B deficiency, leading to GM2 ganglioside accumulation. It presents with similar neurodegenerative symptoms as Tay-Sachs but with visceral involvement, unlike Gaucher's disease.

Fabry's disease (Option D) is caused by a deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A, leading to the accumulation of globotriaosylceramide. It presents with neuropathic pain, angiokeratomas, corneal opacities, and renal/cardiac complications. No Gaucher cells are observed.

question_text: Reticular fibers are not seen as the structural framework of:
explanation:
The fully developed thymus is composed of two fused, well-encapsulated lobes. Fibrous extensions of the capsule divide each lobe into numerous lobules, each with an outer cortical layer enclosing the central medulla. Diverse types of cells populate the thymus, but thymic epithelial cells and immature T lymphocytes, also called thymocytes, predominate.

Epithelial cells in the cortex are polygonal in shape and have an abundant cytoplasm with dendritic extensions that contact adjacent cells. In contrast, the epithelial cells in the medulla are densely packed, often spindle-shaped, and have scant cytoplasm devoid of interconnecting processes. Whorls of medullary epithelial cells create Hassall corpuscles, with their characteristic keratinized cores. HOWEVER IT DOESN'T HAVE RETICULAR FIBRES

RETICULAR FIBRES ARE RICH IN LIVER, BONE MARROW, SPLEEN AND LYMPH NODE

Reference: Robin's basic pathology 10th edition, 631

question_text: Biopsy of a long bone was taken and the histology is shown below. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Paget's Disease of Bone (Osteitis Deformans) is a chronic bone disorder characterized by abnormal bone remodeling, leading to enlarged, deformed, and structurally weak bones.

Histological Findings in Paget’s Disease:

  • Mosaic pattern of lamellar bone ("jigsaw puzzle" or "mosaic-like" appearance) due to irregular cement lines.
  • Increased osteoclastic activity followed by excessive, disorganized osteoblastic activity.
  • Hypervascular marrow with fibrotic changes.
  • Thickened trabeculae with disorganized architecture.

Incorrect Choices explanation :

  • (Choice A) Osteoporosis
    • Bone mass is reduced, but histology shows thinning of trabeculae, not a mosaic pattern.
    • No abnormal remodeling, only increased bone resorption.
  • (Choice B) Osteosclerosis
    • Characterized by increased bone density, but without disorganized remodeling.
    • Seen in osteopetrosis and myelofibrosis, not Paget's.
  • (Choice C) Osteomalacia
    • Due to defective mineralization of bone matrix from vitamin D deficiency.
    • Histology shows excess unmineralized osteoid, not the mosaic pattern of Paget’s.

 Key takeaway:

  • Commonly affects long bones (femur, tibia), pelvis, skull, and spine.
  • Patients often have bone pain, deformities (bowing of long bones), and fractures.
  • Elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP) with normal calcium and phosphate levels.
  • Radiology: Enlarged bones with cortical thickening and lytic ("osteolytic-blastic") lesions.

question_text: A 50-year-old female on corticosteroids from a long duration presented with pain in the right hip region initially associated with activity and later on becomes constant. Fracture at neck along with irregular densities of the cancellous bone of femur is noticed in X-ray. The head of femur is replaced by artificial head. The histopathological examination of the head shows empty lacunae and necrotic adipocytes. What is the probable diagnosis based on histology?
explanation:
Infarction of bone and marrow is relatively common. It can be limited to the medullary cavity or involve both the medulla and cortex. Fractures and corticosteroid administration are the two most common causes. Microscopically, dead bone is characterized by empty lacunae surrounded by necrotic adipocytes. The released fatty acids bind calcium and form insoluble calcium soaps. The remaining trabeculae act as scaffolding for deposition of new bone, while osteoclasts resorb necrotic trabeculae.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition, chapter 26, pg 1185

question_text: A 50-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of left leg pain. His temperature is 38.7°C (103°F). He has a harsh systolic murmur and echocardiographic evidence of bacterial endocarditis. If this patient has developed hematogenous osteomyelitis, his bone infection would most likely be found in which of the following anatomic locations?
explanation:
Hematogenous osteomyelitis primarily affects the metaphyseal area of the long bones (knee, ankle, hip) because of the unique vascular supply in this region. Normally, arterioles enter the calcified portion of the growth plate, form a loop, and then drain into the medullary cavity without establishing a capillary bed. This vascular loop permits slowing and sludging of blood flow, allowing bacteria time to penetrate the walls of the blood vessels and establish an infective focus within the bone marrow. Osteomyelitis may break into the periosteum (choice e) but does not originate there. Vascular loops do not reach the epiphysis (choice c). Choices a and b would be distinctly uncommon.

Reference:Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition , chapter 26, pg 1171

question_text: A 30-year-old woman presents with left knee pain for the past month. Examination shows tenderness over the knee joint. X-ray demonstrates a 5 cm epiphyseal lesion in the distal femur with a"soap bubble" appearance. Microscopic findings are shown in the accompanying image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation (epiphyseal knee pain), radiographic finding (soap bubble appearance), and histology showing numerous multinucleated giant cells are typical of Giant Cell Tumour (Osteoclastoma).

Key features of Giant Cell Tumour (GCT):

  • Benign but locally aggressive tumour.
  • Occurs in third to fifth decades.
  • Common sites: Epiphysis of long bones (distal femur, proximal tibia, around knee).
  • Pathogenesis: Neoplastic osteoblast precursors overexpress RANKL, stimulating osteoclast formation → uncontrolled bone resorption.
  • Histology: Uniform oval mononuclear tumour cells + abundant multinucleated osteoclast-type giant cells (100+ nuclei).
  • Grossly: Large, red-brown, often cystic masses.
  • Rarely metastasises (lungs) but generally non-fatal.
  • Radiology: "Soap bubble" appearance = expansile, lytic lesion.
  • Clinical relevance: Though benign, its local aggressiveness can cause pathological fractures.

Explanation of other options:

Chondroblastoma (Option A): Benign chondroid tumour in skeletally immature patients; arises in epiphysis/apophysis. Painful but usually lacks soap bubble radiology.

Osteosarcoma (Option C): Malignant bone tumour of metaphysis, common in children/young adults. Produces osteoid, not multinucleated giant cells.

Osteochondroma (Option D): Benign cartilage-capped bony projection, usually near growth plates. Does not occur in epiphysis or show soap bubble pattern.

Key Takeaways:

  • Osteoclastoma (GCT) = Epiphyseal tumour with soap bubble appearance.
  • Histology hallmark: Numerous multinucleated giant cells.
  • Most common sites: Distal femur, proximal tibia.

question_text: A 43-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of increasing abdominal girth. On physical examination, there is pronounced ascites. Pelvic examination reveals a left adnexal mass. A 6 cm ovarian tumor is removed. The tumor is solid and white. Histologically, it is composed of cells resembling normal ovarian stroma surrounded by collagen fibers and histopathological image is shown below. Which of the following is the appropriate diagnosis?
explanation:
(a) Fibromas are the most common ovarian stromal tumors, accounting for 75% of all stromal tumors and 7% of all ovarian tumors. They occur at all ages and are virtually always benign. The tumors are solid, firm, and white. Microscopically, the cells resemble the stroma of the normal ovarian cortex, being composed of welldifferentiated fibroblasts and variable amounts of collagen.

(b) Microscopically, granulosa cell tumors display haphazard orientation of the nuclei about a central degenerative space (Call-Exner bodies), which results in a characteristic follicular histologic pattern.

(c) Leiomyosarcoma is a malignant tumor of smooth muscle cell origin. It should be suspected, if an apparent leiomyoma is soft, shows areas of necrosis on gross examination, has irregular borders, or does not bulge above the surface when cut. The following features are considered evidence for the diagnosis of leiomyosarcoma: (1) ten or more mitoses per highpowered field (HPF); (2) five or more mitoses per 10 HPFs, with nuclear atypia and necrosis

(d) It will show papillary formation having fibrovascular core.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition, Chapter - 22 pg 1027

question_text: A 40-year-old woman presents with pain and swelling in her left elbow that has lasted 6 months. Physical examination reveals a 0.5 cm soft tissue mass. explanation:

question_text: An 11-year-old girl with no past medical history is evaluated by her paediatrician for pain in the bilateral hands, wrists, and feet that began 3 weeks earlier. Her physical examination is normal except for tenderness in the aforementioned joints. Her paediatrician orders plain films of the hands and wrists, which are normal, as well as a complete blood count, which showed a slightly decreased hemoglobin, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 55 mm/hr. Which of the following additional tests would likely be positive?
explanation:
• The clinical scenario is consistent with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA). Positive antinuclear antibodies are common in JRA; however, the other autoantibodies listed are rarely present in these patients. A positive rheumatoid factor in a patient with polyarticular arthritis should prompt consideration of a diagnosis other than JRA.
  • Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is a heterogeneous group of disorders of unknown cause that present with arthritis before age 16 and persist for at least 6 weeks. In contrast to RA, in JIA:
    1. oligoarthritis is more common,
    2. systemic disease is more frequent,
    3. large joints are affected more often than small joints,
    4. rheumatoid nodules and rheumatoid factor are usually absent, and
    5. anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) seropositivity is common.
  • The pathogenesis is unknown but similar to adult RA; risk factors include HLA and PTPN22 variants. Also, like adult RA, damage in JIA appears to be caused by TH1 and TH17 cells and cytokines produced by these and other inflammatory cells.
  • Treatment is similar to adult RA with some success in using an IL-6 receptor antibody in the systemic form. Long-term prognosis of JIA is very variable. Although many affected individuals have chronic disease, only about 10% develop serious functional disability.

Reference: Robbins, 10th edition, page number - 821

question_text: A 36-year-old male patient with gluten sensitivity presents with intensely itchy, grouped vesicular lesions on the extensor surfaces. A skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence shows the following finding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis based on the given features of pruritic vesicular lesions on extensor surfaces in a patient with gluten sensitivity and direct immunofluorescence showing deposits on the tips of dermal papillae is suggestive of dermatitis herpetiformis.

  • Dermatitis herpetiformis is a rare, chronic, intensely pruritic disorder characterised by urticaria-like papules, grouped vesicles, or urticarial plaques that are symmetrically distributed, most often on extensor surfaces such as the elbows, knees, buttocks, and back with occasional excoriations and crusted papules due to scratching.
  • The disease affects predominantly men, typically presenting in the third to fourth decades, though it can occur at any age, including childhood, and has a chronic course.
  • Pruritus may have a burning or stinging quality, with lesions appearing 12-24 hours after symptom onset.
  • Almost all patients have associated, usually subclinical, gluten-sensitive enteropathy or celiac disease, and over 90% express the HLA-B8/DRw3 and HLA-DQw2 haplotypes.
  • Pathogenesis involves genetically predisposed individuals developing IgA antibodies against dietary gluten (gliadin) that cross-react with reticulin in the anchoring fibrils between the epidermal basement membrane and superficial dermis, producing injury, inflammation, and subepidermal blisters.
  • Biopsy of early lesions reveals neutrophil-rich infiltrates with fibrin, oedema, and microvesicles at the tips of dermal papilla.
  • Direct immunofluorescence of normal-appearing perilesional skin shows discontinuous, granular IgA deposits (with or without complement) localised to dermal papillae and along the basement membrane zone.
  • These deposits remain unaffected by medication but diminish or disappear after long-term adherence to a strict gluten-free diet. This finding distinguishes the disease from linear IgA deposition disorders.
  • Gastrointestinal involvement in celiac disease, when present, includes blunting of intestinal villi and lymphocytic infiltration of the lamina propria, reversible with a gluten-free diet. Gluten exposure can trigger both cutaneous and intestinal flares.
  • The condition is associated with IgA anti-endomysial autoantibodies targeting tissue transglutaminase. There is also an increased incidence of autoimmune conditions such as thyroid abnormalities, achlorhydria, atrophic gastritis, and autoantibodies to gastric parietal cells, likely linked to the high prevalence of HLA-B8/DRw3 in affected patients.
  • Treatment relies on dapsone, a sulfone, which provides rapid (24-48 hours) relief but requires pretreatment screening (e.g., for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency) and ongoing monitoring to avoid complications such as hemolysis and methemoglobinemia, especially at doses above 100 mg/day.
  • Gluten restriction is essential, often reducing dapsone needs and preventing relapses.

Explanation of other options:

Bullous pemphigoid (Option A): Bullous pemphigoid primarily affects the elderly, presenting with tense, clear-fluid-filled bullae on erythematous or normal skin, often involving thighs, flexor forearms, axillae, groin, and lower abdomen, with oral lesions in some cases. Morphologically, the bullae are subepidermal and nonacantholytic, with eosinophil-rich inflammatory infiltrates beneath the epidermal basal layer. Direct immunofluorescence typically shows continuous linear antibody deposition at the dermoepidermal junction, as shown below, reflecting antibodies against BPAG antigens that disrupt epidermal attachment.

Pemphigus vulgaris (Option B): Pemphigus vulgaris, the most common pemphigus variant, affects mucosa and skin, often beginning with persistent oral ulcers before skin involvement. Lesions are superficial vesicles and bullae that rupture easily, leaving shallow erosions with crust. Histology shows acantholysis with suprabasal blister formation where basal cells form a row of tombstones, accompanied by dermal lymphocytes, macrophages, and eosinophils. On direct immunofluorescence, there is intercellular IgG deposition throughout the epidermis in a fish-net pattern, as shown below.

Psoriasis (Option D): Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis with a probable autoimmune basis, commonly affecting extensor surfaces like the elbows, knees, and scalp, \may be associated with arthritis, nail changes, or systemic conditions. Lesions are typically well-demarcated, pink to salmon-colored plaques with loosely adherent silvery-white scales, and histology shows marked acanthosis with elongation of rete ridges, as shown below, thinning or absence of the stratum granulosum, and extensive parakeratosis.

question_text: A 55-year-old man is found to have hepatomegaly on physical examination. He also complains of dark tan skin despite avoiding sun exposure. His liver microscopy is provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of hepatomegaly, darkened skin, and liver histology showing iron deposits is characteristic of hemochromatosis. This condition involves increased iron absorption and storage in multiple organs such as the liver, pancreas, and heart, eventually causing organ dysfunction. Microscopy demonstrates golden-brown deposits in hepatocytes that stain positively with Prussian blue. The hallmark triad consists of cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus, and skin hyperpigmentation ("bronze diabetes").

Explanation of other options:

Wilson's disease (Option A): A genetic disorder of copper metabolism causing copper accumulation in the liver, brain, and eyes, usually presenting in younger individuals with neurological and hepatic manifestations.

Autoimmune hepatitis (Option B): An immune-mediated disorder resulting in chronic liver inflammation, presenting with fatigue, joint pain, and liver enzyme elevation.

α-1 antitrypsin deficiency (Option C): A hereditary condition leading to deficient α-1 antitrypsin, causing both liver disease and emphysema.

Key Takeaways:

  • Hemochromatosis causes excess iron deposition with a classic triad of cirrhosis, diabetes, and pigmentation.
  • Prussian blue stain confirms iron accumulation in hepatocytes.
  • Differentiated from Wilson's disease, autoimmune hepatitis, and α-1 antitrypsin deficiency by histology and clinical features.

question_text: A 29-year-old man comes with joint pain in his right knee and left ankle for 2 weeks. He also complains of burning urination. His past history reveals a self-limiting episode of dysentery 3 weeks ago. Laboratory results show he is HLA-B27 positive. Which of the following additional findings may be seen in this patient?
option_c: Bony ankylosis of the sacroiliac joint
option_d: Psoriatic skin lesions with nail pitting
explanation:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario of arthritis, uveitis, and urethritis along with HLAB27-positivity is suggestive of reactive arthritis which includes clinical features such as uveitis and circinate balanitis.

Explanation of other options:

Presence of subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules (Option A): Rheumatoid nodules are solid nodules measuring 0.5-4 cm, typically located on the extensor surfaces of joints such as the elbows. They occur in about 20% of individuals with rheumatoid arthritis. The given clinical scenario is more suggestive of reactive arthritis.

Bony ankylosis of the sacroiliac joint (Option C):Ankylosing spondylitis leads to loss of articular cartilage and fusion of bones, most notably affecting the sacroiliacand vertebral apophyseal joints. It typically appears in the second or third decade with symptoms of low back pain and reduced spinal mobility. Peripheral joints like the hips, knees, and shoulders are affected in about one-third of patients, and nearly 90% show HLA-B27 positivity. Reactive arthritis better fits the given clinical features.

Psoriatic skin lesions with nail pitting (Option D): Psoriasis is an immune-mediated -skin disorder that presents with red, well-defined papules and round plaques topped with silvery, scaly surfaces. The lesions often cause itching of varying intensity. Fingernail involvement may present as punctate pitting, onycholysis, thickening of the nails, or subungual hyperkeratosis. The given clinical features are not suggestive of psoriaisis.

question_text:
UV-B light is carcinogenic
BECAUSE
UV-B light stimulates formation of pyrimidine dimers in DNA.
option_a: If both statements are true and causally related
option_b: If both statements are true but not causally related
option_c: If the first statement is true and second is false
option_d: If the first statement is false and second is true
explanation:
• Ionizing radiation causes chromosome breakage, chromosome rearrangements and less frequently, point mutations, any of which may affect cancer genes and thereby drive carcinogenesis.
  • UV rays in sunlight induce the formation of pyrimidine dimers within DNA, leading to mutations that can give rise to squamous cell carcinomas and melanomas of the skin.
  • UV-B lamps are lamps that emit a spectrum of ultraviolet light with wavelengths ranging from 290–320 nanometers. This spectrum is also commonly called the biological spectrum due to the human body's sensitivity to light of such a wavelength The main diseases that are treated with UV-B lamps are psoriasis, lichen planus and atopic dermatitis(eczema), vitiligo(loss of skin color) and some other skin diseases.
  • There are thousands of dermatology clinics around the world that treat skin ailments with UV-B lamps. Many people who suffer from psoriasis or other skin diseases have their own UV-B lamp for home treatment. A small lamp is used to treat limited areas of the skin, while full body cabins are available in clinics and hospitals.
  • Overexposure to UV-B light can burn the skin, so the exposure time must be regulated by a timer that turns off the lamp.
  • UV-B treatments for treating skin diseases(psoriasis, vitiligo, atopic dermatitis, etc.) are given in a very low dosage. The treatments take only few minutes.
  • The maximum dose of broadband UV-B is 0.5 Joules per treatment. The maximum dose for narrowband UV-B is 3 Joules per treatment. This low dosage does not increase the risk of skin cancer and UV-B phototherapy remains a very safe treatment.
  • Too much UV ultraviolet radiation of an undesirable wavelength may lead to direct DNA damage, sunburn and skin cancer.

Reference: Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed, Pg 231.

question_text: An 18-year-old man suffers massive trauma in a motorcycle accident. A CT scan shows multiple intracerebral hemorrhages. The patient expires after 6 months in a coma. At autopsy, there are cystic cavities within the frontal and temporal lobes, corresponding to the areas of prior hemorrhage. These cavities were formed in large measure due to the phagocytic activity of which of the following cell types?
explanation:
Microglia are phagocytic macrophage-derived cells of the CNS, accounting for 5% of all glial cells. In response to necrosis, macroglia become phagocytic, accumulate lipids and other cellular debris, and are designated gitter cells. Some reactive microglia exhibit a prominent elongated nucleus, in which case they are referred to as rod cells. After microglial phagocytosis, astrocytosis (choice a) then leads to local scar formation, which persists as telltale evidence of a prior injury.

Reference: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Diseases 10th edition, Chapter – 28 pg 1243

question_text: Ribbon candy appearance on immunofluorescence is seen in?
explanation:
• Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by linear deposits of IgG and C3 at the dermo-epidermal junction, which on immunofluorescence shows a characteristic "Ribbon candy" appearance due to smooth, continuous linear staining along the basement membrane zone.

Incorrect choices explanation:

  • (Choice A) Pemphigus vulgaris: Immunofluorescence shows a "fish-net" or reticular pattern due to intercellular IgG deposits.
  • (Choice C) Pemphigus foliaceous: Similar to pemphigus vulgaris, it also shows an intercellular "fish-net" pattern.
  • (Choice D) Dermatitis herpetiformis: Immunofluorescence reveals granular deposits of IgA at dermal papilla tips, not a linear "ribbon candy" appearance.

Thus, option (B) is correct.
